definition: Sung without instrumental accompaniment.
example: They sang an a cappella Mass.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian a cappella (“in the manner of the [Sistine] chapel”), referring to non-instrumental choirs.

definition: Involving deductive reasoning from a general principle to a necessary effect; not supported by fact.
example: An a priori judgment.
etymology: First attested in 1610. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).

definition: To a small degree; somewhat.
example: It's a bit warm.

definition: Express admiration and pleasure by uttering ‘ooh’ or ‘aah’.
example: They oohed and aahed when they unwrapped the presents.

definition: Having the wind against the forward side of the sails.
example: The ship came up into the wind with all yards aback.
etymology: From Middle English abak, from Old English onbæc, equivalent to a- (“towards”) + back. Compare West Frisian tebek (“aback”, adverb, literally “to/at back”), Swedish tillbaka (idem.).

definition: A formal resignation and renunciation of powers.
example: Abdication of the throne, government, power, authority.
etymology: First attested in 1552. From Latin abdicātiō (“renunciation”), from abdicō. By surface analysis, abdicate + -ion.

definition: A branch of the descending aorta.
In bed.
etymology: From Middle English abedde, o bedde, from Old English on (“in”) + bedde (“bed”). Equivalent to a- (“in, on”) + bed.

definition: A state or condition markedly different from the norm.
example: The aberration of youth.
etymology: A learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration.

definition: Surgical removal of a body part or tissue.
etymology: From Late Middle English ablacioun (“removal”), from Late Latin ablātiō (“a taking away”), from auferō (“to take away, carry off, withdraw, remove”) + -tiō (“-tion”, nominal suffix). Doublet of ablatio.

definition: An abnormal physical condition resulting from defective genes or developmental deficiencies.
etymology: From abnormal + -ity. First attested in the mid 19th century.

definition: Unequivocally detestable.
example: Abominable treatment of prisoners.

definition: An abraded area where the skin is torn or worn off.
example: The metal surface showed signs of abrasion after years of use.
etymology: First attested in 1656. From French abrasion (attested since 1611), from Medieval Latin abrasio (“a scraping”), from Latin abrādō (“scrape off”). See also abrade.

definition: Being up to particular standard or level especially in being up to date in knowledge.
example: Kept abreast of the latest developments.
etymology: From Middle English abrest. By surface analysis, a- (“on, at”) + breast, meaning “breasts (chests) in line, side-by-side and exactly equally advanced”; roughly “breast-by-breast”.

definition: Symptom consisting of a localized collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin abscessus (“a going away; gathering of humors, abscess”), from abscēdō (“go away, depart”), from abs (“away from”) + cēdō (“go”). See cede.

definition: The condition of being formally forgiven by a priest in the sacrament of penance.
example: Governments granting absolution to the nation.
etymology: From Middle English absolucion, absolucioun, from Old French absolution, from Latin absolūtiōnem, accusative singular of absolūtiō (“acquittal”), from absolvō (“absolve”). See also absolve.

definition: Grant remission of a sin to.
example: The priest absolved him and told him to say ten Hail Marys.
etymology: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English absolven, from Latin absolvere (“set free, acquit”), from ab (“away from”) + solvō (“loosen, free, release”). Doublet of assoil.

definition: Having power or capacity or tendency to absorb or soak up something (liquids or energy etc.).
example: As absorbent as a sponge.
etymology: From Latin absorbēns, present active participle of absorbeō (“absorb”).

definition: Cotton made absorbent by removal of the natural wax.
A material having capacity or tendency to absorb another substance.
Lost in thought; showing preoccupation.
example: An abstracted scholar.
etymology: From abstract + -ed.

definition: In an absurd manner or to an absurd degree.
example: An absurdly rich young woman.
etymology: From absurd + -ly.

definition: Very great; limitless.
example: Abysmal misery.
etymology: From abysm + -al. Compare abyssal.

definition: (used of syllables) bearing the principle stress, usually accompanied by a change in pitch.
To stress, single out as important.
etymology: First attested in 1731; borrowed from Medieval Latin accentuātus, perfect passive participle of accentuō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin accentus. accent + -u- + -ate.

definition: (chemistry) in the formation of a coordinate bond it is the compound to which electrons are donated.
etymology: From Middle English acceptour, from Latin acceptor, with the meanings from accept.

definition: A tangible symbol signifying approval or distinction.
example: The scientist received the highest accolade in her field for the groundbreaking discovery.
etymology: First use appears c.

definition: A creditor's accounts of money owed to them; normally arise from the sale of products or services.
An increase by natural growth or addition.
example: A mineral augments not by growth, but by accretion.
etymology: PIE word *h₂éd Learned borrowing from Latin accrētiō (“increase, increment”) + English -ion (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or processes, or their results).

definition: Grow by addition.
example: The interest accrues.
etymology: First attested in mid 15th century.

definition: Someone who imputes guilt or blame.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English acuser, accusour, borrowed from Old French accusour, from Latin accūsātor, from accūsāre. Equivalent to accuse + -er. Doublet of accusator.

definition: A fabric made from fibers of cellulose acetate.
The simplest ketone; a highly flammable liquid widely used as an organic solvent and as material for making plastics.
etymology: From acet- from acētum (“vinegar”). The -one was taken from margarone but further etymology is unclear. Doublet of ketone.

definition: The highest level or degree attainable; the highest stage of development.
example: His landscapes were deemed the acme of beauty.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point; high point”).

definition: Squash plant bearing small acorn-shaped fruits having yellow flesh and dark green or yellow rind with longitudinal ridges.
A buoy that can be heard (at night).
Vigorously active.
example: An acrobatic dance.
etymology: From acrobat + -ic.

definition: A stunt performed by an acrobat.
A stunt performed by an acrobat.
The gymnastic moves of an acrobat.
etymology: From acrobat + -ics. By surface analysis, acrobatic + -s.

definition: Act in an uncontrolled manner.
(biology) any agency bringing about activation; a molecule that increases the activity of an enzyme or a protein that increases the production of a gene product in DNA transcription.
etymology: From activate + -or.

definition: Of or relating to the work of an actuary.
etymology: From actuary + -al.

definition: A table of statistical data.
A mechanism that puts something into automatic action.
example: The mind is the actuator of the body.
etymology: From actuate + -or. First attested in 1652.

definition: Sharpness of vision; the visual ability to resolve fine detail (usually measured by a Snellen chart).
example: The old woman with dementia lost her mental acuity.
etymology: From Middle English acuite, acuyte, from Middle French acuité, from Medieval Latin acuitas, irreg., from Latin acuō (“sharpen”).

definition: A tapering point.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin acūmen (“sharp point”).

definition: Glaucoma in which the iris blocks the outflow of aqueous humor.
A condensed but memorable saying embodying some important fact of experience that is taken as true by many people.
example: According to an old adage, oysters are best in months containing the letter R.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French adage, from Latin adā̆gium.

definition: The ability to change (or be changed) to fit changed circumstances.
etymology: From adaptable + -ity or adapt + -ability.

definition: Textual matter that is added onto a publication; usually at the end.
example: An addendum was added to the contract to clarify payment terms.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin addendum, inflection of addendus (“annexed”), future passive participle of addō (“to add”).

definition: A sweetened beverage of diluted fruit juice.
etymology: Back-formation from lemonade, orangeade, etc.

definition: The quality of being able to meet a need satisfactorily:.
example: His zeal is, of course, unquestionable; his adequacy, however, I doubt.
etymology: From adequ(ate) + -acy.

definition: A farewell remark.
example: We bid our final adieus to our family, then boarded the ship, bound for America.
etymology: From Middle English adieu also adew, adewe, adue, from Old French adieu (“to God”), a shortening of a Dieu vous comant (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Doublet of adios.

definition: Composed of animal fat.
example: Adipose tissue constitutes the fat of meat.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin adipōsus, from Latin adeps (“fat, lard”). By surface analysis, adip- + -ose;

definition: Cells composed of fat.
A kind of body tissue containing stored fat that serves as a source of energy; it also cushions and insulates vital organs.
A pronoun acting as an adjective, such as which in which dictionaries?
example: Others is a compound pronoun, including both an adjective pronoun and a noun, and is equivalent to other men.

definition: The final judgment in a legal proceeding; the act of pronouncing judgment based on the evidence presented.
example: 16 June, 1784, Edmund Burke, speech on reform of representation in the House of Commons An adjudication in favour of natural rights.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin adiudicatio, adiudicationem. By surface analysis, adjudicate + -ion.

definition: In an admirable manner.
example: The children's responses were admirably normal.
etymology: From admirable + -ly.

definition: Deserving to be admitted.
example: Admissible evidence.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French admissible. Equivalent to admit + -ible

definition: The right to enter.
etymology: From admit + -ance. Sense 5 was coined by electrical engineer, mathematician and physicist Oliver Heaviside in 1887.

definition: Any handsome young man.
Showing adoration.
Of or pertaining to the adrenal glands or their secretions.
etymology: From ad- (“near”) + renal (“pertaining to the kidneys”), from Latin rēn (“kidney”).

definition: Either of a pair of complex endocrine glands situated near the kidney.
The accumulation of molecules of a gas to form a thin film on the surface of a solid.
etymology: Borrowed from German Adsorption, from ad- + (Ab)sorption.

definition: A conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers.
Exercise that increases the need for oxygen.
The branch of mechanics that deals with the motion of gases (especially air) and their effects on bodies in the flow.
example: He specializes in aerodynamics.
etymology: From aero- + dynamics. Compare French aérodynamique, German Aerodynamik, and Italian aerodinamica.

definition: A dispenser that holds a substance under pressure and that can release it as a fine spray (usually by means of a propellant gas).
Any mental disorder not caused by detectable organic abnormalities of the brain and in which a major disturbance of emotions is predominant.
Firmly attached.
example: The affixed labels.

definition: Traveling by foot.
example: She was afoot when I saw her this morning.
etymology: From a- + foot.

definition: Again but in a new or different way.
example: Start afresh.
etymology: From Middle English a-fresche, equivalent to a- + fresh. Compare Old English afersċean (“to freshen; become fresh”).

definition: Thinking again about a choice previously made.
example: She packed her sandals only as an afterthought, but she was glad she did.
etymology: From after- + thought, probably modelled on forethought. Compare also the verb afterthink.

definition: An impure form of quartz consisting of banded chalcedony; used as a gemstone and for making mortars and pestles.
etymology: From Middle French agathe, from Latin achatēs, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”).

definition: Space for one line of print (one column wide and 1/14 inch deep) used to measure advertising.
Make worse.
example: This drug aggravates the pain.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1471 in Middle English, the verb in 1530;

definition: An exasperated feeling of annoyance.
etymology: From Middle French aggravation.

definition: A person who collects things.
etymology: From aggregate + -or.

definition: The quality of being bold and enterprising.
example: The aggressiveness of various sulfate salts towards concrete is partly related to solubility.
etymology: From aggressive + -ness.

definition: The principal character in a work of fiction.
Extremely painful.
example: It was an agonizing twenty-minute wait for the results.

definition: A large-scale farming enterprise.
etymology: From agri- + business, or a blend of agriculture + business, coined by American academic and diplomat John Herbert Davis (1904–1988).

definition: A person who tills the soil for a living.
A person who tills the soil for a living.
Stuck in a place where a ship can no longer float.
example: A ship aground offshore.
etymology: From Middle English agrounde, on grounde (“on ground”), equivalent to a- + ground.

definition: Largest known toad species; native to Central America; valuable destroyer of insect pests.
An often persistent bodily disorder or disease; a cause for complaining.
etymology: From ail + -ment.

definition: Without aim; in an aimless manner.
example: He wandered around aimlessly.
etymology: From aimless + -ly.

definition: Obstruction of the circulatory system caused by an air bubble as, e.g., accidentally during surgery or hypodermic injection or as a complication from scuba diving.
The fare charged for traveling by airplane.
example: I'd love to visit Paris, but I can't afford the airfare.
etymology: From air + fare.

definition: The airborne branch of a country's armed forces.
Transportation of people or goods by air (especially when other means of access are unavailable).
etymology: From air + lift; compare sealift.

definition: A male who operates an aircraft.
etymology: From air + -man.

definition: An airfield without normal airport facilities.
example: The outfitter deposited us at a small airstrip out in the bush, promising to pick us up again in a week's time.
etymology: From air + strip.

definition: Having no weak points.
example: An airtight defense.
etymology: From air + tight.

definition: (figurative) something that hinders or handicaps.
example: She was an albatross around his neck.
etymology: Uncertain. Probably from Spanish or Portuguese alcatraz (“pelican, gannet, albatross”), probably derived from Arabic الْغَطَّاس (al-ḡaṭṭās, “the diver”) (compare Alcatraz);

definition: Wood of any of various alder trees; resistant to underwater rot; used for bridges etc.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English aldre, alder, aller, from Old English alor, from Proto-West Germanic *aluʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aluz, *alusō, *alizō, *alisō.

definition: A disease of alders caused by the woolly alder aphid (a plant louse).
Dark-colored insect having predaceous aquatic larvae.
North temperate shrubs or trees having toothed leaves and conelike fruit; bark is used in tanning and dyeing and the wood is rot-resistant.
The process of paying close and continuous attention.
etymology: From alert + -ness.

definition: Important European leguminous forage plant with trifoliate leaves and blue-violet flowers grown widely as a pasture and hay crop.
etymology: PIE word *h₁éḱwos Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *HéHḱus Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćwas Proto-Iranian *Hácwah Proto-Iranian *Hástiš Proto-Iranian *HacwaHastiš Old Median *aspāstišder.

definition: Of or relating to or having the characteristics of an algorithm.
etymology: From algorithm + -ic.

definition: An artificial language designed to express algorithms.
A precise rule (or set of rules) specifying how to solve some problem.
A precise rule (or set of rules) specifying how to solve some problem.
Any of various water-soluble compounds capable of turning litmus blue and reacting with an acid to form a salt and water.
etymology: From French alcali, from Medieval Latin alcali, ultimately from Arabic اَلْقِلْي (al-qily, “alkali, ashes (in reference to ashes of the saltwort)”), related to قَلَى (qalā, “to roast in a pan, fry”).

definition: A common solitary bee important for pollinating alfalfa in the western United States.
Plant of western North America having grasslike leaves and greenish-white flowers.
Any of the monovalent metals of group I of the periodic table (lithium or sodium or potassium or rubidium or cesium or francium).
example: The hydroxides of the alkali metals are strongly alkaline.

definition: Poisoning resulting from the ingestion of an alkali compound (as lye or ammonia).
Any of a series of univalent groups of the general formula CnH2n+1 derived from aliphatic hydrocarbons.
etymology: From alc(ohol) + -yl.

definition: Any of a series of univalent groups of the general formula CnH2n+1 derived from aliphatic hydrocarbons.
Any of a series of univalent groups of the general formula CnH2n+1 derived from aliphatic hydrocarbons.
(of animals) both plant-eating and flesh-eating.
Used in or characteristic of or containing allegory.
example: Allegorical stories.
etymology: From Latin allēgoricus + -al. By surface analysis, allegory + -ical.

definition: Eczema caused by an allergic reaction.
A narrow street with walls on both sides.
etymology: From alley + way.

definition: Large species having three ridges on its back; found in southeastern United States.
Give out.
example: Each candidate was allotted five minutes to make a presentation in front of the judges.
etymology: From Middle English allotten, from Old French aloter (Modern French allotir). à + lot. By surface analysis, al- + lot.

definition: Deductible according to the tax laws.
etymology: From Middle English allowable, alowable, a borrowing from Old French alouable (Modern French allouable), from allouer, equivalent to allow + -able.

definition: Passing reference or indirect mention.
etymology: From Latin allūsiōnem, accusative singular of allūsiō (“the act of playing with”), from allūdō (“play with; allude”), from al-, combining form of ad (“to”), + lūdō (“play”): compare French allusion.

definition: Of or relating to alluvium.
etymology: From Latin alluvius (“alluvial”), from alluviō (“an overflowing, inundation”), from alluō (“wash against”). By surface analysis, alluvium + -ial.

definition: A fan-shaped deposit where a fast flowing stream flattens out.
Clay or silt or gravel carried by rushing streams and deposited where the stream slows down.
A fan-shaped deposit where a fast flowing stream flattens out.
A flat resulting from repeated deposits of alluvial material by running water.
A flat resulting from repeated deposits of alluvial material by running water.
Clay or silt or gravel carried by rushing streams and deposited where the stream slows down.
A fine-grained fertile soil deposited by water flowing over flood plains or in river beds.
Money or goods contributed to the poor.
Box for collecting alms, especially one in a church.
A tray for collecting the offering from a congregation.
A tray for collecting the offering from a congregation.
Making voluntary contributions to aid the poor.
Remote in manner.
example: Stood apart with aloof dignity.

definition: A form of interferon that is produced endogenously and commercially for its pharmacological effects (including regulation of the immune system and antiviral and antineoplastic effects).
Creeping mat-forming evergreen shrub of high mountain regions of Northern Hemisphere grown for its rose-pink flowers.
A method of childbirth that avoids intrusive high-tech medicine in favor of more natural and homely settings.
An old term for an electric generator that produces alternating current (especially in automobiles).
etymology: From alternate + -or.

definition: The quality of unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
etymology: From French altruisme, which was coined in 1830 by Auguste Comte from autrui (“of or to others”) + -isme, from Old French, from Latin alteri, dative of alter (“other”) (whence also English alter).

definition: Showing unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
example: His helping the old woman with her shopping was deemed highly altruistic by everyone, especially since her home was a mile away.
etymology: From altruist + -ic. See altruism.

definition: White crystalline compound that occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite.
White crystalline compound that occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite.
A male person who has received a degree from a school (high school or college or university).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin alumnus (“foster child, nourished one”).

definition: Pertaining to the tiny air sacs of the lungs.
etymology: From alveolus + -ar.

definition: The part of the upper or lower jawbones in which the teeth are set.
Lung tissue densely packed with alveoli.
Craniometric point that is the most anterior point in the midline on the alveolar process of the maxilla.
A ridge that forms the borders of the upper and lower jaws and contains the sockets of the teeth.
etymology: From New Latin processus alveolaris (“protuberance of tooth sockets”).

definition: A ridge that forms the borders of the upper and lower jaws and contains the sockets of the teeth.

An alloy of mercury with another metal (usually silver) used by dentists to fill cavities in teeth; except for iron and platinum all metals dissolve in mercury and chemists refer to the resulting mercury mixtures as amalgams.
etymology: From Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient;

definition: Joined together into a whole.
example: The amalgamated colleges constituted a university.

definition: Increase in amount by collecting or gathering.
example: To amass a treasure or a fortune.
etymology: From Middle English *amassen (found only as Middle English massen (“to amass”)), from Anglo-Norman amasser, from Medieval Latin amassāre, from ad + massa (“lump, mass”). See mass.

definition: A particular environment or surrounding influence.
etymology: From ambient + -ence.

definition: Mixed feelings or emotions.
etymology: Borrowed from German Ambivalenz (“simultaneous conflicting feelings”), from Latin ambi- (“both”) and valentia (“strength”), from the verb valere (“to be strong”) (see valiant);

definition: Relating to or adapted for walking.
example: An ambulatory corridor.
etymology: From Latin ambulatorius. By surface analysis, ambulate + -ory, or, by surface analysis, ambulator + -y.

definition: A mild form of bubonic plague.
Disposed or willing to conform.
example: Someone amenable to the instruction of others.

definition: Pleasantness resulting from agreeable conditions.
example: He discovered the amenities of reading at an early age.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English amenite, amenyte, partly from Middle French amenité and partly from its etymon, Latin amoenitās (“pleasantness, delightfulness”), from amoenus (“pleasant, delightful”), of unknown origin.

definition: Disposed to please.
example: An amiable villain with a cocky sidelong grin.
etymology: From Middle English amyable, from Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”, verb).

definition: Characterized by friendship and good will.
example: An amicable agreement.
etymology: From Middle English amicable (“agreeable; pleasant”), from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”). Doublet of amiable.

definition: A friend or comrade.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish amigo (“friend”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), derived from amāre (“to love”). Compare French ami, Italian amico, Portuguese amigo and Romanian amic. Doublet of amicus.

definition: A compound derived from ammonia by replacing hydrogen atoms by univalent hydrocarbon radicals.
etymology: From ammonia + -ine.

definition: Away from the correct or expected course.
example: Something went badly amiss in the preparations.
etymology: From a- + miss.

definition: A cordial disposition.
etymology: From Middle English amite, from Old French amisté, amitie, amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”).

definition: A white crystalline double sulfate of aluminum: the ammonium double sulfate of aluminum.
A carbonate of ammonium; used in the manufacture of smelling salts and baking powder and ammonium compounds.
A white salt used in dry cells.
Used as an explosive and fertilizer and rocket propellant.
Wildly; without self-control.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese amouco, from Malay amuk (“to go on a killing spree”).

definition: Inclined toward or displaying love.
example: Feeling amorous.
etymology: From Middle English amorous, amerous (14th century), from Old French amoros, amoreus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, from Latin amor (“love”), related to amāre (“to love”). Compare French amoureux (“in love”).

definition: Having no definite form or distinct shape.
example: Amorphous clouds of insects.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos, “without form, shapeless, deformed”) (itself from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”) + -ous. By surface analysis, a- + -morphous.

definition: An ill-defined or arbitrary shape.
The reduction of the value of an asset by prorating its cost over a period of years.
etymology: From Middle English amortisen (“to kill, alienate in mortmain”), from Anglo-Norman amorteser, alteration of Old French amortir, from Vulgar Latin *admortire (“to kill”), from Latin ad- and mors, mortem (“death”).

definition: A central nervous system stimulant that increases energy and decreases appetite; used to treat narcolepsy and some forms of depression.
etymology: Shortened form of a(lpha-)m(ethyl)ph(en)et(hyl)amine.

definition: A sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater).
example: The symphony warmed up inside the amphitheater while the audience crowded around outside.

definition: A sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater).
etymology: From Latin amphitheatrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + θέᾱτρον (théātron, “theatre”).

definition: Modulation of the amplitude of the (radio) carrier wave.
A trinket or piece of jewelry usually hung about the neck and thought to be a magical protection against evil or disease.
example: The soldier wore an amulet for protection.
etymology: From Middle French amulette, from Latin amuletum.

definition: A non-nitrogenous food substance consisting chiefly of starch; any substance resembling starch.
etymology: From amyl + -oid.

definition: A plaque consisting of tangles of amyloid protein in nervous tissue (a pathological mark of Alzheimer's disease).
Of or related to the synthetic phase of metabolism.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw”) + -ic.

definition: Large arboreal boa of tropical South America.
example: My anaconda don't want none / Unless you got buns, hon.

definition: Living or active in the absence of free oxygen.
example: Anaerobic bacteria.
etymology: From French anaérobie, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic. By surface analysis, an- + aerobic.

definition: Exercise that builds muscles through tension.
Relating to or producing insensibility.
A drug that causes temporary loss of bodily sensations.
A detested person.
example: He is an anathema to me.

definition: Lacking vigor or energy.
example: An anemic attempt to hit the baseball.
etymology: From anemia + -ic.

definition: Any of various tall and stout herbs of the genus Angelica having pinnately compound leaves and small white or greenish flowers in compound umbels.
etymology: From French angélique. Doublet of angelic and angélique (“plucked bowl lute”).

definition: Any disease of the throat or fauces marked by spasmodic attacks of intense suffocative pain.
etymology: From Latin angina (“quinsy; strangling, choking”), from angō (“to press together, to choke, to hurt (cause pain)”).

definition: A vise that can hold a workpiece at a variety of different angles (usually offers a full 90 degree adjustment).
A scheming person; someone who schemes to gain an advantage.
example: A throng of anglers lined the trout stream on opening day of trout season.
etymology: From Middle English angler, angleer, angeler, equivalent to angle + -er.

definition: Fishes having large mouths with a wormlike filament attached for luring prey.
(Jungian psychology) the inner self (not the external persona) that is in touch with the unconscious.
example: The projection-making factor is the anima, or rather the unconscious as represented by the anima.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin anima (“a current of air, wind, air, breath, the vital principle, life, soul”), sometimes equivalent to animus (“mind”), both from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”); see animus.

definition: Breeding and caring for farm animals.
Mediterranean oat held to be progenitor of modern cultivated oat.
etymology: So called because its spikelets can move in response to moisture.

definition: Giving spirit and vivacity.
Someone who imparts energy and vitality and spirit to other people.
example: In recent years, animators using computer rendering have largely superseded artists working by hand.
etymology: From Latin animātor. By surface analysis, animate + -or. Piecewise doublet of animateur.

definition: Destroyed completely.
A comment or instruction (usually added).
example: She added an annotation in the margin to clarify the text.
etymology: From Latin annotātiōnem, accusative singular of annotātiō (“remark, annotation”), from annotātus, perfect passive participle of annotō (“note down, remark”). Equivalent to annotate + -ion.

definition: The parallax of a celestial body using two points in the earth's orbit around the sun as the baseline.
Shaped like a ring.
example: Annular fiber.
etymology: From Latin ānulāris (“ring-shaped”); (possibly through French annulaire), from ānulus (“ring”).

definition: A positively charged electrode by which electrons leave an electrical device.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) and ὁδός (hodós, “path”), forming the New Greek compound ἄνοδος (ánodos). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year.

definition: The act of applying oil or an oily liquid.
example: The anointings of Jesus.

definition: Deviating from the general or common order or type.
example: Advanced forms of life may be anomalous in the universe.
etymology: From Late Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμᾰλος (anṓmălos).

definition: A common way to make software available; users are allowed to log in as ‘guest’ without a password and copy whatever has been made available.
A kind of antbird, with species spanning the genera Formicarius and Chamaeza.
etymology: From ant + thrush.

definition: Belonging to a period before a war especially the American Civil War.
Small ground squirrel of western United States.
etymology: So called, possibly, from the white underside of the tail of most species which, when arched over the back, is reminiscent of similar behavior by pronghorn antelopes.

definition: The anterior lobe of the pituitary body; primarily glandular in nature.
Of or relating to the study of the origins and development of human beings.
example: Anthropogenic climate change.
etymology: From anthropo- + -genic. First use appears c. 1883.

definition: Destroying bacteria or inhibiting their growth.
example: This drug has an antibacterial effect.
etymology: From anti- + bacterial.

definition: Any drug that destroys bacteria or inhibits their growth.
Any of a class of drugs used to treat depression; often have undesirable side effects.
etymology: From anti- + depressant.

definition: Any of a class of drugs used to treat depression; often have undesirable side effects.
Substance that inhibits oxidation or inhibits reactions promoted by oxygen or peroxides.
etymology: From anti- + oxidant.

definition: Of or relating to persons who study or deal in antiques or antiquities.
example: Antiquarian literature.
etymology: From antiquary + -an.

definition: Relating to or characterized by anti-Semitism; hating Jews.
Thoroughly clean and free of or destructive to disease-causing organisms.
example: Doctors in antiseptic green coats.
etymology: From anti- + septic.

definition: Exact opposite.
example: His theory is the antithesis of mine.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin antithesis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis). By surface analysis, anti- + thesis.

definition: Inhibiting or stopping the growth and reproduction of viruses.
etymology: From anti- + viral.

definition: Any drug that destroys viruses.
Any drug that destroys viruses.
The large trunk artery that carries blood from the left ventricle of the heart to branch arteries.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).

definition: An aneurysm of the aorta.
Showing little or no emotion or animation.
example: A woman who became active rather than apathetic as she grew older.
etymology: From apathy + -etic.

definition: Situated at an apex.
etymology: From apic- + -al.

definition: Politically neutral.
example: The Queen is an apolitical figure.
etymology: From a- + political.

definition: Offering or expressing apology.
example: An apologetic note.
etymology: From French apologétique, from Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós, “of or suitable for defense”), from ἀπολογέομαι (apologéomai, “to speak in defense of”); see more at English apology.

definition: A person who argues to defend or justify some policy or institution.
example: An apologist for capital punishment.
etymology: From apology + -ist.

definition: Address to an absent or imaginary person.
etymology: From Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).

definition: A ghostly appearing figure.
example: We were unprepared for the apparition that confronted us.
etymology: From Middle French apparition, from Latin apparitio, from appareo.

definition: The act of appeasing (as by acceding to the demands of).
etymology: From Middle English appesement, from Old French apaisement.

definition: Of or relating to or taking account of appeals (usually legal appeals).
example: Appellate court.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French apelant.

definition: Identifying word or words by which someone or something is called and classified or distinguished from others.
etymology: From late Middle English appellacion, from Old French apellatiun, from Latin appellātiō (“a naming”).

definition: An external body part that projects from the body.
example: Bodily appendage.
etymology: From append + -age.

definition: Inflammation of the vermiform appendix.
etymology: From appendic- + -itis.

definition: Strong alcoholic beverage with apple flavour.
Larvae bore into and feed on apples.
Relevance by virtue of being applicable to the matter at hand.
etymology: From applicable + -ity.

definition: An official who is appointed.
example: The ambassador is a political appointee, not a career diplomat.
etymology: French appointé, from appointer.

definition: One who estimates officially the worth or value or quality of things.
etymology: From appraise + -er.

definition: Enough to be estimated or measured.
example: Appreciable amounts of noxious wastes are dumped into the harbor.
etymology: From French appréciable. By surface analysis, appreci(ate) + -able.

definition: Capable of being read with comprehension.
example: The tales seem more approachable than his more difficult novels.
etymology: From approach + -able.

definition: Appropriate conduct; doing the right thing.
etymology: From appropriate + -ness.

definition: Asian tree having clusters of usually white blossoms and edible fruit resembling the peach.
example: Pickled apricots.

definition: Fruit bar containing apricot jam.
For Chinese dishes: apricot preserves and chutney.
Asian tree having clusters of usually white blossoms and edible fruit resembling the peach.
Animal living wholly or chiefly in or on water.
A conduit that resembles a bridge but carries water over a valley.
etymology: Adapted borrowing from Latin aquaeductus (“conveyance of water”), from aqua (“water”) + dūcō (“to lead”, “to bring”); compare the French aqueduc.

definition: Underground bed or layer yielding ground water for wells and springs etc.
example: The water in the well came from an aquifer.
etymology: From aqui- + -fer.

definition: (of farmland) capable of being farmed productively.
etymology: From Middle English arable, from Middle French arable, from Old French arable, from Latin arābilis, formed from arō (“plow”) + -bilis (“able to be”). Cognate with earable (“arable”).

definition: Someone with the power to settle matters at will.
example: She was the final arbiter on all matters of fashion.
etymology: From Middle English arbiter, arbytour, arbitre, from Old French arbitre, from Latin arbiter (“a witness, judge, literally one who goes to see”).

definition: A kind of hedged investment meant to capture slight differences in price; when there is a difference in the price of something on two different markets the arbitrageur simultaneously buys at the lower price and sells at the higher price.
etymology: An unadapted borrowing from French arbitrage, from arbitrer (“to arbitrate”); see arbitrate.

definition: Someone chosen to judge and decide a disputed issue.
example: The critic was considered to be an arbiter of modern literature.
etymology: From Middle English arbitrator, from Late Latin arbitrātor, from arbitror.

definition: A facility where trees and shrubs are cultivated for exhibition.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin arborētum (“place with trees growing, plantation of trees”), from arbor (“tree”).

definition: Requiring secret or mysterious knowledge.
example: The arcane science of dowsing.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arceō (“to shut up, enclose”); cognate with Latin arca (“a chest”).

definition: An angel ranked above the highest rank in the celestial hierarchy.
etymology: From Middle English archangel, from Old French archangele, from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from Ancient Greek prefix ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”).

definition: A sovereign prince of the former ruling house of Austria.
example: World War I traditionally started with the assassination of Archduke Francis (Franz) Ferdinand.
etymology: From Middle French archeduc (modern French archiduc), from Latin archidux. Equivalent to arch- + duke.

definition: Related to or dealing with or devoted to archaeology.
etymology: From archeology + -ical.

definition: A relic that has been excavated from the soil.
The site of an archeological exploration.
The branch of anthropology that studies prehistoric people and their cultures.
etymology: From Middle French archéologie, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογία (arkhaiología, “antiquarian lore, ancient legends, history”), from ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “primal, old, ancient”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”).

definition: Representing or constituting an original type after which other similar things are patterned.
example: Archetypal patterns.
etymology: From archetype + -al.

definition: Something that serves as a model or a basis for making copies.
A person in charge of collecting and cataloguing archives.
example: The billionaire’s will established a trust to create a staff of archivists that would chronicle and preserve his rise to prominence.
etymology: From archive + -ist.

definition: A simple light plough without a mouldboard.
A colorless and odorless inert gas; one of the six inert gases; comprises approximately 1% of the earth's atmosphere.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀργός (argós, “idle, lazy”), because of its inertness, + -on, used for all noble gases.

definition: Given to or characterized by argument.
example: An argumentative discourse.

definition: A covered gravy holder of silver or other metal containing a detachable central vessel for hot water to keep the gravy warm.
etymology: From the Argyll branch of the Scottish Campbell clan, named after their tartan.

definition: A covered gravy holder of silver or other metal containing a detachable central vessel for hot water to keep the gravy warm.
A member of the aristocracy.
A hydrocarbon that contains one or more benzene rings that are characteristic of the benzene series of organic compounds.
Call forth (emotions, feelings, and responses).
example: Arouse pity.
etymology: From a- + rouse.

definition: A legal document calling someone to court to answer an indictment.
etymology: From arraign + -ment.

definition: The pointed head or striking tip of an arrow.
etymology: From Middle English arewehede, arowhede, arowheved. By surface analysis, arrow + head.

definition: A stream or brook.
Shrubby willow of the western United States.
Sclerosis of the arterial walls.
Not straightforward or candid; giving a false appearance of frankness.
A truck consisting of a tractor and trailer together.
An implanted electronic device that takes over the function of the natural cardiac pacemaker.
A public performer (a dancer or singer).
etymology: Borrowed from French artiste. Doublet of artist.

definition: In an artistic manner.
example: It was artistically decorated.
etymology: From artistic + -ally.

definition: Pretentiously artistic; cloyingly charming.
The state that exists when one person or group has power over another.
etymology: From ascend + -ancy or ascendant + -cy. The use in ecology is due to Robert Ulanowicz.

definition: Tending or directed upward.

etymology: PIE word *h₂éd The adjective is derived from Late Middle English ascendent (“ascending, rising; increasing in quantity;

definition: The ascending part of the aorta as it emerges from the left ventricle.
Discovered or determined by scientific observation.
example: Variation in the ascertained flux depends on a number of factors.

definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of an ascetic or the practice of rigorous self-discipline.
example: Ascetic practices.
etymology: First use appears c. 1646. From Medieval Latin asceticus, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητικός (askētikós), from ἀσκητής (askētḗs, “monk, hermit”), from ἀσκέω (askéō, “to exercise”).

definition: Attribute or credit to.
example: One may ascribe these problems to the federal government; however, at this stage it is unclear what caused them.
etymology: From Middle English ascriben, from Old French ascrivre (“inscribe, attribute, impute”), from Latin āscrībere (“to state in writing”), equivalent to a- + scribe.

definition: Reproduction without the fusion of gametes.
Spice derived from the dried fruit of Piper guineense; very similar to cubeb pepper but is much less bitter and has a fresher more herbaceous flavour.
example: Even in West Africa, Ashanti pepper is an expensive spice and is used sparingly.

definition: A place of religious retreat modeled after the Indian ashram.
example: The entire ashram was excited.
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit आश्रम (āśrama).

definition: Of southern Europe; similar to but smaller than the adder.
A fernlike plant native to South Africa.
A poplar that is widely cultivated in the United States; has white bark and leaves with whitish undersurfaces.
A group of persons together in one place.
example: The assemblage of words and recordings.
etymology: Borrowed from French assemblage. By surface analysis, assemble + -age.

definition: A man who is a member of a legislative assembly.
etymology: From assembly + -man.

definition: An official who evaluates property for the purpose of taxing it.
etymology: From Middle English assessour, from Old French assessour, from Latin assessor (“assistant judge; assessor of taxes”). Cognate with French assesseur.

definition: Characterized by or causing or resulting from the process of bringing ideas or events together in memory or imagination.
example: Associative learning.

definition: Without a doubt.
example: The grammar schools were assuredly not intended for the gentry alone.
etymology: From assured + -ly.

definition: Any of various chiefly fall-blooming herbs of the genus Aster with showy daisylike flowers.
etymology: From Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr). Doublet of star; related to estoile, étoile, stella, and stelo.

definition: Plants with heads composed of many florets: aster, daisy, dandelion, goldenrod, marigold, lettuces, ragweed, sunflower, thistle, zinnia.
In an amazing manner; to everyone's surprise.
example: The advertisements made the place look promising, but the food was astonishingly bad.
etymology: From astonishing + -ly.

definition: The feeling that accompanies something extremely surprising.
example: He looked at me in astonishment.
etymology: From astonish + -ment.

definition: Filled with the emotional impact of overwhelming surprise or shock.
example: Astounded viewers wept at the pictures from the Oklahoma City bombing.

definition: Someone who predicts the future by the positions of the planets and sun and Moon.
example: Nicolaus Copernicus and Johannes Kepler both made a living as astrologers.
etymology: From Middle English astrologer, astrologier, astrologere, formed from Middle English astrologie or Latin astrologus + Middle English -ere, equivalent to astrology + -er.

definition: Relating to or concerned with astrology.
example: Astrological chart.
etymology: From Latin astrologicus + -al. By surface analysis, astrology + -ical.

definition: (mathematics) a lack of symmetry.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρία (asummetría), from ἀσύμμετρος (asúmmetros) + -ία (-ía), from ἀ- (a-) + σύμμετρος (súmmetros); equivalent to a- + symmetry.

definition: Having no symptoms of illness or disease.
etymology: PIE word *ḱóm The adjective is derived from a- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + symptomatic. The noun is derived from the adjective.

definition: (digital communication) pertaining to a transmission technique that does not require a common clock between the communicating devices; timing signals are derived from special characters in the data stream itself.
etymology: From a- + synchronous.

definition: An induction or asynchronous motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding.
Operations that occur without a regular or predictable time relation to other events.
A studio especially for an artist or designer.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French atelier, from Middle French astelier, from astelle (“small piece of wood, etc., to hold a broken bone in place, splint”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis;

definition: A stage of arteriosclerosis involving fatty deposits (atheromas) inside the arterial walls, thus narrowing the arteries.
etymology: From athero- + sclerosis.

definition: Intense energy.
example: His music is characterized by a happy athleticism.
etymology: From athletic + -ism.

definition: An island consisting of a circular coral reef surrounding a lagoon.
The warhead of a missile designed to deliver an atom bomb.
Make amends for.
example: He tried to atone for his mistakes by working harder.
etymology: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”, literally “at one”), equivalent to at + one. Compare Latin adūnō (“to unite, make one”) for the similar formation.

definition: Of or relating to a cavity or chamber in the body (especially one of the upper chambers of the heart).
etymology: From atrium + -al.

definition: The branch of the coronary artery that supplies the muscles of the atria.
A decrease in size of an organ caused by disease or disuse.
Of an electrical signal; reduced in amplitude with little or no distortion.
example: Attenuated power.

definition: Weakening in force or intensity.
example: Attenuation in the volume of the sound.
etymology: From Middle English attenuacioun, a borrowing from Latin attenuātiō (“a diminishing”). Equivalent to attenuate + -ion.

definition: Being up to particular standard or level especially in being up to date in knowledge.
example: Constant revision keeps the book au courant.
etymology: Borrowed from French au fait (literally “at the fact”).

definition: Invulnerable to fear or intimidation.
example: Audacious explorers.
etymology: From Latin audacia (“boldness”) + -ious, from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

definition: Involving both hearing and seeing (usually relating to teaching aids).
example: The school's audiovisual department.
etymology: From audio- + visual.

definition: Materials using sight or sound to present information.
example: Language tapes and videocassettes and other audiovisuals.

definition: A long flexible steel coil for dislodging stoppages in curved pipes.
etymology: From a rebracketing of Middle English a nauger (seen as an + auger), from Old English nafugār (“nave drill”, literally “nave spear”), from Proto-West Germanic *nabugaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz.

definition: A Scottish word.
example: Auld lang syne.
etymology: From Scots auld or from Northern Middle English auld, aulde, awld, awlde, ald, alde, from Northumbrian Old English ald, variant of Old English eald (“old, mature, venerable;

definition: Of or pertaining to hearing or the ear.
example: An animal with a very sensitive aural apparatus.
etymology: From Latin auralis, from auris (“ear”).

definition: Established as genuine.
Give or delegate power or authority to.
example: She authorized her assistant to sign the papers.

definition: A system for automatically correcting text.
etymology: From auto- + correct.

definition: Bearing an autograph.
example: An autographed copy of his latest book.
etymology: From autograph + -ed.

definition: Of or characteristic of or occurring in autumn.
example: The autumnal equinox.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin autumnāl(is). By surface analysis, autumn + -al.

definition: For which vengeance has been taken.
example: An avenged injury.

definition: Someone who operates an aircraft.
etymology: Borrowed from French aviateur. By surface analysis, avi- + -ator

definition: Science and technology of electronic systems and devices for aeronautics and astronautics.
example: Avionics has become even more important with the development of the space program.
etymology: Blend of aviation + electronics.

definition: Capable of being avoided or warded off.
etymology: From avoid + -able.

definition: Covered with water.
example: The main deck was afloat (or awash).
etymology: From a- + wash.

definition: Turned or twisted toward one side.
example: A … youth with a gorgeous red necktie all awry.
etymology: From Middle English awry, awrie. By surface analysis, a- + wry.

definition: The 2nd cervical vertebra; serves as a pivot for turning the head.
A high-ranking Shiite religious leader who is regarded as an authority on religious law and its interpretation and who has political power as well.
etymology: Borrowed from Iranian Persian آیَتُاللّٰه (âyato-l-lâh), from Classical Persian آیَةُاللّٰه (āyatu-l-lāh), from Arabic آيَةُ ٱللَّٰهِ (ʔāyatu llāhi, “sign of God”, from آيَة (ʔāya, “sign”) + اللّٰه (allāh, “God”)).

definition: The cry made by sheep.
etymology: Compare German bäh, mäh; an imitative word. Notes on phonological development The pronunciation /bɑː/ is perhaps a development from earlier /bæː/ reflecting the shift of /æː/ to /ɑː/ during the 18th and 19th centuries.

definition: Child's word for a sheep or lamb.
Utter meaningless sounds, like a baby, or utter in an incoherent way.
example: The old man is only babbling — don't pay attention.

definition: Divulge confidential information or secrets.
Gibberish resembling the sounds of a baby.
etymology: From Middle English bablyng, babelynge, equivalent to babble + -ing.

definition: A confusion of voices and other sounds.
A farewell sermon to a graduating class at their commencement ceremonies.
etymology: First attested in 1625;

definition: (of racket strokes) made across the body with back of hand facing direction of stroke.
example: He scored on a backhand shot.
etymology: From back + hand.

definition: A hard straight return made on the backhand side.
A return made with the back of the hand facing the direction of the stroke.
A return made with the back of the hand facing the direction of the stroke.
A tent that can be carried in a backpack.
The meeting place of a group of leaders who make their decisions via private negotiations.
example: Backroom deals.

definition: A male expert adviser involved in making important decisions but usually lacking official status.
A female expert adviser involved in making important decisions but usually lacking official status.
A body of water that was created by a flood or tide or by being held or forced back by a dam.
example: The bayous and backwaters are breeding grounds for mosquitos.
etymology: From back + water.

definition: Deeply eroded barren land.
The basic unit of money in Thailand.
etymology: Borrowed from Thai บาท (bàat), from Pali pāda (quarter of a larger valued coin), ultimately from Sanskrit पाद (quarter).

definition: The basic unit of money in Panama; equal to 100 centesimos.
etymology: Named after Vasco Núñez de Balboa. See also Balboa.

definition: Getting bald.
A resistor inserted into a circuit to compensate for changes (as those arising from temperature fluctuations).
The trajectory of an object in free flight.
etymology: From New Latin ballistica + -s, use as noun of feminine of ballisticus (“ballistic”). Compare later ballistic and French balistique. By surface analysis, ballista + -ics or ballistic + -s.

definition: Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
example: Banal clichés.

definition: Large and brightly colored handkerchief; often used as a neckerchief.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi बंधन (bandhan, “the act of binding, a bond”), from Sanskrit बध्नाति (badhnāti, “he binds”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind, bond”). Related to Hindi बाँधना (bāndhnā, “to tie”).

definition: A stripe or stripes of contrasting color.
example: The black and yellow banding of bees and wasps.
etymology: From band + -ing.

definition: A roll of currency notes (often taken as the resources of a person or business etc.).
example: Phil kept his bankroll in his front pocket, as it made too much of a lump to sit on.
etymology: Compound of bank + roll.

definition: A railing at the side of a staircase or balcony to prevent people from falling.
Very small.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch Bantam (Banten province in Java).

definition: A small loaf or roll of soft bread.
example: He lost the bap.
etymology: Originally Scottish English, of unknown origin.

definition: Having undergone the Christian ritual of baptism.
A table game in which short cues are used to knock balls into holes that are guarded by wooden pegs; penalties are incurred if the pegs are knocked over.
(Judaism) an initiation ceremony marking the 13th birthday of a Jewish boy and signifying the beginning of religious responsibility.
example: A bar mitzvah is an important social event.
etymology: From Hebrew בר מצווה / בַּר מִצְוָה (literally “of the age of mitzvah”).

definition: A brutal barbarous savage act.
example: These barbarisms can not be allowed to continue; they must be crushed or civilization will collapse.

definition: A shop where men can get their hair cut.
etymology: Compound of barber + shop.

definition: An unaccompanied quartet of (usually male) voices singing sentimental songs in four-part harmony.
(used informally) completely unclothed.
Riding without a saddle.
example: A bareback rider.
etymology: From bare + back.

definition: The removal of covering.
The second lowest brass wind instrument.
The second lowest adult male singing voice.
A male employee who mixes and serves alcoholic drinks at a bar.
A coarse annual panic grass; a cosmopolitan weed; occasionally used for hay or grazing.
A member of the British order of honor; ranks below a baron but above a knight.
example: Since he was a baronet, he had to be addressed as Sir Henry Jones, Bart.

definition: Lodge in barracks.
etymology: Borrowed from French baraque, from Spanish barraca or Catalan barraca, which is of uncertain origin.

etymology: First attested in the 1670s, from Latin American Spanish barracuda, perhaps from a Cariban word. Doublet of barracouta.

definition: A Spanish-speaking quarter in a town or city (especially in the United States).

Fragrant European mint having clusters of small violet-and-white flowers; naturalized especially in eastern North America.
etymology: From basil + thyme.

definition: Derive or receive pleasure from; get enjoyment from; take pleasure in.
example: She relished her fame and basked in her glory.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English basken, from Old Norse baðask (“to take a bath”, literally “to bathe oneself”), mediopassive form from underlying baða (“to bathe”) + sik (“oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *baþōną and *sek.

definition: A hilt with a basket-shaped guard for the hand.
Large harmless plankton-eating northern shark; often swims slowly or floats at the sea surface.
(Judaism) an initiation ceremony marking the 12th birthday of a Jewish girl and signifying the beginning of religious responsibility.
etymology: Borrowed from Hebrew בַּת מִצְוָה (bát mitsvá, “bat mitzvah, someone who has come of age”).

definition: Moderate or restrain; lessen the force of.
example: He bated his breath when talking about this affair.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English baten (“to abate”), an apheretic form of abaten, from Old French abatre (“to knock down”).

definition: (Judaism) an initiation ceremony marking the 12th birthday of a Jewish girl and signifying the beginning of religious responsibility.
The act of subjecting to strong attack.
A ram used to break down doors of fortified buildings.
etymology: The heads of some battering rams were carved in the shape of a ram, an animal renowned for butting with its head.

definition: The line along which opposing armies face each other.
etymology: From battle + front.

definition: Loud cries made while weeping.
example: E. F. Benson Nobody could call Major Flint, with his bawlings and his sniffings, the least mysterious.

definition: A severe scolding.
Muscle of small choice shallow-water scallops.
A computer that is running software that allows users to leave messages and access information of general interest.
