Having brown speckles.
Having brown stripes.
The inedible nutlike seed of the horse chestnut.
etymology: The name stems from Native Americans, who called the nut "hetuck," which means "buck eye" (because the markings on the nut resemble the eye of a deer).

definition: A pancake made with buckwheat flour.
example: There's buckwheat cakes and Injun batter, Makes you fat or a little fatter;.

definition: Tree of low-lying coastal areas of southeastern United States having glossy leaves and racemes of fragrant white flowers.
Perennial vine of dry parts of central and southwestern United States and Mexico having small hard mottled green inedible fruit.
A brass instrument without valves; used for military calls and fanfares.
example: The bugle of an elk.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English bugle, from Anglo-Norman bugle (“young ox, heifer; bugle”), from Latin būculus (“young ox, steer”).

definition: A signal broadcast by the sound of a bugle.
A partition that divides a ship or plane into compartments.
etymology: From Old Norse bálkr (“partition”) + head, anglicised as bulk + head.

definition: Large powerful tractor; a large blade in front flattens areas of ground.
etymology: Originally bull-dozer (1875, Louisiana, US), in the bullier and terrorizer sense; bulldoze + -er. The name for the earthmoving machine came later, figuratively, from that sense.

definition: An embankment built around a space for defensive purposes.
example: The party stalwarts constitute the bulwark that ensures the president's term of office.
etymology: From Middle English bulwerk, from Middle Dutch bolwerk, bolwerc and Middle Low German bolwerk, equivalent to bole (“tree trunk”) + work. Cognate with German Bollwerk, Danish bolværk, Swedish bålverk, Dutch bolwerk.

definition: Make a mess of, destroy or ruin.
example: Spiders build webs and wait for insects to bumble into them.
etymology: Onomatopoeia. Compare bungle, jumble, and fumble.

definition: Robust hairy social bee of temperate regions.
etymology: 1520s from bumble + bee, replacing Middle English humbul-be. Merged with Middle English bombeln (“to boom, buzz”), in the late 14th century. The name of the drink is a semantic loan from Ukrainian джміль (džmilʹ).

definition: Lacking physical movement skills, especially with the hands.
example: A bumbling mechanic.

definition: An elasticized rope.
etymology: Probably from slang, possibly derived from bouncy + spongy.

definition: An elasticized rope.
(baseball) the act of hitting a baseball or softball lightly by holding the bat in a stationary position rather than swinging it.
example: The bunt of the sail was green.
etymology: Unknown. Perhaps a nasalised variant of butt.

definition: Cheerfulness that bubbles to the surface.
etymology: From buoyant + -cy or buoy + -ancy.

definition: Tending to float on a liquid or rise in air or gas.
example: Buoyant balloons.
etymology: From buoy + -ant.

definition: Seed vessel having hooks or prickles.
etymology: From Middle English burre, of unknown origin but probably from North Germanic (Scandinavian) source or from Old English byrst (“bristle”). See also burr.

definition: Not easily borne; wearing.
example: The burdensome task of preparing the income tax return.
etymology: From burden + -some.

definition: An official of a bureaucracy.
etymology: From French bureaucrate, equivalent to bureau + -crat.

definition: Colloquial American term for a town.
example: I've lived in this burg all my life.
etymology: The historical sense is from Late Latin burgus, from Frankish *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“borough, fortification”). Doublet of borough, Brough, burgh, burh, and bury. Also compare burgess.

definition: A borough in Scotland.
etymology: From Middle English borwe, borgh, burgh, buruh, from Old English burh, from Proto-West Germanic *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“city, stronghold”). Cf. Strasbourg.

definition: Muscular and heavily built.
example: Had a tall burly frame.
etymology: From Middle English burly, burely, borly, burlich, borlich, borlic (“tall, stately”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Scots burely, burly (“rough, stout, sturdy, strong”).

definition: Facial hair that has grown down the side of a man's face in front of the ears (especially when the rest of the beard is shaved off).
etymology: From Ambrose Burnside.

definition: A shade of brown with a tinge of red.
A reflex that expels gas noisily from the stomach through the mouth.
example: Lennon let out a burp after downing the beer.
etymology: Originally from American English, of imitative origin.

definition: Southern and western Australian shrub with unlobed or shallowly lobed toothed leaves and purple flowers; sometimes placed in genus Hibiscus.
A United States dry measure equal to 4 pecks or 2152.42 cubic inches.
example: A heap containing ten bushels of apples.

definition: A basket large enough to hold a bushel.
Used of hair; thick and poorly groomed.
example: Bushy locks.
etymology: From bush + -y.

definition: A woman engaged in commercial or industrial business.
etymology: From business + -woman.

definition: A rapid active commotion.
example: The hum and bustle; a din and bustle.
etymology: From Middle English bustlen, bustelen, bostlen, perhaps an alteration of *busklen (> Modern English buskle), a frequentative of Middle English busken (“to prepare;

definition: Move or cause to move energetically or busily.
example: The cheerleaders bustled about excitedly before their performance.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Ranunculus.
etymology: From butter + cup. Both sense 1 and 2 are from the flowers' association with butter, from their yellow colour. Compare butterflower for a similar derivation;

definition: Residue from making butter from sour raw milk; or pasteurized milk curdled by adding a culture.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English butter-melke, equivalent to butter + milk.

definition: Very tender biscuit partially leavened with buttermilk and soda.
A pancake made with buttermilk.
Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech.
example: Buttery praise.
etymology: From Middle English buttry, equivalent to butter + -y. Piecewise doublet of butyric, butter ultimately being from Latin būtȳrum and -y being a doublet of -ic.

definition: Evergreen tree or shrub with fruit resembling buttons and yielding heavy hard compact wood.
Furnished or closed with buttons or something buttonlike.
example: A buttoned sofa.

definition: Unimaginatively conventional.
example: A colorful character in the buttoned-down, dull-grey world of business.

definition: (British colloquial) not inclined to conversation.
Well in the past; former.
example: Bygone days.
etymology: From by (adverb) + gone. See go by.

definition: A capacitor that provides low impedance over certain (high) frequencies.
A conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers.
Tropical American tree producing cacao beans.
etymology: From Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl. Doublet of cocoa.

definition: Seed of the cacao tree; ground roasted beans are source of chocolate.
Small moth whose larvae feed on tobacco and other dried plant products.
Tropical American tree producing cacao beans.
Large harsh-voiced American wren of arid regions of the United States southwest and Mexico.
A can for storing tea.
example: Place the disc in the DVD caddy.
etymology: A variant of caddie (etymology 1).

definition: A soft bluish-white ductile malleable toxic bivalent metallic element; occurs in association with zinc ores.
etymology: Borrowed from German Cadmium. from Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía, “calamine”), a cadmium-bearing mixture of minerals, which was named after the king Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”).

definition: A standard voltaic cell (trademark Weston).
Orange-hued cadmium yellow pigment.
Pigment of cadmium sulfide and barium sulfate varying in hue from lemon yellow to orange.
A mound of stones piled up as a memorial or to mark a boundary or path.
etymology: From Scots cairn, from Scottish Gaelic càrn, from Old Irish carn, from Proto-Celtic *karnos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Compare Welsh carn, Cornish carn. Doublet of carn and horn.

definition: A grey salt of calcium (CaC) used in making acetylene.
A caustic substance produced by heating limestone.
A caustic substance produced by heating limestone.
Make fine adjustments or divide into marked intervals for optimal measuring.
example: Calibrate an instrument.
etymology: From calibre + -ate.

definition: Made of calico or resembling calico in being patterned.
example: Calico dresses.
etymology: From Calicut, from where the cloth was originally exported, from Malayalam കോഴിക്കോട് (kōḻikkōṭŭ, “Kozhikode”), from കോഴി (kōḻi, “palace”) + കോട് (kōṭŭ, “fortified palace”).

definition: A North American evergreen shrub having glossy leaves and white or rose-colored flowers.
A cat having black and cream-colored and yellowish markings.
Brightly spotted crab of sandy beaches of the Atlantic coast of the United States.
The civil and religious leader of a Muslim state considered to be a representative of Allah on earth.
etymology: From Middle English calife, caliphe, from Old French caliphe, from Medieval Latin calipha, from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) and خَلِيف (ḵalīf, “successor”).

definition: A request by the manufacturer of a defective product to return the product (as for replacement or repair).
etymology: Deverbal from call back.

definition: Steadiness of mind under stress.
etymology: From calm + -ness.

definition: Relating to or associated with heat.
example: The caloric effect of sunlight.
etymology: From calorie + -ic. From French calorique, coined by French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin calor (“heat”).

definition: Any experience that causes intense suffering.
etymology: From Late Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calavera and calvaria.

definition: Rare north temperate bog orchid bearing a solitary white to pink flower marked with purple at the tip of an erect reddish stalk above 1 basal leaf.
etymology: Originally Trinidad English, an alteration of kaiso, perhaps ultimately of African origin; Allsopp 1996 suggests Ibibio ka iso (“come on”), used to urge dancers on.

definition: The quality of affording easy familiarity and sociability.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French camaraderie. Recent American pronunciations such as /ˌkɑməˈɹɑdəɹi/ and /ˌkɑmˈɹɑdəɹi/ are influenced by the cognate comrade.

definition: Made invisible by means of protective coloring.
A climber having flowers that are the color of canaries.
Any of the yeastlike imperfect fungi of the genus Candida.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Candida, from Latin candida.

definition: (used as intensives reflecting the speaker's attitude) it is sincerely the case that.
example: Candidly, I think she doesn't have a conscience.
etymology: From candid + -ly.

definition: A holder with sockets for candles.
etymology: From Middle English candelstik, candelstikke, from Old English candelsticca (“candlestick”), equivalent to candle + stick. Cognate with Scots candilsteke, candilstik (“candlestick”).

definition: Ability to make judgments free from discrimination or dishonesty.
etymology: From Latin candor (“brightness, whiteness”), from candeō (“to shine”).

definition: Ground beef mixed with raw egg and e.g. onions and capers and anchovies; eaten raw.
A solid projectile that in former times was fired from a cannon.
example: The cannonball could be called the S.U.V. of the pool — oversized, brash, hormonally hardwired.
etymology: From cannon + ball from being a round ball that is fired from a cannon.

definition: Move hurridly.
Showing self-interest and shrewdness in dealing with others.
example: The politician gave a canny response to the reporter’s questions.
etymology: Northern English dialect, from can (“to know”) ( + -y), from Middle English can, first and third person singular of cunnen, connen (“to be able, know how to”), from Old English cunnan (“to know how to, be able to”).

definition: The highest part (usually the melody) in a piece of choral music.
etymology: From Italian canto (“song”). Doublet of chant.

definition: The setting for a narrative or fictional or dramatic account.
example: The crowded canvas of history.
etymology: The verb is derived from canvas (“type of coarse cloth woven from hemp”). The connection between “to toss (someone) in a (canvas) sheet; (by extension) to batter, beat, or thrash (someone or something);

definition: Persuasion of voters in a political campaign.
An electrical phenomenon whereby an electric charge is stored.
etymology: From capacity + -ance.

definition: A measure of the capacity of a circuit component to store charge.
Any of numerous plants of the genus Capparis.
etymology: Clipping of capriole.

definition: A dilleniid dicot family of the order Rhoeadales that includes: genera Capparis, Cleome, Crateva, and Polanisia.
Allemande sauce with capers.
Shrub or small tree of southern Florida to Central and South America.
Of or relating to hair.
etymology: From Latin capillāris (“pertaining to the hair”), from capillus (“the hair, properly of the head”), from caput (“head”).

definition: A phenomenon associated with surface tension and resulting in the elevation or depression of liquids in capillaries.
One of the small thin-walled arteries that end in capillaries.
A layer of tissue densely packed with capillaries.
A fracture without separation of the fragments and the line of the break being very thin.
A tube of small internal diameter; holds liquid by capillary action.
A minute vein continuous with a capillary.
Any of the minute blood vessels connecting arterioles with venules.
Water that remains in the soil after gravitational water is drained out, that is subject to the laws of capillary movement, and that is in the form of a film around the soil grains.
A document containing the terms of surrender.
etymology: From Middle French capitulation; equivalent to capitulate + -ion. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.

definition: Equal parts of espresso and hot milk topped with cinnamon and nutmeg and usually whipped cream.
Equal parts of espresso and hot milk topped with cinnamon and nutmeg and usually whipped cream.
A sudden desire.
etymology: Borrowed from French caprice, from Italian capriccio, from caporiccio (“fright, sudden start”). Doublet of capriccio.

definition: Changeable.
example: A capricious summer breeze.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French capricieux, from Italian capriccioso, from capriccio. By surface analysis, caprice + -ious.

definition: The post of captain.
etymology: From captain + -cy. Piecewise doublet of chieftaincy.

definition: A binary compound of carbon with a more electropositive element.
Light automatic rifle.
etymology: Ca. 1600, from French carabine. Doublet of carabine.

definition: A colorless nonflammable liquid used as a solvent for fats and oils; because of its toxicity its use as a cleaning fluid or fire extinguisher has declined.
Having carbonation (especially artificially carbonated).
example: Soda pop, lemon soda and soda water are carbonated drinks. Champagne and beer are naturally carbonated through fermentation.

definition: Effervescent beverage artificially charged with carbon dioxide.
Of or relating to the Carboniferous geologic era.
example: Carboniferous rock system.
etymology: From carbon + -i- + -ferous.

definition: Mixes air with gasoline vapor prior to explosion.
etymology: Attested from 1862, from carburet (“enrich an illuminating gas with carbon-rich fuel”) + -or. The motor vehicle sense is attested since 1896

definition: Causing or tending to cause cancer.
example: The carcinogenic action of certain chemicals.
etymology: From carcino- + -genic.

definition: An abnormal sound of the heart; sometimes a sign of abnormal function of the heart valves.
A specialized bit of heart tissue that controls the heartbeat.
A plexus of nerves supplying the heart and nearby structures.
A specialist in cardiology; a specialist in the structure and function and disorders of the heart.
etymology: From cardio- + -logist.

definition: Without care or concern.
example: Carelessly raised the children's hopes without thinking of their possible disappointment.
etymology: From careless + -ly.

definition: The quality of not being careful or taking pains.
example: This accident was caused by carelessness.
etymology: From Middle English *carelesnes, *carlesnesse, from Old English carlēasnes (“freedom from care, security, carelessness”), equivalent to careless + -ness.

definition: A gentle affectionate stroking (or something resembling it).
example: He showered her with caresses.
etymology: From French caresse, from Italian carezza (“dear”), from Latin cārus (“dear”), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂-, akin to Sanskrit काम (kāma, “love”). Doublet of karezza.

definition: Of a color at the end of the color spectrum (next to orange); resembling the color of blood or cherries or tomatoes or rubies.
etymology: PIE word *kʷŕ̥mis Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥mis Proto-Indo-Iranian *kŕ̥miš Persian کرمست* (*kermest)bor. Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz)bor. Medieval Latin *carminium? French carminder.

definition: Marked by the appetites and passions of the body.
example: Carnal knowledge.
etymology: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).

definition: Relating to or characteristic of carnivores.
example: The lion and other carnivorous animals.
etymology: From Latin carnivorus (“flesh-eating”).

definition: Typically having large ears and feeding primarily on insects; worldwide in distribution.
Plants adapted to attract and capture and digest primarily insects but also other small animals.
Of or relating to either of the two major arteries supplying blood to the head and neck.
Either of two major arteries of the neck and head; branches from the aorta.
A chemoreceptor located near the bifurcations of the carotid arteries; monitors oxygen content of the blood and helps control respiration.
The craft of a carpenter: making things out of wood.
example: Fine carpentry for sale.
etymology: From Middle English carpentrie, from Anglo-Norman carpenterie, from Old Northern French (compare French charpenterie). See carpenter.

definition: A cleaning implement with revolving brushes that pick up dirt as the implement is pushed over a carpet.
One of the two sides of a motorway where traffic travels in one direction only usually in two or three lanes.
etymology: From carriage + way.

definition: Complete freedom or authority to act.
etymology: Borrowed from French carte blanche, referring to a blank or white card.

definition: Mountain frog found near water; of United States Northwest to California.
A secondary menu that appears while you are holding the cursor over an item on the primary menu.
Tropical American evergreen tree bearing kidney-shaped nuts that are edible only when roasted.
etymology: Reanalysis of French acajou as a + cajou, from Old Tupi akaîu. Doublet of acajou.

definition: Tropical American evergreen tree bearing kidney-shaped nuts that are edible only when roasted.
The quantity a cask will hold.
etymology: From Middle French casque. Doublet of casco and casque.

definition: A starch made by leaching and drying the root of the cassava plant; the source of tapioca; a staple food in the tropics.
A good hard soap made from olive oil and sodium hydroxide.
Street names for ketamine.
An eye disease that involves the clouding or opacification of the natural lens of the eye.
Eye surgery that involves removing all or part of the lens and replacing it with an intraocular lens implant.
The entire geographical area drained by a river and its tributaries; an area characterized by all runoff being conveyed to the same outlet.
A phrase that has become a catchword.
etymology: From catch + phrase, from the notion that the phrase will catch in the mind of the user.

definition: A series of questions put to an individual (such as a political candidate) to elicit their views.
Relating to or included in a category or categories.
etymology: From Late Latin catēgoricus + -al. By surface analysis, category + -ical.

definition: The moral principle that behavior should be determined by duty.
etymology: From German kategorischer Imperativ.

definition: A group of people or things arranged by class or category.
etymology: From categorize + -ation.

definition: Place into or assign to a category.
example: Children learn early on to categorize.
etymology: From category + -ize.

definition: Emotionally purging.
example: Shaving, my favorite activity, is very cathartic.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós).

definition: A positively charged ion.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κᾰτῐόν (kătĭón), neuter present participle of κᾰ́τειμῐ (kắteimĭ, “to go down, come down”), from κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, “downwards, down, cata-”) + εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go, come”).

definition: Narrow platform extending out into an auditorium.
example: Models displayed clothes on a catwalk at the fashion show.
etymology: From cat + walk.

definition: Constituting or relating to a tail.
example: Caudal appendage.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin caudālis (“having a tail”).

definition: Regional anesthesia resulting from injection of an anesthetic into the caudal end of the spinal canal; now largely replaced by epidural anesthesia.
The relation between causes and effects.
etymology: From Latin as if *causalitas, from causalis (“causal”), from causa (“cause”). By surface analysis, causal + -ity = cause + -ality.

definition: Harsh or corrosive in tone.
example: Caustic jokes about political assassination, talk-show hosts and medical ethics.
etymology: From the Latin causticus (“burning”), from Ancient Greek καυστικός (kaustikós, “burning”), from καυστός (kaustós, “burnt”) + -ικός (-ikós).

definition: A caustic substance produced by heating limestone.
Witty language used to convey insults or scorn.
A strongly alkaline caustic used in manufacturing soap and paper and aluminum and various sodium compounds.
Warding off.
example: Most parents were optimistic, but others sounded a cautionary note.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cautiōnārius.

definition: Being or suggesting a cavern.
example: Vast cavernous chambers hollowed out of limestone.
etymology: Late Middle English cavernous, cavernose, borrowing from Old French caverneux or Latin cavernōsus (“full of hollows or cavities”), from caverna (“a hollow, cavity, cave”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix);

definition: Plant bearing very hot and finely tapering long peppers; usually red.
example: What's the difference between a cayenne and a jalapeno?

definition: Commonly cultivated Old World woody herb having large pinkish to red flowers.
Plant bearing very hot and finely tapering long peppers; usually red.
etymology: From Old Tupi ky'ynha (“hot pepper”), later associated with Cayenne.

definition: Give over; surrender or relinquish to the physical control of another.
example: Edward decided to cede the province.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French ceder, from Old French ceder, from Latin cēdō (“to yield”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱyesdʰ- (“to drive away; to go away”). Cognate with Tocharian B kätk- (“to cross, pass”).

definition: A fungous leaf spot disease of the celery plant.
Belonging to or prescribed for celiac disease.
example: A celiac diet.
etymology: From Latin coeliacus, from Ancient Greek κοιλιακός (koiliakós), from κοιλία (koilía, “belly”). Cognate with coelom.

definition: An artery that originates from the abdominal aorta just below the diaphragm and branches into the left gastric artery and the common hepatic artery and the splenic artery.
A disorder in children and adults; inability to tolerate wheat protein (gluten); symptoms include foul-smelling diarrhea and emaciation; often accompanied by lactose intolerance.
An artery that originates from the abdominal aorta just below the diaphragm and branches into the left gastric artery and the common hepatic artery and the splenic artery.
An unmarried status.
etymology: From Latin caelibātus (“celibacy, a single life”), from caelebs (“unmarried”). By surface analysis, celib(ate) + -acy.

definition: Lumpy deposits of body fat especially on women's thighs etc.
etymology: Borrowed from French cellulite. By surface analysis, cellule + -ite. Doublet of cellulitis. First attested in the 1960s.

definition: An ester of acetic acid; used in fibers and fabrics; photographic films and varnishes.
Any ester of cellulose with an acid.
A nitric acid ester; used in lacquers and explosives.
Counterintelligence achieved by banning or deleting any information of value to the enemy.
Harsh criticism or disapproval.
etymology: From 1350–1400 Middle English censure, from Old French, from Latin censūra (“censor's office or assessment”), from censēre (“to consider, to assess, to value, to judge, to tax, etc.”).

definition: (classical mythology) a mythical being that is half man and half horse.
etymology: From Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros), from Κένταυρος (Kéntauros, “a member of a savage race from Thessaly”).

definition: The concentration of attention or energy on something.
A metric unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter.
Chiefly nocturnal predacious arthropod having a flattened body of 15 to 173 segments each with a pair of legs, the foremost pair being modified as prehensors.
etymology: From French centipède, from Latin centipeda, centipēs, from centi- (“hundred”) + pēs (“foot”); equivalent to centi- + -pede.

definition: Black-faced chimpanzees of central Africa; closely related to eastern chimpanzees.
Drawn toward a center or brought under the control of a central authority.
example: Centralized control of emergency relief efforts.

definition: Tending to move away from a center.
example: Centrifugal force.
etymology: From New Latin centrifugālis, coined by Christiaan Huygens from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”) + -al.

definition: The outward force on a body moving in a curved path around another body.
A pump that use centrifugal force to discharge fluid into a pipe.
An apparatus that uses centrifugal force to separate particles from a suspension.
etymology: From French centrifuge, from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”). Equivalent to centri- + -fuge.

definition: Widely cultivated in temperate regions for its edible grains.
An aneurysm of the carotid artery.
A canal connecting the third and fourth ventricles.
Swelling of the brain due to the uptake of water in the neuropile and white matter.
Bleeding from a ruptured blood vessel in the brain.
A blood clot in a cerebral artery or vein.
Material consisting of seed coverings and small pieces of stem or leaves that have been separated from the seeds.
example: To separate out the chaff, early cultures tossed baskets of grain into the air and let the wind blow away the lighter chaff.
etymology: From Middle English chaf, from Old English ċeaf, from Proto-West Germanic *kaf. Cognate with Scots caff, Saterland Frisian Sääf, West Frisian tsjêf, Dutch kaf, German Low German Kaff, regional German Kaff.

definition: Strong feelings of embarrassment.
example: Much to the chagrin (of).

definition: A pipe wrench used for turning large pipes; an adjustable chain circles the pipe with its ends connected to the head whose teeth engage the pipe.
The position of chairman.
etymology: From chairman + -ship.

definition: The female officer who presides at the meetings of an organization.
etymology: From chair + -woman.

definition: Special linen which pertain to the Eucharist.
Mexican evergreen climbing plant having large solitary funnel-shaped fragrant yellow flowers with purple-brown ridges in the throat.
Sheet of slate; for writing with chalk.
etymology: From chalk + board.

definition: A court with jurisdiction in equity.
etymology: From Middle English chancerie, a reduced form of chancellerie. See chancellery.

definition: Capable of or tending to change in form or quality or nature.
example: The weather is very changeable today: we've had bright sunshine, clouds, wind and rain in the same half-hour.
etymology: From Middle English chaungeable, from Old Northern French chaungeable, from Late Latin cambiāre (“to change”), equivalent to change + -able.

definition: Sung or uttered rhythmically in a monotone.
example: A chanted psalm.

definition: One who accompanies and supervises a young woman or gatherings of young people.
etymology: See chaperon.

definition: A graphic or vivid verbal description.
example: The pamphlet contained brief characterizations of famous Vermonters.
etymology: From characterise + -ation.

definition: In characteristic manner.
example: He arrived characteristically late.
etymology: From characteristic + -ally.

definition: A word acted out in an episode of the game of charades.
example: This whole charade is absurd.
etymology: From French charade, charrade (“prattle, idle conversation; a kind of riddle”), probably from Occitan charrada (“conversation; chatter”), from charrar (“to chat; to chatter”) + -ada.

definition: White wine grape.
A deep opening in the earth's surface.
etymology: From Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα (khásma, “abyss, cleft”). Doublet of chasma. Compare schism. Displaced native Old English swelh and Old English elh.

definition: The rapid series of noises made by the parts of a machine.
Full of trivial conversation.
example: Chatty error messages may help attackers to compromise your server.
etymology: From chat (“informal conversation”) + -y.

definition: Patterned with alternating squares of color.
example: That is a checkered tablecloth.
etymology: From checker + -ed.

definition: Any liliaceous plant of the genus Fritillaria having nodding variously colored flowers.
In a cheerful manner.
example: He cheerfully agreed to do it.

definition: Any foodstuff made by combining different ingredients.
example: He volunteered to taste her latest concoction.
etymology: From Latin concoctiō.

definition: Occurring with or following as a consequence.
etymology: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).

definition: A large gathering of people.
etymology: From Middle English concours, from Middle French concours and its etymon Latin concursus, concursum, from concurrere (“to run together”). See concur. Doublet of concours.

definition: A woman who cohabits with an important man.
etymology: From Middle English concubine (first attested 1250–1300), from Anglo-Norman concubine, from Latin concubīna, equivalent to concub- (variant stem of concumbō (“to lie together”)) + feminine suffix -īna.

definition: A product of condensation.
etymology: From condense + -ate (noun-forming suffix). Alternatively, back-formation from condensation.

definition: An electrical device characterized by its capacity to store an electric charge.
etymology: From condense + -er.

definition: Microphone consisting of a capacitor with one plate fixed and the other forming the diaphragm moved by sound waves.
Microphone consisting of a capacitor with one plate fixed and the other forming the diaphragm moved by sound waves.
An expression of sympathy with another's grief.
example: They sent their condolences.
etymology: From condole + -ence, or from Middle French condoléance, or formed from the root of Latin condoleō (“to sympathize”), from con- (“together, with”) and doleō (“to hurt, suffer, have pain”).

definition: The largest flying birds in the western hemisphere.
etymology: From Spanish cóndor, from Classical Quechua kuntur. The change /t/ to /d/ was characteristic of the "coastal" variety of the language.

definition: The transmission of heat or electricity or sound.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin conductio, conductionem (“a bringing together”); equivalent to conduct + -ion.

definition: Anesthesia of an area supplied by a nerve; produced by an anesthetic agent applied to the nerve.
Candy and other sweets considered collectively.
example: The business decided to concentrate on confectionery and soft drinks.
etymology: From confectioner + -y.

definition: A priest who hears confession and gives absolution.
example: Long before Edward I, the English had a King Edward who they considered a martyr and a King Edward who they considered a confessor.
etymology: From Middle English confessor, confessour, from Anglo-Norman confessour, and its source, Latin cōnfessor, from cōnfiteor (“confess, admit, acknowledge”). By surface analysis, confess + -or.

definition: Someone to whom private matters are confided.
Reveal in private; tell confidentially.
example: I confide in her judgement in this matter.
etymology: From Middle Scots confide, confyde (“to put trust in”), from Latin confīdere (“to put trust in, have confidence in”), from con- (“together”) + fidēre (“to trust”). First attested in English use in the early 17th century.

definition: Place limits on (extent or amount or access).
etymology: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.

definition: Restrict or confine within limits.
example: Please confine your questions to the topic.

definition: Surrendered as a penalty.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnfiscātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin cōnfiscō (“to seize for the public treasury (fiscus)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: Seizure by the government.
etymology: From Latin cōnfiscātiō. By surface analysis, confiscate + -ion.

definition: A symmetrical arrangement of the parts of a thing.
etymology: From Latin confōrmātiō. By surface analysis, conform + -ation.

definition: Perplexed by many conflicting situations or statements; filled with bewilderment.
example: A cloudy and confounded philosopher.

definition: That confounds or contradicts or confuses.
etymology: By surface analysis, confound + -ing.

definition: Come together, usually for a purpose.
example: The crowds congregated in front of the Vatican on Christmas Eve.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1400–1450, in Middle English, the verb c. 1513; from Middle English congregat(e) (“(of people) banded together; (of liquids) accumulated; (of muscles) contracted;

definition: A female member of the United States House of Representatives.
etymology: From congress + -woman.

definition: A buoy resembling a cone.
Consisting of two or more associated entities.
example: The interplay of these conjoined yet opposed factors.
etymology: From conjoin + -ed.

definition: One of a pair of identical twins born with their bodies joined at some point.
Joined together especially in a pair or pairs.
etymology: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1530;

definition: A mixture of two partially miscible liquids A and B produces two conjugate solutions: one of A in B and another of B in A.
Formed by the union of two compounds.
example: A conjugated protein.
etymology: Inflected form of conjugate. Adjective sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Konjugation, konjugieren, coined 1899 by German chemist Johannes Thiele.

definition: A protein complex combining amino acids with other substances.
Calling up a spirit or devil.
An illusory feat; considered magical by naive observers.
Tissue of mesodermal origin consisting of e.g. collagen fibroblasts and fatty cells; supports organs and fills spaces between them and forms tendons and ligaments.
An expert able to appreciate a field; especially in the fine arts.
example: Beer connoisseur.
etymology: Around 1705–1715, from French connoisseur, from the verb connoître (obsolete pre-1835 spelling of connaître (“to know”)).

definition: What you must know in order to determine the reference of an expression.
example: The word "advisedly" has a connotation of "wisely", although it denotes merely "intentionally" and "deliberately.".
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from connotō (“to mark in addition”), from Latin con- (“together, with”) + notō (“to note”); equivalent to connote + -ation.

definition: Affected by conscience.
Compulsory military service.
etymology: From Middle French conscription, from Latin cōnscriptiō (“levying of troops”).

definition: A solemn commitment of your life or your time to some cherished purpose (to a service or a goal).
example: His consecration to study.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsecrātiō, cōnsecrātiōnem.

definition: In a consecutive manner.
example: He was consecutively ill, then well, then ill again.
etymology: From consecutive + -ly.

definition: In a conservative manner.
example: We estimated the number of demonstrators conservatively at 200,000.
etymology: From conservative + -ly.

definition: Change in a consonant in a word according to its morphological or syntactic environment.
example: Welsh is a language with a rich and productive system of initial consonant mutation.

definition: The repetition of consonants (or consonant patterns) especially at the ends of words.
In a manner tending to attract attention.
example: There have been plenty of general declarations about willingness to meet and talk, but conspicuously no mention of time and place.
etymology: From conspicuous + -ly.

definition: A member of a conspiracy.
example: The conspirators were rounded up by the police and arrested.
etymology: From Middle English conspyratour, from Anglo-Norman conspiratour. By surface analysis, conspire + -ator.

definition: Engage in plotting or enter into a conspiracy, swear together.
example: They conspired to overthrow the government.
etymology: From Middle English conspiren, from Old French conspirer, from Latin conspirare, conspīrō, from con- (combining form of cum (“with”)) + spīrō (“breathe”).

definition: The force of policemen and officers.
etymology: From mediaeval Latin conestabularia, a noun use of the feminine version of conestabularius, from Latin constabulus, from comes stabuli, literally ‘master of the stables’.

definition: Fear resulting from the awareness of danger.
etymology: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. By surface analysis, consternate + -ion.

definition: Have difficult or incomplete or infrequent evacuation of the bowels.
Compel to behave in a certain way.
example: Duty constrains one to act often contrary to one's desires or inclinations.

definition: In a constructive manner.
example: It is my task to look critically and constructively at the flaws and the failures.
etymology: From constructive + -ly.

definition: Someone who contracts for and supervises construction (as of a building).
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnstrūctor, from Latin cōnstruō + Medieval Latin -or. By surface analysis, construct + -or.

definition: The theory that an increasing consumption of goods is economically beneficial.
etymology: From consumer + -ism.

definition: Brought to completion.
example: A consummated transaction.

definition: A delayed type of allergic reaction of the skin resulting from skin contact with a specific allergen (such as poison ivy).
Make impure.
example: This water is contaminated. It isn't safe to drink.
etymology: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; from Middle English contaminaten (“to defile; to infect with desease”), from contaminat(e) (“sullied, defiled;

definition: Deeply or seriously thoughtful.
example: Contemplative faculties.
etymology: From Middle English contemplatyve, contemplatyf, from Old French contemplatif, from Latin contemplātīvus.

definition: Occurring in the same period of time.
example: A rise in interest rates is often contemporaneous with an increase in inflation.
etymology: From Latin contemporāneus (“contemporary”), from con- (“with”) + tempus (“time”) + -aneus (“of or pertaining to”) (compare Late Latin temporāneus (“opportune, timely”)).

definition: Satisfied or showing satisfaction with things as they are.
example: A contented smile.

definition: Capable of being controlled.
etymology: From control + -able.

definition: Involving controversy.
etymology: From controversial + -ly.

definition: Things that make you comfortable and at ease.
The act of convening.
Tending to come together from different directions.
example: Convergent direction.

definition: Thinking that brings together information focussed on solving a problem (especially solving problems that have a single correct solution).
etymology: Coined by Joy Paul Guilford in 1956.

definition: The act of converging (coming closer).
Lens such that a beam of light passing through it is brought to a point or focus.
A polygon such that no side extended cuts any other side or vertex; it can be cut by a straight line in at most two points.
Document effecting a property transfer.
etymology: From Middle English conveiance, conveyaunce, equivalent to convey + -ance.

definition: A group gathered in response to a summons.
etymology: From Middle English convocacioun, from Old French convocation, from Latin convocatio, convocationem.

definition: Calm and unruffled self-assurance.
example: He performed with all the coolness of a veteran.
etymology: From Middle English colnes, colnesse, from Old English cōlnes, cœ̄lnes, cēlnes (“coolness; cool air, breeze”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlinassī, equivalent to cool + -ness.

definition: Having a bottom of copper or sheathed with copper.
example: Copper-bottomed pots.
etymology: From the copper sheathing applied to the bottom of a wooden ship to prevent damage from marine organisms. In literal sense 18th century, in figurative sense attested since at least 1807.

definition: The basic unit of money in Nicaragua; equal to 100 centavos.
Either of two Welsh breeds of long-bodied short-legged dogs with erect ears and a fox-like head.
Old World herb with aromatic leaves and seed resembling parsley.
Old World herb with aromatic leaves and seed resembling parsley.
Dried coriander seeds used whole or ground.
Of or pertaining to the Corinthian style of architecture.
Chowder containing corn.
A smut fungus attacking Indian corn.
The transparent dome-shaped anterior portion of the outer covering of the eye; it covers the iris and pupil and is continuous with the sclera.
etymology: From Latin cornea tela (“horny tissue”), from cornu (“horn”).

definition: Of or related to the cornea.
etymology: From cornea + -al.

definition: A surgical procedure in which part or all of a damaged or diseased cornea is replaced by healthy corneal tissue from a donor.
A brass musical instrument with a brilliant tone; has a narrow tube and a flared bell and is played by means of valves.
example: This cornet [translating Cornet] was a brave young cavalier and not more than two years older than me.
etymology: From Middle English cornet, from Old French cornet, a diminutive of a popular reflex of Latin cornū (“horn”).

definition: Obstruction of blood flow in a coronary artery by a blood clot (thrombus).
In a corresponding manner.
example: The temperature decreases correspondingly.
etymology: From corresponding + -ly.

definition: A steep-walled semicircular basin in a mountain; may contain a lake.
etymology: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic coire.

definition: Establish or strengthen as with new evidence or facts.
etymology: First attested in the 1530s;

definition: Seducing into corrupt practices.
A pirate along the Barbary Coast.
etymology: Borrowed from French corsaire, from Medieval Latin cursārius (“pirate”), from Latin cursus (“course, a running; plunder, hostile inroad”). Doublet of courser and hussar.

definition: Epilepsy in which the attacks begins with an isolated disturbance of cerebral function (as a twitching of a limb or an illusory sensation or a mental disturbance).
Pertaining to the branch of astronomy dealing with the origin and history and structure and dynamics of the universe.
example: Cosmologic science.
etymology: From cosmology + -ical.

definition: An arbitrary constant in the equations of general relativity theory.
The metaphysical study of the origin and nature of the universe.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”).

definition: A small shelter for domestic animals (as sheep or pigeons).
etymology: From Middle English cote, from the Old English cote, the feminine form of cot (“small house”); doublet of cot (in the sense of “cottage”) and more distantly related to cottage. Cognate to Dutch kot.

definition: Someone who lives in a cottage.
A peasant farmer in the Scottish Highlands.
etymology: From Middle English cotter, cotere, kottere, koter, cotier, equivalent to cot (“cottage”) + -er, from Old English cot. Compare Old French coter, cotier.

definition: A cotter consisting of a split pin that is secured (after passing through a hole) by splitting the ends apart.
Any of several North American trees of the genus Populus having a tuft of cottony hairs on the seed.
etymology: From cotton + wood.

definition: A count who exercised royal authority in his own domain.
etymology: Calque of Medieval Latin comes palātīnus.

definition: The appearance conveyed by a person's face.
example: A pleasant countenance.
etymology: From Middle English contenaunce, countenaunce, from Anglo-Norman countenance and Old French contenance, from the present participle of contenir, or from Late Latin continentia, and therefore a doublet of continence.

definition: An attack by a defending force against an attacking enemy force in order to regain lost ground or cut off enemy advance units etc.
A strategy intended to prevent or counter terrorism.
A man from your own country.
etymology: From country + -man.

definition: The territory of a count palatine.
A smut fungus causing a smut disease of grains in which the spore masses are covered or held together by the grain membranes.
In a covert manner.
example: He did it covertly.
etymology: From Middle English covertli, equivalent to covert + -ly.

definition: Wish, long, or crave for (something, especially the property of another person).
example: She covets her sister's house.
etymology: From Middle English coveten, coveiten, coveyten, from Old French covoitier (modern French convoiter), from covoitié (“desire”), presumably modified from Latin cupiditas.

definition: A woman cowboy.
etymology: From cow + girl.

definition: Protective covering consisting of a metal part that covers the engine.
example: The mechanic removed the cowling in order to repair the plane's engine.
etymology: From Middle English coule, from Old English cūle, from earlier cugele (“hood, cowl”), from Ecclesiastical Latin cuculla (“monk's cowl”), from Latin cucullus (“hood”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of cagoule.

definition: Either of two flat triangular muscles of the shoulder and upper back that are involved in moving the shoulders and arms.
Shaped like a cowl.
Make a crackling sound.
example: My Rice Krispies crackled in the bowl.
etymology: From Middle English crakelen, equivalent to crack + -le (frequentative suffix). The physics sense is part of a facetious sequence "snap, crackle, pop", after the mascots of Rice Krispies cereal.

definition: Glazed china with a network of fine cracks on the surface.
The residue that remains after animal fat has been rendered.
example: The bangs and cracklings of fireworks.
etymology: By surface analysis, crackle + -ing.

definition: Of or relating to the cranium which encloses the brain.
example: Cranial pressure.
etymology: From cranium + -al. By surface analysis, crani- + -al.

definition: The cavity enclosed by the cranium.
Ratio (in percent) of the maximum breadth to the maximum length of a skull.
example: The width of the skull is 18 cm and the length 24 cm, so the cranial index is 75.

definition: Any of the 12 paired nerves that originate in the brain stem.
The bony cavity in the skull containing the eyeball.
A rotating shaft driven by (or driving) a crank.
etymology: From crank + shaft.

definition: (of persons) so unrefined as to be lacking in discrimination and sensibility.
etymology: From Middle English cras, craas, from Old French cras, from Latin crassus (“dense, thick, gross, fat, heavy”). Doublet of grease.

definition: Wanted intensely.
example: The child could no longer resist taking one of the craved cookies.

definition: A person who tries to please someone in order to gain a personal advantage.
etymology: From crawl (“to move slowly, by dragging the body along the ground”) + -er.

definition: Warm-water lobsters without claws; those from Australia and South Africa usually marketed as frozen tails; caught also in Florida and California.
etymology: Alteration (by folk etymological influence of fish) of Middle English crevis (whence modern dialectal crevis), from Old French crevice ("crayfish";

definition: A squeaking sound.
example: The creak of the floorboards gave him away.

definition: An amino acid that does not occur in proteins but is found in the muscle tissue of vertebrates both in the free form and as phosphocreatine; supplies energy for muscle contraction.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κρέας (kréas, “meat”) (genitive κρέατος (kréatos)) + -ine. Not related to create.

definition: The literal belief in the account of Creation given in the Book of Genesis.
example: Creationism denies the theory of evolution of species.
etymology: From creation + -ism.

definition: Credibility among young fashionable urban individuals.
A document attesting to the truth of certain stated facts.
example: May I see your credentials, please?
etymology: From Medieval Latin crēdentiālis (“giving authority”), from Latin crēdentia (“trust”).

definition: Any system of principles or beliefs.
example: Credo III is so beautiful!
etymology: Inherited from Middle English credo, from Old French credo, from Latin crēdō (“to believe”); doublet of creed.

definition: Low rhizomatous European carpeting plant having spikes of blue flowers; naturalized in parts of United States.
Aromatic dwarf shrub common on banks and hillsides in Europe; naturalized in United States.
Baked custard topped with caramel.
A skin cleanser that comes in a thick liquid form, similar in texture to a lotion.
Paper with a crinkled texture; usually colored and used for decorations.
example: The policeman wore crepe-soled shoes.
etymology: Borrowed from French crêpe, from Latin crispus. Doublet of crisp and crape.

definition: Ornamental shrub from eastern India commonly planted in the southern United States.
Tropical shrub having glossy foliage and fragrant nocturnal flowers with crimped or wavy corollas; northern India to Thailand.
Paper with a crinkled texture; usually colored and used for decorations.
Crude natural rubber; used mainly for shoe soles.
(music) gradually increasing in volume.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian crescendo, gerund of crescere (“to grow, to increase”).

definition: Bearing an heraldic device.
Small penguin of the Falkland Islands and New Zealand.
Birds of southeast Asia and East Indies differing from true swifts in having upright crests and nesting in trees.
A painful muscle spasm especially in the neck or back (‘rick’ and ‘wrick’ are British).
etymology: From Middle English crike, crykke (“muscular spasm of the neck”), attested since the 1400s. Likely related to Old Norse kriki (“bend; nook”), whence also crick (“creek”) and creek.

definition: Magenta tinged with crimson.
A bicycle race held on a short course (usually less than 5 km or 3 miles).
etymology: From criticism, critique, critical, criterium, and critical hit, by shortening.

definition: A regional term for ‘creature’ (especially for domestic animals).
etymology: First attested 1815, from a dialectal pronunciation of creature.

definition: Characterized by self-willed opposition.
Fertilization by transfer of pollen from the anthers of one flower to the stigma of another.
etymology: From cross- + pollination.

definition: A horizontal bar that goes across something.
etymology: From Middle English crose bar, equivalent to cross- + bar.

definition: A long racket with a triangular frame; used in playing lacrosse.
etymology: From French crosse (“stick”), of Germanic origin. Doublet of crutch.

definition: Long-tailed American blackbird having iridescent black plumage.
Common coucal of India and China.
A fungous disease of alfalfa which forms white excrescences at the base of the stem.
To a crucial degree.
example: Crucially important.
etymology: From crucial + -ly.

definition: Excessively.
example: A cruelly bitter winter.
etymology: From Middle English cruelly; equivalent to cruel + -ly.

definition: A very small quantity of something.
example: He gave only a crumb of information about his plans.
etymology: From Middle English crome, cromme, crumme, crume, from Old English cruma (“crumb, fragment”), from Proto-Germanic *krumô, *krūmô (“fragment, crumb”).

definition: Cake or coffeecake topped with a mixture of sugar and butter and flour.
etymology: From crumb + cake.

definition: Make a noise typical of an engine lacking lubricants.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: Of metal e.g.
example: A car with a crumpled front end.

definition: A wooden or metal staff that fits under the armpit and reaches to the ground; used by disabled person while walking.
example: He walked on crutches for a month until the cast was removed from his leg.

definition: Small South American spiny tree with dark crimson and scarlet flowers solitary or clustered.
Of or relating to very low temperatures.
etymology: From cryo- + -genic.

definition: Coloring that conceals or disguises an animal's shape.
Crossword puzzles in which each clue is a word puzzle in and of itself.
example: Many Canadian newspapers, including the Ottawa Citizen, Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail, carry cryptic crosswords.

definition: The science of analyzing and deciphering codes and ciphers and cryptograms.
example: We might abate...the strange cryptography of Gaffarell in his Starrie Booke of Heaven.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cryptographia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κρῠπτογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (krŭptogrăphĭ́ā). By surface analysis, crypto- + -graphy.

definition: An oscillator that produces electrical oscillations at a frequency determined by the physical characteristics of a piezoelectric quartz crystal.
A metric unit of volume equal to one thousandth of a liter.
A man whose wife committed adultery.
example: If I never marry, I shall never be a cuckold.
etymology: From Middle English cokolde, cokewold, cockewold, kukwald, kukeweld, from Old French cucuault; a compound of cucu (“cuckoo”) and Old French -auld.

definition: A passage with access only at one end.
Remove something that has been rejected.
example: Cull the sick members of the herd.
etymology: From Middle English cullen, cuilen, coilen, from Old French cuillir (“collect, gather, select”), from Latin colligō (“gather together”). Doublet of coil.

definition: Select desirable parts from a group or list.
example: Cull out the interesting letters from the poet's correspondence.

definition: Deserving blame or censure as being wrong or evil or injurious.
example: Culpable negligence.
etymology: From Middle English culpable, from Old French culpable, from Latin culpābilis (“blameworthy”), from culpō (“to blame, condemn”), from culpa (“a fault, crime, mistake”). Compare also culprit.

definition: With honor; with academic distinction.
example: A cum laude graduate.
etymology: From Latin cum (“with”) + laude (ablative of laus, "praise").

definition: Aromatic seeds of the cumin herb of the carrot family.
An inferior dog or one of mixed breed.
example: A fals double tunge is more fiers and fell Then Cerberus the cur couching in the kenel of hel; Wherof hereafter, I thinke for to write,.
etymology: From Middle English curre (“watchdog, small hunting dog, mongrel, mutt”), perhaps of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, possibly from Old Norse kurr (“grumbling”), itself of imitative origin.

definition: An edge between a sidewalk and a roadway consisting of a line of curbstones (usually forming part of a gutter).
A coagulated liquid resembling milk curd.
example: Lemon curd.
etymology: From Middle English curd, a metathetic variant of crud, crudde (“coagulated substance”). Doublet of crud.

definition: Of timber; having fibers running irregularly rather than in parallel.
A summary of your academic and work history.
etymology: From Latin curriculum (“course”) + vītae, genitive of vīta (“life”).

definition: Having successive letters joined together.
example: Cursive script.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

definition: Rapid handwriting in which letters are set down in full and are cursively connected within words without lifting the writing implement from the paper.
Hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough.
example: A casual (or cursory) inspection failed to reveal the house's structural flaws.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

definition: Place restrictions on.
example: Curtail drinking in school.
etymology: Alteration of curtal, from Old French courtault (“which has been shortened”), itself from court (“short”) (from Latin curtus) + -ault

definition: A safety device installed in cars that deploys by rapidly inflating to protect the head and provide rollover protection.
example: Curtain airbags have been said to reduce brain injury or fatalities by up to 45% in a side impact with an SUV.

definition: Any preliminary activity.
A persistently annoying person.
example: He's an abrupt-sounding cuss, but good-hearted too.
etymology: An American English variant of curse; for a similar phonetic development, compare ass (“buttocks”), from arse, in which the r was originally pronounced (as in curse).

definition: Relating to or existing on or affecting the skin.
example: Cutaneous nerves.
etymology: From New Latin cutaneus, from Latin cutis (“skin”).

definition: A sensation localized on the skin.
The faculty by which external objects or forces are perceived through contact with the body (especially the hands).
One of a number of veins in the subcutaneous tissue that empty into deep veins.
The quality of being appealing in a delicate or graceful way (of a girl or young woman).
etymology: From cute + -ness.

definition: A switch that interrupts an electric circuit in the event of an overload.
Ruthless in competition.
example: Cutthroat competition.
etymology: From cut + throat.

definition: A programmer who breaks into computer systems in order to steal or change or destroy information as a form of cyber-terrorism.
example: The film The Matrix redefined what a cyberpunk looked like.
etymology: From cyber- + -punk, coined by American writer and software developer Bruce Bethke as the title of a 1983 short story, and later popularized by Gardner Dozois.

definition: A computer network consisting of a worldwide network of computer networks that use the TCP/IP network protocols to facilitate data transmission and exchange.
A tricycle (usually propelled by pedalling); used in the Orient for transporting passengers for hire.
A machine for separating grain by kernel length.
Having a cylindrical stem.
Someone who is critical of the motives of others.
A mathematical element that when added to another number yields the same number.
A branch of the hepatic artery; supplies the gall bladder and the surface of the liver.
The most common hereditary disease; the child's lungs and intestines and pancreas become clogged with thick mucus; caused by defect in a single gene; no cure is known.
Vein that drains the gallbladder.
The protoplasm of a cell excluding the nucleus; is full of proteins that control cell metabolism.
etymology: Borrowed from German Zytoplasma, Cytoplasma. Equivalent to cyto- (“cell”) + -plasm (“contents of a cell”).

definition: An evil supernatural being.
etymology: A borrowing of Latin daemōn (“tutelary deity”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, tutelary deity”).

definition: Any of several plants of or developed from the species Dahlia pinnata having tuberous roots and showy rayed variously colored flower heads; native to the mountains of Mexico and Central America and Colombia.
etymology: Named 1791 after Anders Dahl, by Spanish botanist Antonio José Cavanilles.

definition: Behave carelessly or indifferently.
example: 2024, The November Nethack Tournament achievements Dally with a foocubus.
etymology: From Middle English dalien, from Anglo-Norman delaier. Doublet of delay.

definition: The act of damning.
etymology: From Middle English dampnacioun, from Old French dampnacion, from Latin damnatio.

definition: Suppress or constrain so as to lessen in intensity.
example: We won't let the bad news dampen our spirits.
etymology: From damp + -en.

definition: A movable iron plate that regulates the draft in a stove or chimney or furnace.
etymology: From damp (verb) + -er. The name of the type of bread is first attested in 1825, and originally likely refers to damping the appetite.

definition: Damper consisting of a small felted block that drops onto a piano string to stop its vibration.
A plant disease caused by a fungus; diseased condition of seedlings in excessive moisture.
A young unmarried woman.
etymology: From Middle English dameisele, from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, a diminutive from Classical Latin domina (“mistress, lady”), from dominus, from *demh₂-.

definition: Any of several herbs of the genus Taraxacum having long tap roots and deeply notched leaves and bright yellow flowers followed by fluffy seed balls.
etymology: From Middle English dentdelyon, from Old French dent de lion (“lion's tooth”), also in Latin dēns leōnis, referring to the jagged shape of the plant's leaves.

definition: The foliage of the dandelion plant.
Hang loosely.
example: The ornaments dangled from the tree.
etymology: Uncertain, but likely of North Germanic origin, akin to Danish dingle, dangle, Swedish dangla (“to swing about”), Norwegian dangla, perhaps via North Frisian dangeln; all possibly related to Old Norse dengja (“to hit”).

definition: Huckleberry of the eastern United States with pink flowers and sweet blue fruit.
Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners.
example: A dapper young man.
etymology: From Middle English daper (“pretty, neat”), from Middle Dutch dapper (“stalwart, nimble”), Old Dutch *dapar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz (“stout; solid; heavy;

definition: Become dark or darker.
example: The sky darkened.
etymology: From Middle English derkenen, dirkenen, from Old English *deorcnian, *diercnian (“to darken”), from Proto-West Germanic *dirkinōn (“to darken”), equivalent to dark + -en.

definition: Becoming dark or darker as from waning light or clouding over.
example: The darkening sky.

definition: Without light.
example: The river was sliding darkly under the mist.
etymology: From Middle English derkly, derkely, derkliche, derkeliche; equivalent to dark + -ly. Compare Old English deorclīċe, a parallel formation.

definition: A device resembling a sling that is used in various primitive societies to propel a dart or spear.
Formerly, the eldest son of the King of France and direct heir to the throne.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English Dauphin, from Middle French dauphin, from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís); the modern pronunciation is sometimes remodelled on Modern French.

definition: The first light of day.
etymology: From Middle English dawnynge, an alteration of dawing, under the influence of North Germanic cognates (compare Swedish, Danish dagning). See daw (“to dawn”).

definition: A laborer who works by the day; for daily wages.
A laborer who works by the day; for daily wages.
Have a daydream; indulge in a fantasy.
example: Stop daydreaming and get back to work!
etymology: From day + dream. Compare West Frisian deidream (“daydream”), Dutch dagdroom (“daydream”), German Tagtraum (“daydream”), Swedish dagdröm (“daydream”), Icelandic dagdraumur (“daydream”).

definition: Absentminded dreaming while awake.
The feeling of distress and disbelief that you have when something bad happens accidentally.
example: His mother's death left him in a daze.
etymology: From Middle English, back-formation from dazed. Compare Old Norse dasask (“to become weary”), with reflexive suffix -sk, Swedish dasa (“lie idly”), and Icelandic dasask (“to make weary with cold”).

definition: Having vision overcome temporarily by or as if by intense light.
example: She shut her dazzled eyes against the sun's brilliance.

definition: Elegant and sumptuous.
example: A deluxe car.
etymology: Borrowed from French de luxe.

definition: Deprive of energy.
etymology: From de- + energize.

definition: Remove from active military status or reassign.
example: The men were deactivated after five years of service.
etymology: From de- + activate.

definition: A situation in which no progress can be made or no advancement is possible.
example: The negotiation ended in deadlock, with neither party willing to compromise on the price.
etymology: From dead + lock.

definition: Loud enough to cause (temporary) hearing loss.
Partial or complete loss of hearing.
example: Their deafness to her cries.
etymology: From Middle English deefnesse; equivalent to deaf + -ness.

definition: An acute insufficiency.
etymology: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535).

definition: A wild gathering involving excessive drinking and promiscuity.
example: Life of debauchery.
etymology: From debauch + -ery. First use appears c. 1642.

definition: The exposure of falseness or pretensions.
example: The debunking of religion has been too successful.

definition: Having had the head cut off.
Damaged by decay; hence unsound and useless.
example: A decayed foundation.

definition: Involving deception.
example: Deceitful advertising.
etymology: From deceit + -ful.

definition: In a decent manner.
example: They don't know how to dress decently.
etymology: From decent + -ly.

definition: The social process in which population and industry moves from urban centers to outlying districts.
In a misleading way.
example: The exam looked deceptively easy.
etymology: From deceptive + -ly.

definition: A holly tree, also known as possumhaw or swamp holly.
One of the first temporary teeth of a young mammal (one of 20 in children).
Having had security classification removed.
The kind of intellectual who converts messages from a code to plain text.
etymology: From decode + -er.

definition: Separate (substances) into constituent elements or parts.
example: Various fungi can decompose wood.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French décomposer. Equivalent to de- + compose.

definition: Restoring compressed information to its normal form for use or display.
example: The decompression of large data files may take a while.
etymology: From de- + compression.

definition: Pain resulting from rapid change in pressure.
A philosophical theory of criticism (usually of literature or film) that seeks to expose deep-seated contradictions in a work by delving below its surface meaning.
etymology: From de- + construction or deconstruct + -ion.

definition: The removal of contaminants.
etymology: From de- + contamination.

definition: A person who specializes in interior decoration.
etymology: From decorate + -or.

definition: Propriety in manners and conduct.
example: It was sort of a finishing school. You know, to teach proper social decorum and so on and so forth.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin decōrum, neuter form of decōrus (“proper, decent”).

definition: Worn and broken down by hard use.
example: A decrepit bus … its seats held together with friction tape.
etymology: From Middle English decrepyt (ante 1439), from Middle French décrépit, from Latin dēcrepitus (“very old”), from crepō (“to creak”).

definition: Reason by deduction; establish by deduction.
example: To deduce a part from the whole.
etymology: From Late Middle English deducen (“to demonstrate, prove, show; to argue, infer; to bring, lead; to turn (something) to a use;

definition: A kitchen appliance for deep frying; its size depends on intended use.
example: Deep fryers are used for cooking many fast foods, and making them crisp.

definition: Thick in the chest.
example: A deep-chested breed of dog.

definition: (used of statements) harmful and often untrue; tending to discredit or malign.
example: Defamatory statement.
etymology: From Middle French diffamatoire (altered after the prefix de-), from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.

definition: Withdrawing support or help despite allegiance or responsibility.
example: Military defection.
etymology: From Latin dēfectiō (stem dēfectiōn-).

definition: Lacking protection or support.
example: A defenseless child.
etymology: From defence + -less.

definition: Capable of being defended.
etymology: From Old French defensable, from Latin defensibilem. Equivalent to defense + -ible.

definition: A courteous expression (by word or deed) of esteem or regard.
example: His deference to her wishes was very flattering.
etymology: From French déférence. Morphologically defer + -ence.

definition: Brought low in spirit.
example: Left us fatigued and deflated spiritually.

definition: (geology) the erosion of soil as a consequence of sand and dust and loose rocks being removed by the wind.
example: A constant deflation of the desert landscape.
etymology: From deflate + -ion.

definition: An affliction in which some part of the body is misshapen or malformed.
example: Congenital deformity.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English deformite, from Middle French deformite, from Latin dēfōrmitās (“deformity, ugliness”), from dēfōrmis (“deformed, ugly”) + -itās, from dē + fōrma (“shape, form”).

definition: Deprive of by deceit.
example: She defrauded the customers who trusted her.
etymology: From Middle English defrauden, from Old French defrauder, from de- + frauder.

definition: Skillful in physical movements; especially of the hands.
example: A deft waiter.
etymology: From Middle English defte, daft (“gentle”), from Old English dæfte (“mild, gentle, meek”), from Proto-West Germanic *daftī (“fitting, suitable”), derived from *dabaną (“to be suitable”).

definition: With dexterity; in a dexterous manner.
Remove the triggering device from.
example: The diplomats are trying to defuse the escalating crisis.
etymology: From de- + fuse.

definition: Chronic breakdown of cartilage in the joints; the most common form of arthritis occurring usually after middle age.
Condition leading to progressive loss of function.
The experience of thinking that a new situation had occurred before.
etymology: Borrowed from French déjà vu.

definition: Affected or marked by low spirits.
example: Is dejected but trying to look cheerful.
etymology: From deject + -ed.

definition: In a very pleasurable manner.
example: They were walking along the beach slowly and deliciously.
etymology: From delicious + -ly.

definition: In a delightful manner.
example: The farm house, though in itself a small one, is delightfully situated.
etymology: From delightful + -ly.

definition: Nonpayment of a debt when due.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin dēlinquentia, derived from Latin dēlinquēns, present participle of dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”). By surface analysis, delinquent + -cy

definition: Experiencing delirium.
example: Delirious with joy.
etymology: From delirium + -ous; see also Latin delirus (“silly, doting, crazy”).

definition: The boundary of a specific area.
example: There is an alleged, in fact somewhat artificial demarcation in the type of work done by members of different trade unions.

definition: The boundary of a specific area.
Causing awareness of your shortcomings.
example: Demeaning job.

definition: Affected with madness or insanity.
example: A demented idea.
etymology: Past participle of dement + -ed, from Latin dēmentāre.

definition: The action of making something democratic.
etymology: From democratiz(e) + -ation or democrat(ic) + -ization.

definition: The branch of sociology that studies the characteristics of human populations.
etymology: From demo- (“people”) + -graphy (“written representation of”) (From Ancient Greek δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) and Ancient Greek -γραφία (-graphía), from γραφή (graphḗ, “writing, drawing, description”)).

definition: Complete destruction of a building.
In an obvious and provable manner.
example: His documentary sources are demonstrably wrong.
etymology: From demonstrable + -ly. First attested in the early 17th century.

definition: A teacher or teacher's assistant who demonstrates the principles that are being taught.
etymology: From demonstrate + -or.

definition: An infectious disease of the tropics transmitted by mosquitoes and characterized by rash and aching head and joints.
An infectious disease of the tropics transmitted by mosquitoes and characterized by rash and aching head and joints.
etymology: Via Spanish, a corruption of Swahili ki denga pepo, meaning "cramp-like seizure caused by an evil spirit".

definition: Relating to or characteristic of a particular religious denomination.
example: Denominational politics.
etymology: From denomination + -al.

definition: An alloy of mercury with another metal (usually silver) used by dentists to fill cavities in teeth; except for iron and platinum all metals dissolve in mercury and chemists refer to the resulting mercury mixtures as amalgams.
Contingent on something else.
Being determined by conditions or circumstances that follow.
Being determined by conditions or circumstances that follow.
A facility where things can be deposited for storage or safekeeping.
A depository built to contain books and other materials for reading and study.
Moral perversion; impairment of virtue and moral principles.
example: Its brothels, its opium parlors, its depravity.

definition: Lower someone's spirits; make downhearted.
example: These news depressed her.
etymology: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).

definition: (historical linguistics) an explanation of the historical origins of a word or phrase.
Of or relating to a cuticle or cuticula.
example: Near-synonyms: epidermal, epidermo-.
etymology: From derm + -al. First attested in the early 19th century.

definition: Inflammation of the skin; skin becomes itchy and may develop blisters.
etymology: From New Latin dermatītis, from δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, flay”). By surface analysis, dermato- + -itis.

definition: The branch of medicine dealing with the skin and its diseases.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”) + -logy. Analysable as dermato- + -logy.

definition: The removal of salt (especially from sea water).
etymology: From de- + salination.

definition: The descending part of the aorta that branches into the thoracic and abdominal aortae.
The phonological or orthographic sound or appearance of a word that can be used to describe or identify something.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēscrīptōris. Compare describe.

definition: The action of incorporating a racial or religious group into a community.
etymology: From de- + segregation.

definition: Withdrawing support or help despite allegiance or responsibility.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French désertion. By surface analysis, desert + -ion.

definition: As deserved.
example: He chalked up two goals which deservedly gave Bolton their second victory of the season.
etymology: From deserved + -ly.

definition: Become unstable.
example: The economy destabilized rapidly.
etymology: From de- + stabilize.

definition: Destroy (one's own missile or rocket).
example: The engineers had to destruct the rocket for safety reasons.
etymology: Originally a learned borrowing from Latin dēstrūct-, the perfect passive participial stem of dēstruō (“to destroy”). In modern use, probably in part a back-formation from destruction.

definition: Cause to become detached or separated; take off.
example: Detach the skin from the chicken before you eat it.
etymology: From Old French destachier, from the same root as attach; compare French détacher and Portuguese and Spanish destacar.

definition: Designed to be unfastened or disconnected without damage.
example: Shirts with detachable collars.
etymology: From French détachable, detach + -able.

definition: Some held in custody.
etymology: From detain + -ee.

definition: (philosophy) a philosophical theory holding that all events are inevitable consequences of antecedent sufficient causes; often understood as denying the possibility of free will.
etymology: Borrowed from French déterminisme, equivalent to determine + -ism.

definition: A negative motivational influence.
example: The policy relies on nuclear deterrence.
etymology: From the stem of deterrent + -ence.

definition: Dislike intensely; feel antipathy or aversion towards.
example: She detests politicians.

definition: Cause to burst with a violent release of energy.
example: The engineers detonated the dynamite and watched the old building collapse.
etymology: First attested in 1729; either borrowed from French détoner or directly from Latin dētonātus, perfect passive participle of dētonō (“to thunder down (strongly);

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of one and one and one.
An official lowering of a nation's currency; a decrease in the value of a country's currency relative to that of foreign countries.
etymology: From de- + valuation.

definition: Lowered in value.
example: The worth of citizenship is devalued when information is censored.

definition: Showing the cunning or ingenuity or wickedness typical of a devil.
example: Devilish schemes.
etymology: From Middle English develissh, develyssh, equivalent to devil + -ish.

definition: The act that results in something coming to be.
example: The devising of plans.

definition: Pass on or delegate to another.
example: The representative devolved his duties to his aides while he was in the hospital.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēvolvō (“roll or tumble off or down”), from dē- + volvō (“roll”).

definition: Be contingent on.
An ardent follower and admirer.
example: He was a devotee of Arnold Schwarzenegger.
etymology: From devote + -ee. The narrowed meaning in sense 3 arises from the sound similarity with amputee.

definition: (often followed by ‘for’) ardently or excessively desirous.
example: Fierce devouring affection.

definition: Diabetes caused by a relative or absolute deficiency of insulin and characterized by polyuria.
example: When doctors say ‘diabetes’ they usually mean ‘diabetes mellitus’.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).

definition: Showing the cunning or ingenuity or wickedness typical of a devil.
