example: The cold calculation and diabolic art of some statesmen.
etymology: From diabolic + -al.

definition: In a diagonal manner.
example: She lives diagonally across the street from us.
etymology: From Middle English diagonaly, modeled on Medieval Latin diagōnāliter; equivalent to diagonal + -ly.

definition: A claim of rights.
example: I have dibs on that last slice of pizza.
etymology: Since the early 19th century, of disputed origin. Most commonly thought to be from dibstones (“counters used in a game with the same name”).

definition: A small third seat in the back of an old-fashioned two-seater.
etymology: From Dickey.

definition: Small bird; adults talking to children sometimes use these words to refer to small birds.
A small third seat in the back of an old-fashioned two-seater.
A small third seat in the back of an old-fashioned two-seater.
A small third seat in the back of an old-fashioned two-seater.
Of or characteristic of a dictator.
example: Dictatorial powers.
etymology: From dictator + -ial.

definition: One who adheres to traditional views.
etymology: Deverbal from die hard.

definition: A material such as glass or porcelain with negligible electrical or thermal conductivity.
etymology: From dia- (“through”) + electric. Learned 19th-century formation, coined by William Whewell (died 1866).

definition: Heating of an insulator by a high-frequency electric field.
An analog computer designed to solve differential equations.
Optical device consisting of a surface with many parallel grooves in it; disperses a beam of light (or other electromagnetic radiation) into its wavelengths to produce its spectrum.
A cluster of stars within an intricate cloud of gas and dust.
Baffle that distributes sound waves evenly.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Solitary wasp that digs nests in the soil and stocks them with paralyzed insects for the larvae.
Lose clarity or turn aside especially from the main subject of attention or course of argument in writing, thinking, or speaking.
example: She always digresses when telling a story.
etymology: From Latin digressum, past participle of digredi.

definition: A lengthy discussion (spoken or written) on a particular topic.
etymology: From dilate + -ion, late 16th c.

definition: Pickle preserved in brine or vinegar flavored with dill seed.
etymology: From dill + pickle.

definition: In a dim indistinct manner.
example: We perceived the change only dimly.
etymology: From dim + -ly.

definition: Made dim or less bright.
example: The dimmed houselights brought a hush of anticipation.

definition: A small boat of shallow draft with cross thwarts for seats and rowlocks for oars with which it is propelled.
etymology: From Bengali ডিঙি (ḍiṅi), perhaps from Sanskrit द्रोण (droṇa, “wooden trough”).

definition: Wolflike yellowish-brown wild dog of Australia.
etymology: Borrowed from Dharug dingu (“tame or domesticated dingo”).

definition: Thickly covered with ingrained dirt or soot.
example: Dingy linen.
etymology: From ding + -y.

definition: A pail in which a workman carries their lunch or dinner.
Belonging to or governing a diocese.
etymology: From Middle French diocesain.

definition: A pair of equal and opposite electric charges or magnetic poles separated by a small distance.
etymology: From di- + pole.

definition: An aerial half a wavelength long consisting of two rods connected to a transmission line at the center.
A molecule that is a permanent dipole.
The moment of a dipole.
A ladle that has a cup with a long handle.
A distributor who uses direct mail to sell merchandise.
Discontented as toward authority.
etymology: From disaffect + -ed.

definition: Capable of allaying hostility.
example: A disarming smile.

definition: A mental state characterized by a lack of clear and orderly thought and behavior.
etymology: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).

definition: Cause to break up or cease to function.
example: The principal disbanded the political student organization.
etymology: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). By surface analysis, dis- + band.

definition: Perceptible by the senses or intellect.
example: Things happen in the earth and sky with no discernible cause.
etymology: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

definition: The cognitive condition of someone who understands.
etymology: From Middle French discernement, equivalent to discern + -ment.

definition: A soiled or discolored appearance.
etymology: From discolor + -ation.

definition: Causing an emotional disturbance.
example: His disconcerting habit of greeting friends ferociously and strangers charmingly.
etymology: From disconcert + -ing.

definition: An athletic competition in which a disk-shaped object is thrown as far as possible.
etymology: 1656. From Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, dish, disk, and diskos.

definition: Deprived of the rights of citizenship especially the right to vote.
example: Disenfranchised masses took to the streets.

definition: Release from something that holds fast, connects, or entangles.
example: I want to disengage myself from his influence.
etymology: From Middle French désengager; from dis- + engage.

definition: Having the appearance spoiled.
example: A disfigured face.

definition: Made less hopeful or enthusiastic.
example: The disheartened instructor tried vainly to arouse their interest.
etymology: From the verb hearten.

definition: Destructive of morale and self-reliance.
Bring shame or dishonor upon.
example: He dishonored his family by committing a serious crime.
etymology: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honor.

definition: A low-sudsing detergent designed for use in dishwashers.
Freeing from false belief or illusions.
etymology: From dis- + illusion + -ment.

definition: Preventing infection by inhibiting the growth or action of microorganisms.
example: I washed repeatedly with a disinfectant soap but I still caught the flu.
etymology: From disinfect + -ant, borrowed from French désinfectant.

definition: Misinformation that is deliberately disseminated in order to influence or confuse rivals (foreign enemies or business competitors etc.).
etymology: Composed of dis- + information. Attested in the sense “intentional misinformation” in English from 1939. A different usage of disinformation occurred earlier, as early as 1887, as a simple synonym of misinformation.

definition: Not straightforward or candid; giving a false appearance of frankness.
example: An ambitious, disingenuous, philistine, and hypocritical operator, who … exemplified … the most disagreeable traits of his time.
etymology: From dis- + ingenuous.

definition: Break into parts or components or lose cohesion or unity.
example: The material disintegrated.
etymology: Recorded since 1785, from dis- + integrate.

definition: Unaffected by self-interest.
etymology: From disinterest (“to cause to be impartial”, verb) + -ed (suffix forming past tense or past participle forms of verbs), or from dis- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + interested (“having a stake in; showing interest”, adjective).

definition: Lacking orderly continuity.
example: The hours of his illness were disjointed and confusing as he drifted in and out of consciousness.

definition: An event that results in a displacement or discontinuity.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dislocātiō, delocatio.

definition: Remove or force out from a position.
example: The dentist dislodged the piece of food that had been stuck under my gums.
etymology: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

definition: Showing lack of love for your country.
etymology: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman desleal, desloial, equivalent to dis- + loyal.

definition: Struck with fear, dread, or consternation.
example: He was dismayed to find his car had gone.

definition: Refuse to go along with; refuse to follow; be disobedient.
example: He disobeyed his supervisor and was fired.
etymology: From Old French desobeir.

definition: Thrown into a state of disarray or confusion.
example: The small disordered room.

definition: Having lost your bearings; confused as to time or place or personal identity.
example: I frequently find myself disoriented when I come up out of the subway.
etymology: From dis- + oriented or disorient + -ed.

definition: Expressive of low opinion.
example: Disparaging remarks about the new house.

definition: An exemption from some rule or obligation.
example: A fair dispensation of money.
etymology: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. By surface analysis, dispens(e) + -ation.

definition: Distributed or weighted out in carefully determined portions.
example: Medicines dispensed to the sick.

definition: (of colloids) a substance in which another is colloidally dispersed.
(of colloids) a substance in which another is colloidally dispersed.
Cause to move, usually with force or pressure.
example: The refugees were displaced by the war.
etymology: From Middle French desplacer (French: déplacer).

definition: Not pleased; experiencing or manifesting displeasure.
example: A displeased customer.

definition: Physically or spiritually homeless or deprived of security.
example: Made a living out of shepherding dispossessed people from one country to another.

definition: Prove to be false.
example: The physicist disproved his colleagues' theories.
etymology: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

definition: Make unfit or unsuitable.
example: Your income disqualifies you.
etymology: From dis- + qualify.

definition: In spite of everything; without regard to drawbacks.
In need of repairs; in need of repair.
example: The sewing machine is in disrepair.
etymology: From dis- + repair.

definition: Having one or more indentations reaching nearly to the midrib.
A chronic progressive nervous disorder involving loss of myelin sheath around certain nerve fibers.
An act intended to help that turns out badly.
example: He did them a disservice.
etymology: From dis- + service.

definition: To cause to separate and go in different directions.
example: August 1773, James Cook, journal entry I soon dissipated his fears.
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765;

definition: Breaking up and scattering by dispersion.
example: The dissipation of the mist.
etymology: From Middle English dissipacion, dissipacioun, from Late Latin dissipātiō. Morphologically dissipate + -ion.

definition: The act of removing from association.
example: The dissociation of the sulphur molecules.
etymology: Borrowed from French dissociation, from Latin dissociātiō(n).

definition: The equilibrium constant for a reversible dissociation.
The energy needed to break every chemical bond in a molecule and completely separate all its atoms.
A feeling of intense dislike.
etymology: From dis- + taste.

definition: Not pleasing in odor or taste.
example: The food had very distasteful flavour.
etymology: From distaste + -ful or dis- + tasteful.

definition: In an identifiably distinctive manner.
example: The distinctively conservative district of the county.
etymology: From distinctive + -ly.

definition: Capable of being perceived as different or distinct.
example: Only the shine of their metal was distinguishable in the gloom.
etymology: From distinguish + -able.

definition: No longer in use.
The shorter of the two telegraphic signals used in Morse code.
etymology: From Middle English ditten, dutten, from Old English dyttan (“to stop up, close”), from Proto-West Germanic *duttijan, from Proto-Germanic *duttijaną, from *duttaz (“wisp”), akin to Icelandic dytta.

definition: Move or draw apart.
example: The two paths diverge here.
etymology: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

definition: Take away possessions from someone.
example: You shall never divest me of my right to free speech.
etymology: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

definition: A taxonomist who classifies organisms into many groups on the basis of relatively minor characteristics.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From divide + -er.

definition: Successful conjecture by unusual insight or good luck.
etymology: From Old French divination, from Latin divinatio.

definition: Make known to the public information that was previously known only to a few people or that was meant to be kept a secret.
example: I will never divulge that secret to anyone.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).

definition: Willing to be taught or led or supervised or directed.
example: The docile masses of an enslaved nation.
etymology: From Middle English docyle, from Middle French docile, from Latin docilis, from docēre (“teach”).

definition: A laborer who loads and unloads vessels in a port.
etymology: From dock (verb) + -er.

definition: (law) the calendar of a court; the list of cases to be tried or a summary of the court's activities.
etymology: Uncertain; perhaps a diminutive of dock.

definition: Relating to or involving or preoccupied with doctrine.
example: Quibbling over doctrinal minutiae.
etymology: The noun form was from French doctrinal; the adjective form was perhaps from Late Latin doctrīnālis, from doctrīna.

definition: Someone whose style is out of fashion.
etymology: Uncertain. Perhaps from obsolete Portuguese doudo (“fool, simpleton, silly, stupid”) or Dutch dodaars. First attested in the 17th century.

definition: Weedy plant of southeastern United States having divided leaves and long clusters of greenish flowers.
A sled pulled by dogs.
Worn or shabby from overuse or (of pages) from having corners turned down.
example: A somewhat dog-eared duke … a bit run down.
etymology: From dog + eared (“having ears (of a specified type)”), modelled after dog’s-ear (obsolete), due to the similarity of their appearance to the folded ears of certain dogs.

definition: Formerly the chief magistrate in the republics of Venice and Genoa.
etymology: Partly from Middle French doge and partly from its etymon, Italian doge, from Venetan doxe, from Latin ducem, accusative of dux (“leader; commander; ruler”). Doublet of duc, duce, duke, and dux.

definition: Stubbornly unyielding.
example: Dogged persistence.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: A bag for food that a customer did not eat at a restaurant; the transparent pretense is that the food is taken home to feed the customer's dog.
Quietly in concealment.
example: He lay doggo.
etymology: The noun is from dog + -o (colloquializing suffix), perhaps after the adverb. The adverb is probably of the same origin.

definition: Characterized by assertion of unproved or unprovable principles.
etymology: From Middle French dogmatique and its etymon, Late Latin dogmaticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós, “didactic”), from δόγμα (dógma, “dogma”).

definition: The syllable naming the first (tonic) note of any major scale in solmization.
etymology: An anglicised spelling of do.

definition: A house so small that it is likened to a child's plaything.
etymology: From doll + house.

definition: Having a hemispherical vault or dome.
example: A domed hill.
etymology: From dome + -ed.

definition: A stadium that has a roof.
A domesticated gallinaceous bird thought to be descended from the red jungle fowl.
Used in the Andes as a beast of burden and source of wool; considered a domesticated variety of the guanaco.

(law) the residence where you have your permanent home or principal establishment and to where, whenever you are absent, you intend to return; every person is compelled to have one and only one domicile at a time.
example: The call to jury duty was sent to my legal domicile; too bad I was on vacation at the time.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

definition: An allele that produces the same phenotype whether its paired allele is identical or different.
Any of several games played with small rectangular blocks.
A machine used to fry large quantities of doughnuts at once.

A genre (usually a cappella) of Black vocal-harmony music of the 1950s that evolved in New York City from gospel singing; characterized by close four-part harmonies; the name derived from some of the nonsense syllables sung by the backup.
etymology: Coined by DJ Gus Gossert in the 1970s, referring to (mostly) white rock-and-roll groups of the late 1950s and early 1960s. The name is onomatopoeic, representing the nonlexical backing vocals of some songs of the genre.

definition: A man who guards an entrance.
etymology: From door + -man.

definition: Treated or impregnated with a foreign substance.
example: He was so doped after the surgery that it took him 2 hours to remember his name.

definition: To shoot two strokes over par.
Someone who draws two incomes from the government (usually by combining a salary and a pension).
A character used in printing to indicate a third cross reference or footnote after the asterisk and the dagger have been used.
Splitting a ray into two parallel rays polarized perpendicularly.
(golf) a score of two strokes over par for a hole.
A machine used to fry large quantities of doughnuts at once.
Lofty douglas fir of northwestern North America having short needles and egg-shaped cones.
A widow holding property received from her deceased husband.
example: A reclusive dowager owned the pastures across the river, and her farmhands ran beef cattle on them.
etymology: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).

definition: Represent as less significant or important.
etymology: Synthetic form of the phrase play down. By surface analysis, down- + play.

definition: A heavy rain.
example: They got caught in a downpour without an umbrella and came back soaked.
etymology: From down- + pour. Compare typologically Czech liják, Polish ulewa, Slovene naliv, Russian ли́вень (lívenʹ) (akin to лить (litʹ)).

definition: The reduction of expenditures in order to become financially stable.
example: He was excessed in the last downsizing.
etymology: From downsize + -ing.

definition: Sloping down rather steeply.
Someone who writes plays.
etymology: From the stem of Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma) + -ist.

definition: A pleasing country existing only in dreams or imagination.
etymology: From dream + -land.

definition: Maneuvers of a horse in response to body signals by the rider.
example: I'm competing in two dressages and a jumping show this weekend.
etymology: Borrowed from French dressage (“training”).

definition: The propulsion of a ball by repeated taps or kicks.
Apricots preserved by drying.
Small fruit fly used by Thomas Hunt Morgan in studying basic mechanisms of inheritance.
etymology: From taxonomic name Drosophila.

definition: A stonemason's chisel with a broad edge for dressing stone.
Half asleep.
example: Made drowsy by the long ride.
etymology: From drowse + -y, despite the fact that drowsy (1520) is recorded before drowse (1570). Compare Old English drūsian (“to droop, drowse, become languid”).

definition: A power tool used for sanding wood; an endless loop of sandpaper is moved at high speed by an electric motor.
A temporary state resulting from excessive consumption of alcohol.
etymology: From drunken + -ness.

definition: The condition of not containing or being covered by a liquid (especially water).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dryenesse, drynesse; equivalent to dry + -ness.

definition: A wide flat board used to cover walls or partitions; made from plaster or wood pulp or other materials and used primarily to form the interior walls of houses.
etymology: From dry + wall.

definition: A highway divided down the middle by a barrier that separates traffic going in different directions.
example: In Britain they call a divided highway a ‘dual carriageway’.

definition: A new soundtrack that is added to a film.
A pate made from duck liver.
An instrument of punishment consisting of a chair in which offenders were ducked in water.
Someone who is unsuccessful.
example: I got stuck with a seatmate who was a conversational dud.
etymology: From Middle English dudde (“cloak, mantle, kind of cloth;

definition: A canoe made by hollowing out and shaping a large log.
As if struck dumb with astonishment and surprise.
example: A circle of policemen stood dumbfounded by her denial of having seen the accident.

definition: A person who is tricked or swindled.
etymology: From French duper, from Middle French duppe, alteration of huppe (“hoopoe”), from Latin, onomatopoeic.

definition: Lighted by or as if by twilight.
example: The dusky night rides down the sky / And ushers in the morn.
etymology: From dusk + -y.

definition: Relatively slender blue-grey shark; nearly worldwide in tropical and temperate waters.
Having a dark color.
Having a dark color.
A windstorm that lifts up clouds of dust or sand.
example: It was the kind of duster not experienced in years.

definition: A soft quilt usually filled with the down of the eider.
example: He pulled the thick duvet over his head to block out the morning light.

definition: A spreading shrub with pink flowers; found in southeastern United States.
Small yellow-flowered herb resembling dandelions of central and southeastern United States.
A person who inhabits a particular place.
example: The new couple are apartment dwellers.
etymology: From Middle English dweller, equivalent to dwell + -er.

definition: The use of dye to change the color of something permanently.
A loudspeaker that uses a lightweight diaphragm connected to a rigid basket via a flexible suspension that constrains a voice coil to move axially through a cylindrical magnetic gap.
Characterized by action or forcefulness or force of personality.
example: A dynamic market.

definition: (physics) a phase space together with a transformation of that space.
Any of the various theories or doctrines or philosophical systems that attempt to explain the phenomena of the universe in terms of some immanent force or energy.
example: The fact that the war is no longer the main issue in the election points to the dynamism of foreign affairs.
etymology: From English dynam(ic) (or directly from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”)) + ism.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of a dynasty.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δυναστικός (dunastikós). By surface analysis, dynasty + -ic.

definition: An infection of the intestines marked by severe diarrhea.
etymology: From Middle English dissenterie, from Old French dissenterie, from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”).

definition: Any of several hereditary diseases of the muscular system characterized by weakness and wasting of skeletal muscles.
etymology: From dys- + -trophy, literally “bad growth”, as in the opposite of growth.

definition: A positive feeling of wanting to push ahead with something.
etymology: From Middle English egernesse, egrenesse; equivalent to eager + -ness.

definition: Worn or shabby from overuse or (of pages) from having corners turned down.
example: A somewhat dog-eared duke … a bit run down.
etymology: From ear + -ed.

definition: Pinniped mammal having external ear flaps and hind limbs used for locomotion on land; valued for its soft underfur.
Someone who earn wages in return for their labor.
example: Those Japanese radios were a nice little earner: we sold all of them by lunchtime.
etymology: From earn + -er.

definition: In a serious manner.
example: Talking earnestly with his son.
etymology: From Middle English ernestly, from Old English eornostlīċe (“earnestly, strictly”), equivalent to earnest + -ly.

definition: Made of earth (or baked clay).
example: An earthen pot.
etymology: From Middle English erthen, urthen, from Old English eorþen, yrþen, ierþen (“made of earth”), from Proto-Germanic *irþīnaz. Cognate with Dutch aarden (“earthen”), German irden (“earthen”).

definition: (law) the privilege of using something that is not your own (as using another's land as a right of way to your own land).
example: The power company has an easement to put their electricity poles along the edge of this land.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman aisement, easement, eisement, esament, esement, and Middle French aisement (“comfort, convenience, ease, facility, opportunity; a benefit, relief; a right to use land, a thing, etc.;

definition: Lying in or toward the east.
example: Eastern cities.
etymology: From easter + -ly.

definition: Long-haired chimpanzees of east-central Africa; closely related to the central chimpanzees.
Common forest tree of the eastern United States and Canada; used especially for pulpwood.
Of the eastern part of a city e.g. Manhattan.
example: The eastside silk-stocking district.
etymology: From east + side.

definition: A building where people go to eat.
etymology: From eat + -ery.

definition: The overhang at the lower edge of a roof.
etymology: From eave + -s, from a misinterpretation of the -s ending of eaves as forming a plural.

definition: Strange and unconventional behavior.
example: For an ellipse, the eccentricity is the ratio of the distance from the center to a focus divided by the length of the semi-major axis.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin eccentricitās. By surface analysis, eccentric + -ity.

definition: Status in a society or organization.
example: The upper echelon.
etymology: Borrowed from French échelon (“rung; echelon”), from échelle (“ladder”) + -on (diminutive suffix).

definition: With respect to ecology.
example: Ecologically speaking, this idea is brilliant; economically, it is a disaster.
etymology: From ecological + -ly.

definition: Punishment of a group by cutting off commercial dealings with them.
example: The economic strangulation of the Jews by the Nazi Party.

definition: Swelling from excessive accumulation of watery fluid in cells, tissues, or serous cavities.
example: Dependent edema.
etymology: From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

definition: A structure that has a roof and walls and stands more or less permanently in one place.
example: It was an imposing edifice.
etymology: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).

definition: In an unnatural eery manner.
example: It was eerily quiet in the chapel.
etymology: From eerie + -ly. Compare Old English earglīċe, earhlīċe (“in a cowardly manner, timidly, fearfully”).

definition: A representation of a person (especially in the form of sculpture).
example: The coin bears an effigy of Lincoln.
etymology: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).

definition: Characteristic of those having an inflated idea of their own importance.
etymology: From egotistic + -al.

definition: An abrupt emphatic exclamation expressing emotion.
etymology: From French éjaculation, borrowed from Latin ēiaculārī.

definition: Put out or expel from a place.
example: The man started a fight and was ejected from the bar.
etymology: From Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus, perfect passive participle of ēiciō (“to throw out”), or from ēiectō, the frequentative form of the same verb, from ē-, combining form of ex (“out”), + iaciō (“to throw”).

definition: With elaboration.
example: It was elaborately spelled out.
etymology: From elaborate + -ly.

definition: Addition of extra material or illustration or clarifying detail.
example: An elaboration of the sketch followed.
etymology: From Middle French élaboration. Morphologically elaborate + -ion.

definition: A feeling of strong eagerness (usually in favor of a person or cause).
(biology) a hypothetical force (not physical or chemical) once thought by Henri Bergson to cause the evolution and development of organisms.
(of time) having passed or slipped by.
example: Elapsed time.

definition: The time that elapses while some event is occurring.
example: With a bit of tuning, these cars can run 12-second ETs (elapsed times).

definition: Exultantly proud and joyful; in high spirits.
example: The elated winner.
etymology: Latin elatus (“raised”).

definition: A citizen who has a legal right to vote.
etymology: From Middle English electour (“one with a right to vote in electing some office, elector”), borrowed from Late Latin ēlēctor (“chooser, selector;

definition: A dipole with equal and opposite electric charges.
Receptacle providing a place in a wiring system where current can be taken to run electrical devices.
A power tool used for sanding wood; an endless loop of sandpaper is moved at high speed by an electric motor.
A razor powered by an electric motor.
An electrical device characterized by its capacity to store an electric charge.
The passage of electricity through a conductor.
A conductor having low resistance in parallel with another device to divert a fraction of the current.
Causing a surge of emotion or excitement.
example: She gave an electrifying performance.

definition: Of or involving electrochemistry.
etymology: From electro- + chemical.

definition: A serial arrangement of metallic elements or ions according to their electrode potentials determined under specified conditions; the order shows the tendency of one metal to reduce the ions of any other metal below it in the series.
Concerned with or producing or caused by static electricity.
example: An electrostatic generator produces high-voltage static electricity.
etymology: From electro- + static.

definition: A chemical bond in which one atom loses an electron to form a positive ion and the other atom gains an electron to form a negative ion.
The electric charge at rest on the surface of an insulated body (which establishes and adjacent electrostatic field).
Electric field associated with static electric charges.
Electrical device that produces a high voltage by building up a charge of static electricity.
A printer that uses an electric charge to deposit toner on paper.
Any of various units of electricity based on forces of interaction between electric charges.
With elegance; in a tastefully elegant manner.
example: The room was elegantly decorated.
etymology: From elegant + -ly.

definition: Annual of southern United States to Mexico having large whitish or yellowish flowers mottled with purple and a long curving beak.
Called forth from a latent or potential state by stimulation.
example: An elicited response.

definition: An extension at the end and at right angles to the main building.
etymology: From Middle English elle, elne, from Old English eln (“the length of the forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger;

definition: A rod an ell long, used for official measurement.
example: Edward I of England required that every town has at least one ell-wand.

definition: (of a leaf shape) in the form of an ellipse.
example: Elliptic integral.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”). By surface analysis, ellipse + -tic.

definition: (mathematics) a non-Euclidean geometry that regards space as like a sphere and a line as like a great circle.
example: Bernhard Riemann pioneered elliptic geometry.

definition: A simple leaf shaped like an ellipse.
(of a leaf shape) long and narrow.
example: Painted turtles lay oval, elongate eggs.
etymology: From Late Middle English elongat, elongate (“kept away; different or remote in nature”, adjective), borrowed from Late Latin ēlongātus (“having been stretched out, elongated; prolonged, protracted;

definition: A long slender leaf.
Powerful and effective language.
example: His eloquence attracted a large congregation.
etymology: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from Latin.

definition: With eloquence.
example: He expressed his ideas eloquently.
etymology: From Middle English eloquently, eloquentely, equivalent to eloquent + -ly.

definition: Escape, either physically or mentally.
example: The thief eluded the police.
etymology: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”, short form of ex-) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).

definition: Causing embarrassment.
example: The great man was embarrassingly humble and self-effacing.
etymology: From embarrassing + -ly.

definition: (of a person) beset by difficulties or conflict.
example: The state legislature called for the embattled governor's resignation.
etymology: From embattle (“to equip as for battle”) + -ed.

definition: Fix or set securely or deeply.
example: To embed something in clay, mortar, or sand.
etymology: From em- + bed.

definition: A hot fragment of wood or coal that is left from a fire and is glowing or smoldering.
etymology: From Middle English embre, eymbre, aymer, eymere, emeri, from Old English ǣmyrġe, from Proto-West Germanic *aimuʀjā, from Proto-Germanic *aimuzjǭ, a compound of *aimaz + *uzjǭ.

definition: Serving as a visible symbol for something abstract.
example: A crown is emblematic of royalty.
etymology: From French emblématique. See emblem.

definition: Made bold or courageous.
An insertion into a calendar.
etymology: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow.

definition: Embellished with a raised pattern created by pressure or embroidery.
example: An embossed satin.

definition: Deeply involved especially in something complicated.
example: Embroiled in the conflict.

definition: Vigorous Philippine evergreen twining liana; grown for spectacular festoons of green flowers that resemble lobster claws.
Leave one's country of residence for a new one.
example: Many people had to emigrate during the Nazi period.
etymology: From Latin emigratus, perfect passive participle of emigro (“to move away, remove, depart from a place”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + migro (“to move, remove, depart”).

definition: In an eminent manner.
example: Two subjects on which he was eminently qualified to make an original contribution.
etymology: From eminent + -ly.

definition: The domain controlled by an emir.
etymology: From emir + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it).

definition: Someone sent on a mission to represent the interests of someone else.
etymology: From French émissaire, from Latin emissarius (“agent, scout, spy”).

definition: One of several connecting veins in the scalp and head that drain blood from sinuses in the dura mater to veins outside the skull.
The electrode in a transistor where electrons originate.
etymology: From emit + -er.

definition: Characterized by emotion.
Showing empathy or ready comprehension of others' states.
example: A sensitive and empathetic school counselor.
etymology: Derived from empathic, modified to sound more similar to sympathetic.

definition: Be understanding of.
example: Empathize with someone.

definition: In an empirical manner.
example: This can be empirically tested.
etymology: From empirical + -ly.

definition: A large retail store organized into departments offering a variety of merchandise; commonly part of a retail chain.
example: With a name like “The Wine and Spirits Emporium”, no wonder the prices are so high.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station; business district in a city; market town”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “factory, trading station; market”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant, trader;

definition: Someone who copies the words or behavior of another.
(chemistry) a colloid in which both phases are liquids.
example: An oil-in-water emulsion.
etymology: Borrowed from French émulsion, from New Latin ēmulsiō, ēmulsiōnis, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).

definition: Marked by foolish or unreasoning fondness.
example: Narcissus was a beautiful Greek youth who became enamored of his own reflection.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English enamoured, a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer; compare amour and enamor, enamour.

definition: A site where people on holiday can pitch a tent.
etymology: PIE word *h₁én From encamp (“to establish a camp or temporary shelter”) + -ment (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or their results).

definition: Inflammation of the brain usually caused by a virus; symptoms include headache and neck pain and drowsiness and nausea and fever (‘phrenitis’ is no longer in scientific use).
etymology: From encephal- + -itis.

definition: A feeling of great liking for something wonderful and unusual.
etymology: From Middle English enchauntement, from Old French enchantement.

definition: Confined on all sides.
example: The encircled pioneers.

definition: Enclose or enfold completely with or as if with a covering.
example: To enclose lands.

definition: The act of enclosing something inside something else.
Convert information into code.
example: Encode pictures digitally.
etymology: From en- + code.

definition: Gradually intrusive without right or permission.
example: We moved back from the encroaching tide.

definition: Any entry into an area not previously occupied.
etymology: From encroach + -ment.

definition: Having a hardened crust as a covering.
Convert ordinary language into code.

A reference work (often in several volumes) containing articles on various topics (often arranged in alphabetical order) dealing with the entire range of human knowledge or with some particular specialty.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia; the English word is an etymologically restored spelling variant of earlier encyclopedia, q.v.

definition: Any of the glands of the endocrine system that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
The branch of medicine dealing with the endocrine glands and their secretions.
etymology: From French endocrinologie, or endocrine + -ology.

definition: Of or resembling an endogen.
etymology: From endogen + -ous or endo- + -genous. Piecewise doublet of indigenous.

definition: A place where something ends or is complete.
etymology: From end + point.

definition: In an energetic manner.
example: Reiki attempts to heal the body energetically.
etymology: From energetic + -ally.

definition: Cause to be alert and energetic.
example: Whenever we energize that circuit we blow a fuse.
etymology: From energy + -ize.

definition: Giving or marked by complete attention to.
example: That engrossed look of rapt delight.

definition: Anything that serves by contrast to call attention to another thing's good qualities.
etymology: From enhance + -er.

definition: The act of getting recruits; enlisting people for the army (or for a job or a cause etc.).
A period of time spent in military service.
etymology: From enlist + -ment.

definition: Address a question to and expect an answer from.
example: He enquired about the availability of rental bicycles in the town.
etymology: From Old French enquerre, from en- + querre (“to search, to look for”), from Latin quaerere, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

definition: Someone who asks a question.
etymology: From enquire + -er.

definition: Issue or terminate (in a specified way, state, etc.); end.
example: Give three freshmen six bottles of wine, and hilarity will ensue.
etymology: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after;

definition: An intricate trap that entangles or ensnares its victim.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:entanglement.
etymology: From entangle + -ment.

definition: Marked by imagination, initiative, and readiness to undertake new projects.
example: An enterprising foreign policy.

definition: Filled with wonder and delight.
The branch of zoology that studies insects.
example: Entomology is an important field of study within biology.
etymology: From French entomologie, from Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, “insect”) + -logie (from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “-logy”)), equivalent to entomo- + -logy.

definition: A commodity that enters competition with established merchandise.
example: A well publicized entrant is the pocket computer.
etymology: From French entrant, present participle of entrer.

definition: A defense that claims the defendant would not have broken the law if not tricked into doing it by law enforcement officials.
example: The entrapment of the victims in the wreckage made rescue difficult.
etymology: From entrap + -ment.

definition: Confer a trust upon.
example: The messenger was entrusted with the general's secret.
etymology: From en- + trust.

definition: Causing envy.
example: An enviable position.
etymology: From envy + -able (suffix meaning ‘able or fit to be done’ forming adjectives).

definition: Someone who works to protect the environment from destruction or pollution.
etymology: From environmental + -ist.

definition: The area in which something exists or lives.
etymology: From environ + -s.

definition: Of or relating to or produced by an enzyme.
etymology: From enzyme + -atic.

definition: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.
etymology: From epi- + center.

definition: Of or relating to epidemiology.
example: Epidemiological studies.
etymology: From epidemiology + -ical.

definition: On or outside the dura mater.
example: Epidural anesthesia is commonly used for pain relief during childbirth.
etymology: From epi- + dural.

definition: Injection of an anesthetic substance into the epidural space of the spinal cord in order to produce epidural anesthesia.
Of or relating to or characteristic of epilepsy.
example: Epileptic seizure.

definition: Chowder containing fish.
A longitudinal slice or boned side of a fish.
A longitudinal slice or boned side of a fish.
Mousse made with fish.
A long narrow depression in a surface.
etymology: From Middle English fissure, from Old French fissure, from Latin fissūra (“a cleft, chink”), from findō (“to cleave, split, divide”) + -tūra (nominal suffix).

definition: The ordinal number of five hundred in counting order.
The intonation of keyboard instruments where the pitch of each note is fixed and cannot be varied by the performer.
An effervescent beverage (usually alcoholic).
example: I poured a cola and waited for the fizz to settle down before topping off the glass.
etymology: Onomatopoeia.

definition: Hissing and bubbling.
example: Fizzy drinks are also known as carbonated beverages.
etymology: From fizz + -y.

definition: A long narrow inlet of the sea between steep cliffs; common in Norway.
A slick spokesperson who can turn any criticism to the advantage of their employer.
etymology: Most likely flak.

definition: A slick spokesperson who can turn any criticism to the advantage of their employer.
Smut affecting leaves and stems of cereals and other grasses.
Flagstones collectively.
example: There was a pile of flagging waiting to be laid in place.

definition: A tall staff or pole on which a flag is raised.
etymology: From flag + staff.

definition: A slick spokesperson who can turn any criticism to the advantage of their employer.
etymology: Coined by American author and journalist Tom Wolfe in his 1970 book Radical Chic & Mau-Mauing the Flak Catchers, from flak, meaning "criticism".

definition: Made of or resembling flakes.
example: Flaky soap.
etymology: From flake + -y.

definition: Guitar music composed for dancing the flamenco.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish flamenco, from Middle Dutch vlaminc (“Fleming”) (> Dutch Vlaming).

definition: Having a tendency to flap.
etymology: From flap + -y.

definition: Point at which something is ready to blow up.
etymology: From flash + point.

definition: Having a flat bottom.
example: A flat-bottomed boat.

definition: In an unqualified manner.
example: He flatly denied the charges.
etymology: From flat + -ly.

definition: Make flat or flatter.
example: Flatten a road.
etymology: From flat + -en.

definition: Become flat or flatter.
example: The landscape flattened.

definition: Excessive or insincere praise.
example: Don't you know that some of his contributions here are pure flattery?
etymology: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). By surface analysis, flatter + -y (forming abstract nouns).

definition: The act of displaying something ostentatiously.
example: His behavior was an outrageous flaunt.
etymology: Of North Germanic origin. Perhaps related to Norwegian flanta (“to show off, wander about”), Icelandic flana (“to rush about, act rashly or heedlessly”) and then also to French flâner (“to wander around, loiter”).

definition: Something added to food primarily for the savor it imparts.
example: This soda has an aftertaste because of the artificial flavoring.

definition: Smoothly and without difficulty; precisely and deftly.
example: The gymnast landed flawlessly.
etymology: From flawless + -ly.

definition: Fungus causing flax rust.
Usually describes a large person who is fat but has a large frame to carry it.
example: A fleshy wine.
etymology: From Middle English fleisshy, fleischy, fleschi, equivalent to flesh + -y. Piecewise doublet of fleischig.

definition: A harrow that consists of fine spring tines mounted on a contour-flexing frame, used for weeding crops.
Shining unsteadily.
Someone who travels by air.
etymology: From fly + -er (comparative suffix).

definition: A reflex response to sudden pain.
example: My eye doctor hates the flinch I have every time he tries to get near my eyes.
etymology: From Middle French flenchir (“to bend”), from Old French flenchir, flanchir, from Frankish *hlankijan, from Proto-Germanic *hlankijaną (“to bend, twist, flex”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng- (“to bend, turn, wind”).

definition: A shoe for swimming; the paddle-like front is an aid in swimming (especially underwater).
etymology: From flip + -er. Compare Saterland Frisian Flappert (“flipper, wing”).

definition: Having limbs that are used as flippers.
Like a coquette.
example: Yes yes, forgive a young woman her flirtatious pleasantries.
etymology: From flirtation + -ous.

definition: Beating with a whip or strap or rope as a form of punishment.
example: What lawbreakers like that need is a good flogging. Do that and watch the crime rate plummet.

definition: Provided with a floor.
A United States Navy fleet consisting of two or more squadrons of small warships.
example: Toward the horizon a flotilla of fishing-boats showed immutable, pink-lacquered by the evening sun.
etymology: From Spanish flotilla, diminutive of flota (“fleet”), from French flotte.

definition: Flesh of any of various American and European flatfish.
etymology: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. Cognate with Danish flynder, German Flunder, Swedish flundra.

definition: Resembling or made of or suggestive of flowers.
Asiatic ornamental shrub with spiny branches and pink or red blossoms.
Of or relating to or suggestive of flowers.
example: A flowery hat.
etymology: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flower + -y (adjectival suffix). Piecewise doublet of floury.

definition: Cause to fluctuate or move in a wavelike pattern.
example: I fluctuated between wishing he was back home and wishing I'd never met him.
etymology: First attested in 1630; borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell;

definition: A wave motion.
example: The fluctuations of the sea.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fluctuatiōnem, accusative singular of fluctuatiō, from fluctuō, from fluctus. Morphologically fluctuate + -ion.

definition: Flat bladelike projection on the arm of an anchor.
etymology: From Middle English flue, flewe (“mouthpiece of a hunting horn”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps a back-formation from Middle English *flews (mistaken as a plural), from Old English flēwsa (“a flow, flowing, flux”).

definition: Organ pipe whose tone is produced by air passing across the sharp edge of a fissure or lip.
An organ stop with the tone of a flue pipe.
In a fluent manner.
example: She speaks French fluently.
etymology: From fluent + -ly.

definition: A British imperial capacity measure (liquid or dry) equal to 60 minims or 3.5516 cubic centimeters.
A kind of fluid coupling in which the flywheel is the driving rotor.
The property of flowing easily.
example: Adding lead makes the alloy easier to cast because the melting point is reduced and the fluidity is increased.
etymology: Borrowed from French fluidité.

definition: A narrow gorge with a stream running through it.
etymology: From Middle English flum, from Old French flum, flun, from Latin flumen, from fluere (“to flow”).

definition: Thrown into a state of agitated confusion; (‘rattled’ is an informal term).
example: The speaker became quite flustered when she dropped all her notes.

definition: The motion made by flapping up and down.
example: I was entranced by the colorful fluttering of the butterfly's wings.

definition: A gecko that has membranous expansions along the sides of its body and limbs and tail that enable it to glide short distances.
The outermost of two or more jibs.
Bridge formed by the upper level of a crossing of two highways at different levels.
etymology: Deverbal from fly over.

definition: Regulator consisting of a heavy wheel that stores kinetic energy and smooths the operation of a reciprocating engine.
etymology: From fly + wheel.

definition: A young horse.
Emitting or filled with bubbles as from carbonation or fermentation.
A crystal, powder, or liquid preparation that foams in, scents, and softens bathwater.
The concentration of attention or energy on something.
example: The focus of activity shifted to molecular biology.

definition: An unborn or unhatched vertebrate in the later stages of development showing the main recognizable features of the mature animal.
Disappointingly unsuccessful.
example: Their foiled attempt to capture Calais.

definition: A popular but erroneous etymology.
etymology: English from the 1880s (Abram Smythe Palmer, 1882), a calque of German Volksetymologie (1820s, in 1821 as Volks-Etymologie in J. A. Schmeller's Die Mundarten Bayerns grammatisch dargestellt).

definition: Any small spherical group of cells containing a cavity.
A revue with elaborate costuming.
example: The most famous Broadway theatrical revues of all time were the Ziegfeld Follies.
etymology: From French folies.

definition: A piece of work that exploits or builds on earlier work.
example: His new software is a follow-up to the programs they started with.
etymology: Deverbal from follow up.

definition: Without good sense or judgment.
example: He acted foolishly when he agreed to come.
etymology: From Middle English folysly, folysschly; equivalent to foolish + -ly.

definition: Not liable to failure.
example: A foolproof identification system.
etymology: From fool + -proof.

definition: A trodden path.
etymology: From Middle English foot path, footpath; equivalent to foot + path.

definition: Impelled by physical force especially against resistance.
example: Forcible entry.
etymology: From Middle English forcible, forsable, from Old French forcible, from forcier (“to conquer by force”), equivalent to force + -ible.

definition: A feeling of evil to come.
example: A steadily escalating sense of foreboding.
etymology: From Middle English forbodyng, vorboding, equivalent to fore- + bode + -ing. Compare German Vorbote (“harbinger, omen”).

definition: Be earlier in time; go back further.
etymology: From Middle English forgan, from Old English foregān, equivalent to fore- + go.

definition: Well in the past; former.
example: Dreams of foregone times.

definition: An inevitable ending.
A person who goes before or announces the coming of another.
example: Bakelite is a forerunner of today's plastics.
etymology: From Middle English forrenner, foreriner. Calque of Latin praecursor (“one who runs before, a forerunner”). Equivalent to fore- + runner and/or forerun + -er.

definition: Indistinctly prophetic.
etymology: From foreshadow (verb) + -ing (suffix forming nouns denoting the act of doing something, an action, or the embodiment of an action; or forming present participles of verbs).

definition: Someone trained in forestry.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English forester, a borrowing from Old French forestier, from forest + -ier; equivalent to forest + -er. Displaced native Old English wuduweard.

definition: (of memory) deficient in retentiveness or range.
example: A forgetful mapping; a forgetful functor.
etymology: From Middle English *forgetful, *forȝetful (suggested by derivative forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse (“forgetfulness”)), equivalent to forget + -ful.

definition: A flighty and disorganized person.
Easily forgotten.
etymology: From forget + -able.

definition: Do without or cease to hold or adhere to.
example: I've had to forgo my student discount in exchange for taking the job.
etymology: From Middle English forgon (“to go by, pass up”), from Old English forgān (“to go away, forgo”); equivalent to for- + go.

definition: Resembling a fork; divided or separated into two branches.
example: A forked river.

definition: A form of lightning that moves rapidly in a zigzag path with one end divided (fork-like).
A small industrial vehicle with a power operated forked platform in front that can be inserted under loads to lift and move them.
etymology: From fork + lift.

definition: Marked by or showing hopelessness.
example: The last forlorn attempt.

definition: A hopeless or desperate enterprise.
A colorless poisonous gas; made by the oxidation of methanol.
etymology: From form(yl) + aldehyde.

definition: A requirement of etiquette or custom.
example: A mere formality.

definition: Concerned with or characterized by rigorous adherence to recognized forms (especially in religion or art).
example: Highly formalized plays like ‘Waiting for Godot’.

definition: Leave someone who needs or counts on you; leave in the lurch.
etymology: From Middle English forsaken (“to abandon, desert, repudiate, withdraw allegiance from”), from Old English forsacan (“to oppose; to give up, renounce;

definition: Characterized by directness in manner or speech; without subtlety or evasion.
example: Forthright criticism.
etymology: From Middle English forþright, forþriʒt, forþriht, from Old English forþriht (“direct, plain”). By surface analysis, forth + right.

definition: Defensive structure consisting of walls or mounds built around a stronghold to strengthen it.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French fortification, from Late Latin fortificatio, fortificationem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, fort + -ification.

definition: Make strong or stronger.
example: Sherry is made by fortifying wine.
etymology: From Late Middle English fortifien, fortfien (“to strengthen (a castle, etc.) from attack; to strengthen (an army, etc.); to strengthen (a person), aid, support; to reinforce, support; to improve;

definition: Occurring every two weeks.
etymology: From fortnight + -ly.

definition: Sleeping for a short period of time (usually not in bed).
example: As you’re so tired, why not try to catch forty winks before you leave?
etymology: From forty + winks, possibly referring to a nap supposedly lasting as long as it takes a person to wink (i.e., blink) forty times.

definition: The ordinal number of four hundred in counting order.
Having four prongs.
Four people considered as a unit.
example: The foursome teed off before 9 a.m.
etymology: From four + -some.

definition: An acute diarrheal disease (especially of chickens) caused by the microorganism that causes hemorrhagic septicemia.
Either of two acute viral diseases of domestic fowl; characterized by refusal to eat and high temperature and discoloration of the comb.
(mathematics) a geometric pattern that is repeated at every scale and so cannot be represented by classical geometry.
etymology: From French fractal, from Latin fractus (“broken”), perfect passive participle of frangō (“break, fragment”).

definition: (mathematics) the geometry of fractals.
example: Benoit Mandelbrot pioneered fractal geometry.

definition: A rig on a sailing vessel that consists of a foresail, such as a jib or genoa sail, that does not reach all the way to the top of the mast.
Quality of being easily damaged or destroyed.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French fragilité, from Latin fragilitās. Doublet of frailty. Morphologically fragile + -ity.

definition: Consisting of small disconnected parts.
example: Fragmentary remains.
etymology: From fragment + -ary.

definition: European orchid having dense spikes of fragrant pink or lilac or red flowers with conspicuous spurs.
In a dishonest and fraudulent manner.
example: This money was fraudulently obtained.
etymology: From Middle English fraudulently; equivalent to fraudulent + -ly.

definition: Worn away or tattered along the edges.
example: Frayed cuffs.
etymology: From fray + -ed, from Old French froiier (“to rub against, scrape; thrust against”), from Latin fricare (“to rub, rub down”).

definition: Something that is free (usually provided as part of a promotional scheme).
example: The road map was a freebie.
etymology: From free + -b- (epenthetic) + -ie or free + -bie.

definition: An estate held in fee simple or for life.
Affected with or marked by frenzy or mania uncontrolled by reason.
example: A frenzied attack.

definition: Make (to feel) fresh.
example: The cool water refreshed us.
etymology: From fresh + -en.

definition: Make brighter and prettier.
etymology: From freshen + up.

definition: A Roman Catholic friar wearing the black mantle of the Dominican order.
A feeling of liking for another person; enjoyment in their company.
etymology: From Middle English freendlynesse, frendlynes, equivalent to friendly + -ness.

definition: An architectural ornament consisting of a horizontal sculptured band between the architrave and the cornice.
example: The classroom had an alphabet frieze that showed an animal for each letter.
etymology: Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships. Or, from French friser (“to curl”)..

definition: Provoking horror.
example: A frightful crime of decapitation.
etymology: From Middle English frightful (“afraid”), from Old English forhtfull (“fainthearted, timorous”). Equivalent to fright + -ful.

definition: Surrounded as with a border or fringe; sometimes used in combination.
example: A large suburban community … fringed by an industrial area.
etymology: From Middle English frenged; equivalent to fringe + -ed.

definition: Low wiry-stemmed branching herb or southern California having fringed pink flowers.
Play boisterously.
example: The police frisked the suspiciously-acting individual and found a knife as well as a bag of marijuana.

definition: A long, loose outer garment.
etymology: From Middle English frock, froke, from Old Norse frauki (“frog”), related to Old English frocga (“frog”). More at frog.

definition: A man's coat having knee-length skirts front and back; worn in the 19th century.
The extent of land abutting on a street or water.
etymology: From front + -age.

definition: A local road that runs parallel to an expressway and allows local traffic to gain access to property.
The suture between two halves of the frontal bone (usually obliterated by the age of 6).
Upthrust of ground or pavement caused by the freezing of moist soil.
Upthrust of ground or pavement caused by the freezing of moist soil.
Destruction of tissue by freezing and characterized by tingling, blistering and possibly gangrene.
etymology: From frost + bite.

definition: Become bubbly or frothy or foaming.
example: The boiling soup was frothing.
etymology: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ; Old English āfrēoþan (“to foam, froth”) is from same Germanic root. Verb attested from late 14th century.

definition: Hinder or prevent (the efforts, plans, or desires) of.
example: What ultimately frustrated every challenger was Ruth's amazing September surge.
etymology: From Middle English frustraten (“to prevent, disappoint, render useless”), from Latin frūstrātus, perfect passive participle of frūstrō (“to deceive”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French frustrer.

definition: Flesh of a medium-sized young chicken suitable for frying.
example: He learned to work the fryer as part of becoming a competent cook for a commercial kitchen.
etymology: From fry + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix).

definition: The pivot about which a lever turns.
example: It is possible to flick food across the table using your fork as a lever and your finger as a fulcrum.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fulcrum (“bedpost, foot of a couch”), from fulciō (“prop up, support”).

definition: A feeling of satisfaction at having achieved your desires.
example: To achieve fulfilment of one's hopes.
etymology: From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan, from full (“full”) + fyllan (“to fill”). Equivalent to fulfill + -ment.

definition: Showing lack of skill or aptitude.
example: His fumbling attempt to put up a shelf.

definition: The branch of genomics that determines the biological function of the genes and their products.
A form of Protestantism that takes the interpretation of every word in the sacred texts as literal truth.
etymology: From fundamental + -ism. First used in the 1910s by American Christians.

definition: Dismiss, usually for economic reasons.
etymology: From Dutch verlof (“furlough”), probably from Middle Low German verlōf (“furlough, permission”) (possibly via German Verlaub), from the verb verlōven (“to allow”), from Old Saxon far- + lōvian (“to trust, believe”).

definition: An instrument which sets the fuze time on projectiles with mechanical time fuzes.
Uselessness as a consequence of having no practical result.
example: An exercise of futility.
etymology: From Latin fūtilitās (“worthlessness, futility”). By surface analysis, futile + -ity.

definition: Light informal conversation for social occasions.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English gab, gabbe, from Old Norse gabb (“jest, mockery”) (whence also Old French gab, gap (“mockery, derision, scorn”)). Cognate with Icelandic gabb (“hoax”).

definition: Asiatic mustard used as a potherb.
The qualities of a hero or heroine; exceptional or heroic courage when facing danger (especially in battle).
etymology: From French galanterie, equivalent to gallant + -ry.

definition: A muscular sac attached to the liver that stores bile (secreted by the liver) until it is needed for digestion.
etymology: From gall + bladder.

definition: A colorless crystalline acid obtained from tannin.
Cardiac rhythm characterized by the presence of an extra sound; can indicate a heart abnormality.
A herd of whales.
etymology: From Italian gamba (“leg”). Doublet of gamb, gamba, jamb, and jambe. Compare gammon and ham.

definition: A complete extent or range:.
etymology: 1520s, original sense “lowest note of musical scale”, contraction of Medieval Latin gamma ut, from gamma (“Greek letter, corresponding to the musical note G”) + ut (“first solfège syllable, now replaced by do”).

definition: Mature male goose.
example: Have a gander at what he’s written.
etymology: From Middle English gandre, from Old English gandra, ganra (“gander”), from Proto-West Germanic *ganʀō, from Proto-Germanic *ganzô (“gander”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns (“goose”).

definition: A correctional institution used to detain persons who are in the lawful custody of the government (either accused persons awaiting trial or convicted persons serving a sentence).
etymology: From Middle English gayole, gaiol, gaylle, gaille, gayle, gaile, via Old French gaiole, gayolle, gaole, from Medieval Latin gabiola, for Late Latin caveola, a diminutive of Latin cavea (“cavity, coop, cage”).

definition: Primitive predaceous North American fish covered with hard scales and having long jaws with needlelike teeth.
etymology: Clipping of garfish, from Middle English gar (“spear”) + fish. Compare pike.

definition: Minute arthropod often infesting the underground parts of truck-garden and greenhouse crops.
Long cultivated hybrid of Rheum palmatum; stems often cooked in pies or as sauce or preserves.
A loose high-necked blouse with long sleeves; styled after the red flannel shirts worn by Garibaldi's soldiers.
etymology: The jacket is named after Italian patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi, who wore a red shirt of similar appearance. The biscuit is also named after Garibaldi.

definition: One of the small bulblets that can be split off of the axis of a larger garlic bulb.
Lac refined by treating with solvent; garnet-colored.
Floor consisting of open space at the top of a house just below roof; often used for storage.
etymology: From Middle English garett, garite, from Old French garite, guerite (“watchtower”), from garir, guarir (“to defend, protect”) (compare English garrison), ultimately of Germanic origin (see English garage).

definition: A band (usually elastic) worn around the leg to hold up a stocking (or around the arm to hold up a sleeve).
A wide belt of elastic with straps hanging from it; worn by women to hold up stockings.
Any of numerous nonvenomous longitudinally-striped viviparous North American and Central American snakes.
A knitting stitch that results in a pattern of horizontal ridges formed by knitting both sides (instead of purling one side).
Obstruction of the circulatory system caused by an air bubble as, e.g., accidentally during surgery or hypodermic injection or as a complication from scuba diving.
Existing as or having characteristics of a gas.
example: Steam is water in the gaseous state.
etymology: From gas + -eous.

definition: A cluster of stars within an intricate cloud of gas and dust.
Seal consisting of a ring for packing pistons or sealing a pipe joint.
etymology: Perhaps from Middle French garcette (“gasket”), from Old French garce (“young woman”), feminization of garçon.

definition: A basic coil for storing rope.
example: Tie your rope in a gasket coil to prevent it from tangling.

definition: A peptic ulcer of the stomach.
A gangster's pistol.
etymology: Clipping of Gatling gun, after inventor Richard Gatling.

definition: Someone who controls access to something.
example: There are too many gatekeepers between the field officers and the chief.
etymology: From gate + keeper.

definition: A person who gathers.
example: They were a society of hunters and gatherers.
etymology: From Middle English gaderere, gaderare, equivalent to gather + -er.

definition: Tastelessly showy.
example: A gaudy costume.
etymology: From Middle English gaudi, from Old French gaudie, from Medieval Latin gaudia. equivalent to gaud (“ornament, trinket”) + -y.

definition: Very thin especially from disease or hunger or cold.
example: A nightmare population of gaunt men and skeletal boys.
etymology: From Middle English gaunt, gawnt, gawnte, gant (“lean, slender, thin, gaunt”); further etymology uncertain. Speculated origins include: * from a North Germanic/Scandinavian source related to Old Norse gandr (“magic staff;

definition: (medicine) bleached cotton cloth of plain weave used for bandages and dressings.
etymology: Borrowed from French gaze, from Arabic قَزّ (qazz, “silk”).

definition: So thin as to transmit light.
A spectator who stares stupidly without intelligent awareness.
etymology: From gawk + -er.

definition: Old breed of tall swift keen-eyed hunting dogs resembling greyhounds; from Egypt and southwestern Asia.
A Japanese woman trained to entertain men with conversation and singing and dancing.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 芸者(げいしゃ) (geisha, “artisan”), from Middle Chinese 藝 (MC ngjiejH, “art, craft”) + 者 (MC tsyaeX, “-er”).

definition: A Japanese woman trained to entertain men with conversation and singing and dancing.
Jellied dessert made with gelatin and fruit juice or water.
A crystalline rock that can be cut and polished for jewelry.
etymology: From Middle English gimstone, alteration (due to Middle English gemme) of earlier ȝimston, ȝimstan, from Old English ġimstān, ġymstān (“gem; jewel; precious stone”), equivalent to gem + stone.

definition: The technology of preparing recombinant DNA in vitro by cutting up DNA molecules and splicing together fragments from more than one organism.
An anesthetic that anesthetizes the entire body and causes loss of consciousness.
Draw from specific cases for more general cases.
etymology: From general + -ize.

definition: Having the ability to produce or originate.
example: Generative power.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English generatyve. By surface analysis, generate + -ive. Compare French génératif.

definition: (linguistics) a type of grammar that describes syntax in terms of a set of logical rules that can generate all and only the infinite number of grammatical sentences in a language and assigns them all the correct structural description.
A disease or disorder that is inherited genetically.
The special atmosphere of a place.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin genius loci (“tutelary deity of a/the place”), from the singular genitive form of locus (“place”).

definition: The branch of genetics that studies organisms in terms of their genomes (their full DNA sequences).
etymology: From gene + -omics or genome + -ics.

definition: The property possessed by a slope that is very gradual.
etymology: From Middle English gentilnesse; equivalent to gentle + -ness.

definition: Of or relating to or determined by geometry.
etymology: From geometric + -al.

definition: The study of the effects of economic geography on the powers of the state.
etymology: From geo- + politics, calque of Swedish geopolitik, coined in 1900 by Rudolf Kjellén.

definition: The nonstandard dialect of natives of Newcastle-upon-Tyne.
Of or relating to the aged.
example: Geriatric disorder.
etymology: From geriatrics. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek γῆρας (gêras, “old age”) + -iatric.

definition: A pore in the outer wall of a spore or pollen grain through which the germ tube or pollen tube makes its exit on germination.
The process whereby seeds or spores sprout and begin to grow.
Of or relating to gestation.
example: Gestational diabetes.
etymology: From gestation + -al.

definition: The age of an embryo counting from the time of fertilization.
A spring that discharges hot water and steam.
A portable stereo.
example: We got tired of him carrying his ghetto blaster down our street every day.
etymology: From ghetto + blaster. First use appears c. 1980, see quotations.

definition: Spectacular perennial native of wet montane grasslands of Peru; formerly included in genus Ranunculus.
A large variety of conch.
The largest moa; about 12 feet high.
Large (up to more than three feet) edible salamander of Asia.
Extremely lofty evergreen of southern end of western foothills of Sierra Nevada in California; largest living organism.
Large evergreen with extremely large erect or spreading leaves; cultivated widely in tropics for its edible rhizome and shoots; used in wet warm regions as a stately ornamental.
Unintelligible talking.
etymology: First attested mid-16th century. Origin obscure.

definition: Smallest and most perfectly anthropoid arboreal ape having long arms and no tail; of southern Asia and East Indies.
etymology: Reborrowing from French gibbon, folk etymology (compare English Gibbon) ultimately from a Northern Aslian language (compare Batek kəboɲ).

definition: Southwestern United States bird like the yellow-shafted flicker but lacking the red neck.
One of a series of slit openings in the pharynxes of fishes and aquatic amphibians through which water passes.
Of the highest quality or value.
example: Gilt-edged securities.

definition: Aromatic root of ginseng plants.
etymology: Borrowed from Hokkien 人參 /人参 (jîn-sim, “ginseng”). Doublet of ninzin.

definition: An encircling or ringlike structure.
example: The girdle of the world.
etymology: From Middle English girdel, gerdel, gurdel, from Old English gyrdel, from Proto-West Germanic *gurdil, from Proto-Germanic *gurdilaz (“girdle, belt”), equivalent to gird + -le.

definition: A check given by the British government to someone who is unemployed; it can be cashed either at a bank or at the post office.
The distance around a person's body.
etymology: From Middle English girth, gerth, gyrth, from Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to encircle, enclose; belt”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌰 (gairda), Icelandic gjörð.

definition: Any period of time during which glaciers covered a large part of the earth's surface.
A tract of land with few or no trees in the middle of a wooded area.
example: A glade of ice.
etymology: From Middle English glade, glode, glede (“a gleam of light, bright space, an open space; an open or cleared space in a forest; a bright patch of sky;

definition: An article of tableware made of glass.
etymology: From glass + -ware.

definition: Resembling glass in smoothness and shininess and slickness.
example: The glassy surface of the lake.
etymology: From Middle English glasy, equivalent to glass + -y. Compare Saterland Frisian glääsich (“glassy”), Dutch glazig (“glassy”), German Low German glasig (“glassy”), German glasig (“glassy”).

definition: Be shiny, as if wet.
etymology: * Old High German glīmen (“to glow, shine”); gleimo, glīmo (“glowworm”) (Middle High German glīme, gleime)

definition: In a joyous and gleeful manner.
example: The old man had greeted her gleefully.
etymology: From gleeful + -ly.

definition: Reflecting light.
example: Glistening bodies of swimmers.

definition: Growth to a global or worldwide scale.
example: The globalization of the communication industry.
etymology: From global + -isation or globalise + -ation. Popularized by German-American economist and professor at Harvard Business School Theodore Levitt.

definition: With glory or in a glorious manner.
example: Where others had failed he had gloriously succeeded.
etymology: From Middle English gloriously, equivalent to glorious + -ly.

definition: Overeat or eat immodestly; make a pig of oneself.
example: To glut one's appetite.

definition: A salt or ester of glutamic acid.
etymology: From glutamic acid + -ate.

definition: One form in which body fuel is stored; stored primarily in the liver and broken down into glucose when needed by the body.
etymology: Borrowed from French glycogène. By surface analysis, glyco- + -gen.

definition: A sweet but poisonous syrupy liquid used as an antifreeze and solvent.
etymology: From Ancient Greek γλῠκῠ́ς (glŭkŭ́s, “sweet”) + English -ol.

definition: Used of old persons or old trees; covered with knobs or knots.
example: Gnarled and knotted hands.
etymology: From gnarl (“knot in wood”) + -y. The slang senses were particularly popularized by US surf culture in the 1970s.

definition: Possessing intellectual or esoteric knowledge of spiritual things.
Someone whose career progresses rapidly.
example: He's a promising young go-getter, but he needs to learn some things about office politics.

definition: The soccer or hockey player assigned to protect the goal.
etymology: From goal + tender.

definition: Eat a large amount of food quickly.
example: The children gobbled down most of the birthday cake.

definition: A drinking glass with a base and stem.
example: Sup wine from a goblet.
etymology: From Middle English goblet (= Middle Low German gobelet, kobelet (“goblet”)), from Old French gobellet, diminutive of gobel, from or related to the verb gober (“to ingest”).

definition: An epithelial cell that secretes mucous.
etymology: The cell is named for its goblet-like shape. The apical portion is shaped like a cup and the basal portion is shaped like a stem.

definition: Resembling the shape of a goblet.
Any woman who serves as a sponsor for a child at baptism.
etymology: From Middle English godmoder, from Old English godmōdor (“godmother”), equivalent to god- + mother.

definition: A sudden happening that brings good fortune (as a sudden opportunity to make money).
etymology: A variant of God’s send, from God + -’s + send (“(obsolete) act of sending”), in the sense of someone or something sent by God.

definition: Any of several shrubby herbs or subshrubs of the genus Chrysopsis having bright golden-yellow flower heads that resemble asters; throughout much of United States and into Canada.
A jackal native to Europe and Asia with a golden coat.
An English breed having a long silky golden coat.
Yellow-throated American wood warbler.
(Jewish folklore) an artificially created human being that is given life by supernatural means.
etymology: Borrowed from Hebrew גולם \ גֹּלֶם (gólem).

definition: A low flat-bottomed freight car with fixed sides but no roof.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian gondola, from Venetan góndoƚa. Possibly from Medieval Greek κοντοῦρα (kontoûra, “cutter, kind of ship”).

definition: A low flat-bottomed freight car with fixed sides but no roof.
A buoy with a bell on it.
Conspicuously or grossly unconventional or unusual.
etymology: Coined in 1971 by Boston Globe editor Bill Cardoso. Of uncertain origin; OED proposes Italian gonzo (“dolt”) and / or Spanish ganso (“dolt, goose”). The etymology supplied by Cardoso himself (French gonzeaux) is spurious;

definition: A man who is a stupid incompetent fool.
example: I made a goof in that last calculation.
etymology: Perhaps from dialectal English goff (“foolish clown”), from earlier goffe, in which case further etymology is uncertain.

definition: An idle worthless person.
Proof against human misuse or error.
Reflex erection of hairs of the skin in response to cold or emotional stress or skin irritation.
A zealously energetic person (especially a salesman).
A hole in the ground made by gophers.
Large dark-blue nonvenomous snake that invades burrows; found in southern North America and Mexico.
Burrowing edible land tortoise of southeastern North America.
Covered with blood.
example: A gory dagger.
etymology: From gore + -y. Compare Middle English gorry (“muddy”), and güre, gire, girre (“gory, clotted”), from Old English gyr, gyru (“filthy, muddy”), from gor (“dirt, dung”); Old Frisian gere, iere (“muddy water”). More at gore.

definition: A conversation that spreads personal information about other people.
