Bottle made from the dried shell of a bottle gourd.
example: I got so stoned last night. I was out of my gourd.
etymology: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of cucurbit.

definition: Any vine of the family Cucurbitaceae that bears fruits with hard rinds.
A woman entrusted with the care and supervision of a child (especially in a private home).
etymology: From Middle English governesse, a contracted form of governeresse, from Old French governeresse (“female ruler or administrator”). In later senses, equivalent to govern(or) + -ess.

definition: The office of governor.
The act of grafting something onto something else.
Any of several sorghums cultivated primarily for grain.
Composed of or covered with particles resembling meal in texture or consistency.
example: The photographs were grainy and indistinct.
etymology: From Middle English greyny, equivalent to grain + -y. Piecewise doublet of corny.

definition: A variety of grainy club mushrooms.
The domain controlled by a grand duke or grand duchess.
Larceny of property having a value greater than some amount (the amount varies by locale).
The chief mufti of a district.
The father of your father or mother.
Impressive because of unnecessary largeness or grandeur; used to show disapproval.
etymology: From French grandiose, from Italian grandioso, from Latin grandis (“great, grand”) (English grand). Possibly from grand + -ose, though to be debated. Doublet of grandioso.

definition: A player of exceptional or world class skill in chess or bridge.
etymology: From grand + master.

definition: A parent of your father or mother.
etymology: From grand- + parent. Compare French grand-parent.

definition: The audience at a stadium or racetrack.
etymology: From grand + stand.

definition: Cereal made of especially rolled oats with dried fruits and nuts and honey or brown sugar.
etymology: Genericized trademark from Granola, a brand of breakfast cereal registered in 1886 by Will Keith Kellogg and in use into the early 20th century.

definition: Cookie bar made of granola.
etymology: From granola + bar. Attested since the late twentieth century.

definition: A bacterial wilt of tobacco plants.
Gossip spread by spoken communication.
example: Although many grapevines have geographical names, these rarely reflect their real origin, if known at all.
etymology: From grape + vine.

definition: In a diagrammatic manner.
etymology: From graphic + -ally.

definition: Costing nothing.
Without cause.
example: A gratuitous insult.
etymology: From Latin grātuītus (“free”), from Latin grātia (“favor”), grātus (“showing favor”).

definition: Move toward.
example: The conversation gravitated towards politics.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin gravitāt-, past participial stem of gravitō.

definition: Native to Europe but introduced in America.
Flounder found from North Carolina to Florida and the eastern Gulf of Mexico.
Highly valued lean flesh of marine or freshwater mullet.
Found in shallow waters off the coast of Florida.
Scraped or touched lightly in passing.
example: His grazed and bleeding arm proved he had been in the line of fire.

definition: Smeared with oil or grease to reduce friction.
Large (up to 6 ft) greyish-brown barracuda highly regarded as a food and sport fish; may be dangerous to swimmers.
A parent of your grandparent.
Important for human and animal food; growth habit and stem form similar to Indian corn but having sawtooth-edged leaves.
The residue that remains after animal fat has been rendered.
North American shrub with light green leaves and winged nuts.
Disease of rice; grains covered by a green powder consisting of conidia.
Woodpecker of Europe and western Asia.
A belt of parks or rural land surrounding a town or city.
Green foliage.
etymology: From green + -ery.

definition: The phenomenon of vitality and freshness being restored.
Of grey tinged with green.
A belt of parks or rural land surrounding a town or city.
etymology: From green + way.

definition: An infantryman equipped with grenades.
Native to Europe but introduced in America.
Flounder found from North Carolina to Florida and the eastern Gulf of Mexico.
A canid living in the deserts of Northern Africa related to the golden jackal and the grey wolf.
Highly valued lean flesh of marine or freshwater mullet.
Found in shallow waters off the coast of Florida.
A traffic jam so bad that no movement is possible.
etymology: From grid + lock.

definition: Thickly covered with ingrained dirt or soot.
example: Grimy hands.
etymology: From grime + -y.

definition: Informal terms for objecting.
example: I have a gripe about the service here.
etymology: From Middle English gripen, from Old English grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grab, grasp”).

definition: Coarsely ground hulled corn boiled as a breakfast dish in the southern United States.
etymology: See grit (Etymology 2, “hulled oats”).

definition: A small cave (usually with attractive features).
etymology: From Italian grotta, from Vulgar Latin grupta, from Classical Latin crypta. Doublet of crypt. The Philippine sense is from the holy cave in Lourdes, France.

definition: Reddish brown North American marmot.
A thin mortar that can be poured and used to fill cracks in masonry or brickwork.
etymology: From Middle English growte, grut, from Old English grūt (“dregs;

definition: A gruff or angry utterance (suggestive of the growling of an animal).
example: The growling from her stomach told us she was hungry.

definition: Infested with grubs.
example: He's a grubby little boy, always playing around by the stream.
etymology: From grub + -y.

definition: Characterized by effort to the point of exhaustion; especially physical effort.
example: A grueling campaign.

definition: Brusque and surly and forbidding.
example: Gruff manner.
etymology: Perhaps related to Dutch grof (“rough, coarse”).

definition: Show one's unhappiness or critical attitude.
example: We grumbled about the increased work load.
etymology: Probably from Middle French grommeler, from Old French grumeler (“to murmur, grumble”), from Middle Dutch *grommelen ("to murmur, mutter, grunt";

definition: A loud low dull continuous noise.
example: The grumblings of a bad-tempered man.

definition: Communicate by hooting and grunting, as of primates.
A dip made of mashed avocado mixed with chopped onions and other seasonings.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish guacamole, from Classical Nahuatl āhuacamōlli (from āhuacatl (“avocado”) + mōlli (“sauce; broth”)).

definition: Any of several large turkey-like game birds of the family Cracidae; native to jungles of tropical America; resembling the curassows and valued as food.
etymology: From American Spanish, from Kuna kwama.

definition: One who provides a warrant or guarantee to another.
etymology: From guarant(ee) + -or.

definition: Attention and management implying responsibility for safety.
example: He is in the care of a bodyguard.
etymology: From guardian + -ship.

definition: A member of an irregular armed force that fights a stronger force by sabotage and harassment.
etymology: Compare French guérilla and German Guerilla.

definition: An irregular armed force that fights by sabotage and harassment; often rural and organized in large groups.
A variety of the English elm with erect branches and broader leaves.
A house separate from the main house; for housing guests.
etymology: From Middle English gest hous, gistenehus, gystehuse, gesthus, partly from Old English gæsthūs, ġesthūs (“guesthouse, hostel; guest-chamber”), from Proto-West Germanic *gastihūs;

definition: Something that offers basic information or instruction.
Shrewdness as demonstrated by being skilled in deception.
etymology: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”).

definition: A west African bird having dark plumage mottled with white; native to Africa but raised for food in many parts of the world.
etymology: Named after Guinea as it was imported from there.

definition: A Russian prison camp for political prisoners.
A narrow gorge with a stream running through it.
etymology: From earlier gulsh (“sink in, gush out”), from Middle English gulchen (“to gulp, spew”), probably from the source of gulp. Likely not related to gully (“ravine formed by water”) despite the similarities.

definition: A large and hurried swallow.
example: He finished it at a single gulp.
etymology: From Middle English gulpen, probably from West Flemish or Middle Dutch gulpen, golpen, of uncertain origin. Perhaps of imitative origin, or related to Dutch galpen (“to roar, squeal”), English galp, gaup (“to gape”).

definition: Gum from an acacia tree; used as a thickener (especially in candies and pharmaceuticals).
A gum obtained from various tropical plants; used as an astringent and in tanning.
Having the sticky properties of an adhesive.
example: A gummy grin.
etymology: From gum (“flesh around teeth”) + -y.

definition: Gush forth in a sudden stream or jet.
example: Water gushed forth.
etymology: From Middle English guschen, gusshen, gosshien, perhaps from Middle Dutch guysen (“to flow out with a gurgling sound, gush”) or Old Norse gusa (“to gush”), ultimately imitative.

definition: Flowing profusely.
example: A gushing hydrant.

definition: A specialist in gynecology.
etymology: From Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”) (genitive form γυναικός) + -λογία (-logía, “branch of study”), itself the combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “word, knowledge, reason”).

definition: The branch of medicine that deals with the diseases and hygiene of women.
etymology: From French gynécologie, from Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”, stem γυναικ-) + -logie (“-logy”). Replaced earlier gyniatrics. By surface analysis, gyneco- + -logy.

definition: A common white or colorless mineral (hydrated calcium sulphate) used to make cements and plasters (especially plaster of Paris).
etymology: From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso.

definition: Wallboard with a gypsum plaster core bonded to layers of paper or fiberboard; used instead of plaster or wallboard to make interior walls.
etymology: From gypsum + board.

definition: A Greek sandwich: sliced roast lamb with onion and tomato stuffed into pita bread.
example: I'll have a gyro, please.
etymology: Originally a shortening of gyroscope.

definition: A navigational instrument based on a gyroscope; it artificially provides a simulated horizon for the pilot.
A writ ordering a prisoner to be brought before a judge.
etymology: From Latin habeas corpus ad subiciendum (“You (shall) have the body to be subjected to (examination)”), referring to the body of the detainee (not the body of a victim, similar to corpus delicti).

definition: The native habitat or home of an animal or plant.
etymology: From Middle English habitacioun, from Old French habitacion, abitacion (“act of dwelling”), from Latin habitātiōnem, accusative of Latin habitātiō.

definition: According to habit or custom.
example: Her habitually severe expression.

definition: A large estate in Spanish-speaking countries.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish hacienda. Doublet of faena and fazenda.

definition: Lean white flesh of fish similar to but smaller than cod; usually baked or poached or as fillets sauteed or fried.
(Islam) the way of life prescribed as normative for Muslims on the basis of the teachings and practices of Muhammad and interpretations of the Koran.
example: In addition to the Quran, Muslims also look to the hadiths for moral and spiritual guidance in their daily lives.
etymology: From Arabic حَدِيث m (ḥadīṯ, “recent events; story; discourse; hadith”), from حَدَّثَ (ḥaddaṯa, “to tell; to relate; to report”).

definition: Tormented or harassed by nightmares or unreasonable fears.
Showing the wearing effects of overwork or care or suffering.
example: Her face was drawn and haggard from sleeplessness.
etymology: From Middle French haggard, from Old French faulcon hagard (“wild falcon”) ( > French hagard (“dazed”)), from Middle High German hag (“coppice”) ( > archaic German Hag (“hedge, grove”)).

definition: A small tubular cavity containing the root of a hair; small muscles and sebaceous glands are associated with them.
Toiletry consisting of an aerosol foam used in hair styling.
Excitation that makes your hair stand up or that chills your bones.
example: The movie was an old-fashioned hair-raiser.
etymology: From hair-raising + -er.

definition: Having no hair or fur.
example: A Mexican Hairless is about the size of a fox terrier and hairless except for a tufts on the head and tail.
etymology: From hair + -less. Piecewise doublet of hair loss. Cognate with German haarlos.

definition: A fracture without separation of the fragments and the line of the break being very thin.
A double pronged pin used to hold women's hair in place.
A U-shaped bend in a road.
etymology: The shape resembles a hairpin.

definition: An Arabic term of respect for someone who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca.
A Muslim physician.
A Muslim ruler or governor or judge.
etymology: From Hindustani حکیم / हकीम (hakīm), from Classical Persian حکیم (hakīm), from Arabic حَكِيم (ḥakīm, “wise, learned”).

definition: Without enthusiasm; in a half-hearted manner.
example: She tried half-heartedly.

definition: Retarded in intellectual development.
etymology: From half- + witted.

definition: Illusory perception; a common symptom of severe mental disorder.
etymology: From hallucinate + -ion, from Latin hallucinatus. Compare French hallucination. The first known usage in the English language is from Sir Thomas Browne.

definition: Any of five related nonmetallic elements (fluorine or chlorine or bromine or iodine or astatine) that are all monovalent and readily form negative ions.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “salt" or "sea”) + γεν- (gen-), "to produce" (coined by Berzelius in 1842). By surface analysis, halo- (“salt”) + -gen (“forming”).

definition: Rope or canvas headgear for a horse, with a rope for leading.
etymology: From Middle English halter, helter, helfter, from Old English hælfter, hælftre (“halter”), from Proto-West Germanic *halftrijā (“harness”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut”), equivalent to half- + -ter.

definition: A small cut of meat from the leg just above the foot.
One of the tendons at the back of the knee.
A small vise held in the hand in doing small work.
Made on a handloom.
In a convenient manner.
example: He won the election handily.
etymology: From handy + -ly. Compare Middle English hendily, hendiliche.

definition: Act of relinquishing property or authority etc.
example: The handover of occupied territory.
etymology: Deverbal from hand over.

definition: In an attractively handsome manner.
example: The volume was handsomely bound.
etymology: From handsome + -ly (suffix forming adverbs).

definition: A man skilled in various odd jobs and other small tasks.
example: I complained that the heat was not working, and the landlord sent the handyman to fix it.
etymology: From handy + -man.

definition: 10 hao equal 1 dong in Vietnam.
etymology: From Vietnamese hào.

definition: Dependent upon or characterized by chance.
example: A haphazard plan of action.
etymology: From archaic hap (“chance, luck”) + hazard.

definition: Deserving or inciting pity.
example: A hapless victim.
etymology: From about 1400, from hap (“luck”) + -less.

definition: Something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone.
example: Harbinger of danger; harbinger of doom; harbinger of spring.
etymology: Originally, a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings. From Middle English herberjour, herbergeour, from Old French herbergeor (French hébergeur), from herbergier (“to set up camp; to shelter;

definition: Having a hard back or cover.
example: Hardback books.
etymology: From hard + back, formed in analogy to earlier paperback.

definition: A no-nonsense attitude in business or politics.
example: They play hardball in the Senate.
etymology: From hard + ball.

definition: Abnormal hardening or thickening of tissue.
Firm and uncompromising.
example: Smith's hardline approach to drugs gained him the support of many local citizens.
etymology: From hard + line.

definition: Listen; used mostly in the imperative.
Go back to something earlier.
example: This harks back to a previous remark of his.
etymology: From hark (“to listen attentively”) + back (“to or in a previous condition or place”, adverb), originally a hunting command to hounds meaning “Listen! Go back!”.

definition: A clown or buffoon (after the Harlequin character in the commedia dell'arte).
Any of several venomous New World snakes brilliantly banded in red and black and either yellow or white; widely distributed in South America and Central America.
A small rectangular free-reed instrument having a row of free reeds set back in air holes and played by blowing into the desired hole.
etymology: From armonica. Coined by American polymath and statesman Benjamin Franklin to refer to his glass harmonica, an instrument that predated the small wind instrument by several decades. Doublet of harmonic;

definition: The study of musical sound.
Brought under control and put to use.
example: Electricity from the harnessed Colorado River.

definition: A spear with a shaft and barbed point for throwing; used for catching large fish or whales; a strong line is attached to it.
etymology: From Old French harpon, from Latin harpaga, a variant of Latin harpagō, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”).

definition: A strong rope for making the catch fast to the harpooner's boat.
A cylindrical log with a device that registers distance.
Someone who helps to gather the harvest.
etymology: From harvest + -er.

definition: Act at high speed.
etymology: Originally intransitive, from haste + -en (verbal suffix).

definition: A car having a hatchback door.
etymology: From hatch + back.

definition: A sloping rear car door that is lifted to open.
A place where eggs are hatched under artificial conditions (especially fish eggs).
example: The park authorities operated a trout hatchery.
etymology: From hatch (verb) + -ery (suffix denoting a place where an art, craft, or practice is carried out).

definition: Someone who makes and sells hats.
etymology: From Middle English hatter; equivalent to hat + -er.

definition: Trend-setting fashions.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French haute couture (“haute couture, high fashion”), from haute (“high, elegant”) + couture (“sewing”).

definition: A loud laugh that sounds like a horse neighing.
Someone who travels about selling their wares (as on the streets or at carnivals).
etymology: Probably borrowed from Low German or Dutch, from Middle Low German hoker and ultimately from the root of huckster.

definition: A stack of hay.
etymology: From Middle English haystak, haystake, hey stak, equivalent to hay + stack.

definition: Common shrub of the eastern United States with smooth bark.
Any of several shrubs or small trees of the genus Corylus bearing edible nuts enclosed in a leafy husk.
etymology: Equivalent to hazel + nut; from Middle English haselnote, from Old English hæselhnutu (“hazelnut”).

definition: Any of several shrubs or small trees of the genus Corylus bearing edible nuts enclosed in a leafy husk.
An abbreviation for ‘hazardous material’ used on warning signs.
example: No HAZMAT in tunnel.
etymology: Blend of hazardous + material.

definition: A gasket to seal a cylinder head.
Smut fungus attacking heads of corn or sorghum and causing a covered smut.
Clothing for the head.
etymology: From head + gear.

definition: A performer who receives prominent billing.
etymology: From headline (verb) + -er.

definition: A photograph of a person's head.
etymology: From head + shot.

definition: The central building block at the top of an arch or vault.
etymology: From head + stone.

definition: Marked by the exercise of good judgment or common sense in practical matters.
example: The cocktail was a heady mixture of spirits.
etymology: From Middle English hedi, hevedi, equivalent to head + -y.

definition: Conducive to good health of body or mind.
example: A healthful climate.
etymology: From Middle English helthful, helþful, helþeful, equivalent to health + -ful.

definition: A vehicle for carrying a coffin to a church or a cemetery; formerly drawn by horses but now usually a motor vehicle.
etymology: From Middle English herse, hers, herce, from Old French herce in the sense "triangular framework used to support candles".

definition: An abnormal sound of the heart; sometimes a sign of abnormal function of the heart valves.
Sea urchin having a heart-shaped body in a rigid spiny shell.
A painful burning sensation in the chest caused by gastroesophageal reflux (backflow from the stomach irritating the esophagus); symptomatic of an ulcer or a diaphragmatic hernia or other disorder.
etymology: From Middle English hertbryne, herte-bren (“lust", also "heartburn”, literally “heart burn”), equivalent to heart + burn.

definition: A stone that forms a hearth.
etymology: From hearth + stone.

definition: With gusto and without reservation.
example: The boy threw himself heartily into his work.
etymology: From Middle English hertely, herteliche, heorteliche, from Old English ġeheortlīċe (“whole-heartedly, vigorously”), equivalent to hearty + -ly.

definition: Dissipation of heat.
Device that transfers heat from one liquid to another without allowing them to mix.
Common much-branched North American perennial with heathlike foliage and small starry white flowers.
Utter a sound, as with obvious effort.
example: She heaved a deep sigh when she saw the list of things to do.
etymology: From Middle English heven, hebben, from Old English hebban, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to take up, lift”), from Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti, from the root *kap-. See also have.

definition: Lift or elevate.
An upward movement (especially a rhythmical rising and falling).
example: The heaving of waves on a rough sea.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hevynge. By surface analysis, heave + -ing. See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: A lightweight line with a weight attached at the end, thrown between two ships or a ship and the shore to pull a heavier line or rope across.
example: The monkey's fist knot is most often used as the weight in a heaving line.

definition: Any technique designed to reduce or eliminate financial risk; for example, taking two positions that will offset each other if prices change.
A loud laugh that sounds like a horse neighing.
etymology: Onomatopoeic coinage.

definition: Lift or elevate.
example: He hefted the sack of concrete into the truck.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English heft (“heaviness;

definition: Lift or elevate.
Become more extreme.
example: The tension heightened.
etymology: From Middle English heightenen, hyghtenen, equivalent to height + -en (verbal suffix).

definition: A person who expects to inherit but whose right can be defeated by the birth of a nearer relative.
etymology: A calque of French héritier présomptif, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun.

definition: In the shape of a coil.
etymology: By surface analysis, helic- + -al.

definition: A place of eternal fire envisaged as punishment for the damned.
etymology: From Middle English helle fire, helever, from Old English hellefȳr, equivalent to hell + fire. Cognate with West Frisian helfjoer (“hellfire”), Dutch hellevuur (“hellfire”), German Höllenfeuer (“hellfire”).

definition: (informal) very unpleasant.
example: Hellish weather.
etymology: From hell + -ish.

definition: In a helpless manner.
example: The crowd watched him helplessly.
etymology: From helpless + -ly.

definition: Powerlessness revealed by an inability to act.
etymology: From helpless + -ness.

definition: Poisonous drug derived from an Eurasian plant of the genus Conium.
example: Socrates refused to flee and died by drinking hemlock.

definition: An evergreen tree, could refer to any one of a genus of conifers named Tsuga.
A hemoprotein composed of globin and heme that gives red blood cells their characteristic color; function primarily to transport oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues.
example: Fish have simpler hemoglobin than mammals.
etymology: Originally hematinoglobulin, from hematin (from Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -in) + -o- + globulin (from Latin globus (“ball, sphere”) + -in).

definition: Of or relating to a hemorrhage.
A group of illnesses caused by a viral infection (usually restricted to a specific geographic area); fever and gastrointestinal symptoms are followed by capillary hemorrhage.
Stroke caused by the rupture of a blood vessel in the brain.
A man who assists in a plot.
A reddish brown dye used especially on hair.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ), the name of the tree used to make the dye, probably from Middle Persian [script needed] (*hannāy-, “to smear, anoint”). Doublet of alkanet.

definition: Informed about the latest trends.
etymology: Alteration of hip.

definition: Arteries that supply the liver.
Coma that can occur in severe cases of liver disease.
The duct that drains bile from the liver.
Any of the five lobes forming the liver.
A vein that drains the liver; empties into the vena cava.
Characteristic of a nonwoody herb or plant part.
example: The sommelier noted strong herbaceous notes of thyme and lemongrass in the sauvignon blanc.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin herbāceus (“grassy”). By surface analysis, herb + -aceous.

definition: A plant lacking a permanent woody stem; many are flowering garden plants or potherbs; some having medicinal properties; some are pests.
A chemical agent that destroys plants or inhibits their growth.
etymology: From herb + -icide.

definition: In a subsequent part of this document or statement or matter etc.
example: The landlord demises unto the tenant the premises hereinafter called the demised premises.
etymology: From herein + after.

definition: Characterized by departure from accepted beliefs or standards.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French eretical and from Medieval Latin haereticālis, from haereticus, equivalent to heretic + -al. See heretic.

definition: The abode of a hermit.
etymology: From Middle English hermytage, ermitage, from Old French ermitage, hermitaige, from Latin erēmīta, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs, “hermit”). By surface analysis, hermit + -age.

definition: A quatrain consisting of two heroic couplets written in an elevated style; the rhyme scheme is abab.
Ostentatious or vainglorious or extravagant or melodramatic conduct.
example: Heroics are for those epic films they make in Hollywood.
etymology: From hero + -ics.

definition: An infection caused by the herpes simplex virus; affects the skin and nervous system; produces small temporary (but sometimes painful) blisters on the skin and mucous membranes.
Large gull of the Northern Hemisphere.
The quality of being diverse and not comparable in kind.
A six-sided polygon.
etymology: From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon). By surface analysis, hexa- + -gon. Piecewise doublet of sexagon.

definition: Having six sides or divided into hexagons.
example: Nuts in engineering are generally hexagonal.
etymology: From hexagon + -al. Piecewise doublet of sexagonal.

definition: Hernia resulting from the protrusion of part of the stomach through the diaphragm.
Any plant of the genus Hibiscus.
etymology: From Late Latin hibiscus, from Latin hibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos, “marsh mallow”), probably ultimately from Gaulish.

definition: (usually plural) the state of having reflex spasms of the diaphragm accompanied by a rapid closure of the glottis producing an audible sound; sometimes a symptom of indigestion.
example: How do you cure the hiccups?
etymology: From earlier hickop, alteration of earlier hicket, hyckock, from hic (onomatopoeic) + -ock (diminutive suffix).

definition: Ornamental African shrub or climber with red flowers.
A hiding place; usually a remote place used by outlaws.
example: This weekend, let's find some romantic hideaway on the coast.
etymology: From hide + away.

definition: (of persons) excitable.
Elevated ideals or conduct; the quality of believing that ideals should be pursued.
etymology: From high-minded + -ness.

definition: (of a garment) having a high neckline.
example: A high-necked blouse.

definition: A cosmetic used to highlight the eyes or cheekbones.
A foot traveler; someone who goes on an extended walk (for pleasure).
etymology: From hike + -er.

definition: Great merriment.
example: When the new baby's rubber duck squeaked at the wedding, hilarity ensued.
etymology: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful”). By surface analysis, Latin hilar(ō) + -i- + -ty.

definition: Country music originating in mountainous regions of southern United States.
The handle of a sword or dagger.
Ancient Hebrew unit of liquid measure = 1.5 gallons.
example: 500 shekels of cassia — all according to the sanctuary shekel — and a hin of olive oil.
etymology: From Middle English hin, from Latin hin, from Hebrew הִין, from Egyptian h:n-nw-w-W22 (hnw, “jar, unit of liquid volume”).

definition: Preventing movement.
etymology: From hinder + -ing.

definition: A remote and undeveloped area.
etymology: Borrowed from German Hinterland, from hinter (“behind”) + Land (“land”), cognate to English hinder (“back, rear”) + land.

definition: A youth subculture (mostly from the middle class) originating in San Francisco in the 1960s; advocated universal love and peace and communes and long hair and soft drugs; favored acid rock and progressive rock music.
A fricative sound (especially as an expression of disapproval).
example: The performers could not be heard over the hissing of the audience.

definition: A body of historical literature.
etymology: From historio- + -graphy.

definition: To this place (especially toward the speaker).
example: He went hither and thither.
etymology: From Old English hider, from Proto-Germanic *hidrê. Cognate with Latin citer.

definition: (folklore) a small grotesque supernatural creature that makes trouble for human beings.
etymology: Related to hub, but the ultimate origin of both words is obscure.

definition: Any of several white wines from the Rhine River valley in Germany (‘hock’ is British usage).
example: Anyway, you only have one golden retriever, SWORDDOG, and she is already armed to the hocks.
etymology: Clipping of hockamore, from German.

definition: Tarsal joint of the hind leg of hoofed mammals; corresponds to the human ankle.
Extensively cultivated in Europe and Asia for its grain and in United States sometimes for forage.
Large wrasse of western Atlantic; head of male resembles a pig's snout.
Shout out.
example: He hollered out to surrender our weapons.
etymology: American variant of holla, hallo or hollo.

definition: Shout out.
example: He hollered out to surrender our weapons.

definition: Having horns that are hollow.
Hard wood of the holm oak tree.
etymology: Named from a resemblance to the holly plant, also known as holm.

definition: Evergreen oak of southern Europe having leaves somewhat resembling those of holly; yields a hard wood.
A fellow male member of a youth gang.
etymology: 20th-century African-American urban slang. Originated from travelers to metropolitan areas derived from American English as a blend of hometown + boy.

definition: Lacking in physical beauty or proportion.
example: A homely child.

definition: A wife who manages a household while her husband earns the family income.
etymology: From home + maker.

definition: Of or relating to the practice of homeopathy.
example: Homeopathic medicine.
etymology: From homeo- (“similar”) + -pathic (“suffering, disease”).

definition: A method of treating disease with small amounts of remedies that, in large amounts in healthy people, produce symptoms similar to those being treated.
etymology: From German Homöopathie, equivalent to English homeo- + -pathy.

definition: Longing to return home.
example: Feel homesick.
etymology: Back-formation from homesickness, equivalent to home + sick.

definition: Having a feeling of home; cozy and comfortable.
example: A homey little inn.
etymology: From home + -y.

definition: Orienting or directing homeward or to a destination.
example: The homing instinct.

definition: The mechanism in a guided missile that guides it toward its objective.
Pigeon trained to return home.
A torpedo that is guided to its target (as by the sound of a ship's engines).
A polynomial consisting of terms all of the same degree.
All of the same or similar kind or nature.
example: A close-knit homogeneous group.
etymology: From homo- + gene + -ous.

definition: Having the same evolutionary origin but not necessarily the same function.
example: The wing of a bat and the arm of a man are homologous.
etymology: From Late Latin homologus, from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, reckoning”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix).

definition: Old World hawk that feeds on bee larvae and small rodents and reptiles.
etymology: The species was historically assumed to include honey in its diet, due to the fact that it broke open and fed from honeycombs

definition: Tall usually spiny North American tree having small greenish-white flowers in drooping racemes followed by long twisting seed pods; yields very hard durable reddish-brown wood; introduced to temperate Old World.
Carve a honeycomb pattern into.
example: The cliffs were honeycombed.

definition: A machine tool used in the abrasive machining process known as honing.
example: A honing machine, ironically, is relatively inaccurate and compliant.

definition: In an honorable manner.
example: He acted honorably.
etymology: From honorable + -ly.

definition: Conformity with law or custom or practice etc.
Of Mexico and southernmost parts of southwestern United States.
An oriental tobacco pipe with a long flexible tube connected to a container where the smoke is cooled by passing through water.
example: A bipolar world with the hookah and Turkish coffee versus hamburgers and Coca Cola.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani حقہ / हुक़्क़ा (huqqā) and, in turn, derived from Arabic حُقَّة (ḥuqqa, “pot, jar”), from حُقّ (ḥuqq, “cavity, hollow”).

definition: A loud raucous cry (as of an owl).
example: My performance drew hoots of derision from the crowd.
etymology: A variant of utu (influenced by etymology 1), borrowed from Māori utu (“payment, revenge, payback”).

definition: Any owl that hoots as distinct from screeching.
A machine used for picking hops.
The despair you feel when you have abandoned hope of comfort or success.
example: He considered the former tooling hopeless, and he reported its hopelessness to his boss right away.
etymology: From hopeless + -ness.

definition: The maximum parallax observed when the celestial body is at the horizon.
The horizontal airfoil of an aircraft's tail assembly that is fixed and to which the elevator is hinged.
A kind of chameleon.
Any of several four-footed herbivorous dinosaurs with enormous beaked skulls; of the late Cretaceous in North America and Mongolia.
Insectivorous lizard with hornlike spines on the head and spiny scales on the body; of western North America.
Large owls having prominent ear tufts.
Yellow-flowered Eurasian glaucous herb naturalized in along sandy shores in eastern North America.
Insectivorous lizard with hornlike spines on the head and spiny scales on the body; of western North America.
European viola with an unusually long corolla spur.
Highly venomous viper of northern Africa and southwestern Asia having a horny spine above each eye.
A whiff found in waters from the Bahamas and northern Gulf of Mexico to Brazil.
Coarse Eurasian plant cultivated for its thick white pungent root.
A cowboy who takes care of the saddle horses.
A ridge of the earth's crust that has been forced upward between two faults and so is higher than the surrounding land.
Favorable to life and growth.
example: Soil sufficiently hospitable for forest growth.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French hospitable, formed from the root of Latin hospitare with the suffix -able. Displaced native Old English cumlīþe (literally “guest-gentle”).

definition: Someone who performs dangerous stunts to attract attention to themself.
In a heated manner.
example: The children were arguing hotly.
etymology: From Middle English *hotly, *hatliche, from Old English hātlīċe (“ardently, fervently”); equivalent to hot + -ly.

definition: A sandglass that runs for sixty minutes.
example: After each game turn, invert the hourglass to reset the time limit for the next player.
etymology: From hour + glass.

definition: Shaped in the form of an hourglass.
Long-legged centipede common in damp places as e.g. cellars.
etymology: From house + centipede.

definition: A person who specializes in interior decoration.
Someone who owns a home.
etymology: From Middle English housholdere, equivalent to household + -er. The Buddhist sense is a semantic loan from Pali gahapati (literally “house-master”).

definition: Someone who resides in the same house with you.
etymology: From house + -mate.

definition: Overbearing pride or presumption.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὕβρις (húbris, “pride, insolence, outrage”).

definition: Toweling consisting of coarse absorbent cotton or linen fabric.
etymology: Unknown. Perhaps a variant of chuck or hoick.

definition: Plaything consisting of a tubular plastic hoop for swinging around the hips.
The scientific study of human fossils.
The doctrine that people's duty is to promote human welfare.
etymology: From human + -ism, borrowed from German Humanismus, coined by Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer in 1808.

definition: Of or pertaining to a philosophy asserting human dignity and man's capacity for fulfillment through reason and scientific method and often rejecting religion.
example: The humanist belief in continuous emergent evolution.
etymology: From humanist + -ic.

definition: Studies intended to provide general knowledge and intellectual skills (rather than occupational or professional skills).
In the manner of human beings.
example: Humanly possible.
etymology: From human (adjective) + -ly (adverbial suffix). Piecewise doublet of humanely (in Middle English as humanly, when human and humane had not yet become different words).

definition: A singer who produces a tune without opening the lips or forming words.
example: The newlyweds took a hummer limo back to their casino resort.
etymology: From hum + -er.

definition: Tiny American bird having brilliant iridescent plumage and long slender bills; wings are specialized for vibrating flight.
example: Soon I hear the low all-pervading hum of an approaching hummingbird circling above the rock, ….
etymology: From humming (noun) + bird, in reference to the humming sound made by the rapidly moving wings.

definition: Any of various moths with long narrow forewings capable of powerful flight and hovering over flowers to feed.
Large whalebone whale with long flippers noted for arching or humping its back as it dives.
Having the back and shoulders rounded; not erect.
Position 100 in a countable series of things.
etymology: From Middle English hundred (“hundredth”); equivalent to and remodelled after hundred + -th (ordinal suffix), displacing Old English hundtēontigoþa.

definition: Suffering the aftereffects of the consumption of alcohol.
A member of a hunting and gathering society.
etymology: From hunter + gatherer.

definition: A man who hunts game.
etymology: From hunt + -s- + -man.

definition: Throw forcefully.
example: The gangs hurled abuse at each other.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hurlen, of onomatopoeic origin; compare hurry, hurtle.

definition: A victory cheer.
example: Let's give the team a big hurrah.
etymology: Unknown. Possibly adopted from German hurra, itself of uncertain origin, or possibly an alteration of huzzah.

definition: In a hurried or hasty manner.
example: The way they buried him so hurriedly was disgraceful.
etymology: From hurried + -ly.

definition: The practice of cultivating the land or raising stock.
etymology: From Middle English hus-bō̆ndrī, hus-bō̆ndrīe, husbanderi, husbonderie, housbondrye, housebondrie (“household management, housekeeping; household duties; economy, skilful management, thrift;

definition: In a softened tone.
example: Hushed voices.

definition: (used of information or news) kept secret by using influence.
example: Hushed-up stories sometimes leak out.

definition: Material consisting of seed coverings and small pieces of stem or leaves that have been separated from the seeds.
example: A coconut has a very thick husk.
etymology: From Middle English huske, husk (“husk”).

definition: Any of numerous cosmopolitan annual or perennial herbs of the genus Physalis bearing edible fleshy berries enclosed in a bladderlike husk; some cultivated for their flowers.
(genetics) the act of mixing different species or varieties of animals or plants and thus to produce hybrids.
etymology: * hybrid + -ization

definition: Study of the mechanics of fluids.
example: Applied hydraulics.
etymology: From hydraulic + -ics.

definition: A sulfide having the unpleasant smell of rotten eggs.
The branch of geology that studies water on the earth and in the atmosphere: its distribution and uses and conservation.
etymology: From hydro- + -ology.

definition: A chemical reaction in which water reacts with a compound to produce other compounds; involves the splitting of a bond and the addition of the hydrogen cation and the hydroxide anion from the water.
etymology: From hydro- + -lysis.

definition: Lacking affinity for water; tending to repel and not absorb water; tending not to dissolve in or mix with or be wetted by water.
etymology: From hydrophobia + -ic.

definition: The totality of all of the industries involved in the production of electricity and energy harnessed from falling water and running water.
A compound of an oxide with water.
etymology: From hydro- + oxide.

definition: The anion OH having one oxygen and one hydrogen atom.
A powerful doglike mammal of southern and eastern Africa that hunts in large packs; now rare in settled area.
Tending to promote or preserve health.
example: Hygienic habits like using disposable tissues.
etymology: From French hygiénique. Displaced earlier hygienal.

definition: More active than normal.
example: A hyperactive child.
etymology: From hyper- + active.

definition: A condition characterized by excessive restlessness and movement.
etymology: From hyper- + activity.

definition: Extravagant exaggeration.
Pathological sensitivity.
etymology: From hyper- + sensitivity.

definition: A trance induced by the use of hypnosis; the person accepts the suggestions of the hypnotist.
Having your attention fixated as though by a spell.
Subnormal body temperature.
By hypothesis.
example: He offered the proposition hypothetically.
etymology: From hypothetical + -ly.

definition: Oxygen deficiency causing a very strong drive to correct the deficiency.
etymology: By surface analysis, hyp- + ox- + -ia.

definition: Surgical removal of the uterus.
etymology: From hyster- + -ectomy.

definition: In a hysterical manner.
example: She screamed hysterically when she heard the news.
etymology: From hysterical + -ly.

definition: Wading birds of warm regions having long slender down-curved bills.
etymology: Mentioned in the Wycliffe Bible (Lev. 11:17) as ybyn or ibin, as ibys from 16th century and ibis shortly after.

definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory and analgesic medicine (trade names Advil and Motrin and Nuprin) used to relieve the pain of arthritis and as an antipyretic.
example: Daily use of ibuprofen can irritate the stomach.
etymology: From i(so)bu(tyl) + pro(pionic acid) + phen(yl).

definition: Ice cream or water ice on a small wooden stick.
example: In England a popsicle is called an ‘ice lolly’.

definition: Tongs for lifting blocks of ice.
A ship with a reinforced bow to break up ice and keep channels open for navigation.
etymology: From ice + breaker, in the figurative sense from the expression to break the ice.

definition: Very bad.
example: I stepped in something icky and it smells terrible.
etymology: 1935, American English; from icky-boo (circa 1920): sickly, nauseated; baby talk corruption of sick; from a sentimental term for jazz music.

definition: The images and symbolic representations that are traditionally associated with a person or a subject.
example: Religious iconography.
etymology: From icono- + -graphy.

definition: Someone guided more by ideals than by practical considerations.
etymology: From French idéaliste, from Late Latin idealis (“ideal”), from Latin idea (“idea”), equivalent to ideal + -ist.

definition: Exalted to an ideal perfection or excellence.
With complete identity; in an identical manner.
example: He is fitted with an identically similar one.
etymology: From identical + -ly.

definition: A manner of speaking that is natural to native speakers of a language.
example: In English, idiom requires the indefinite article in a phrase such as "she's an engineer", whereas in Spanish, idiom forbids it.

definition: Peculiar to the individual.
example: We all have our own idiosyncratic gestures.
etymology: From idiosyncrasy + -ic. By surface analysis, idio- + syn- + -cratic.

definition: A pulley on a shaft that presses against a guide belt to guide or tighten it.
Having no employment.
example: NO IDLING [sign posted where excess truck exhaust is unwelcome].

definition: In an idle manner.
example: This is what I always imagined myself doing in the south of France, sitting idly, drinking coffee, watching the people.
etymology: From Middle English idely, ydelly, idelliche, from Old English īdellīċe, equivalent to idle + -ly.

definition: The worship of idols; the worship of physical objects or images as gods.
Subject to accident or chance or change.
example: An iffy proposition.
etymology: From if + -y.

definition: Produced under conditions involving intense heat.
example: Igneous rock is rock formed by solidification from a molten state; especially from molten magma.
etymology: From Latin igneus (“fiery”). By surface analysis, Latin ign- + -eous.

definition: Rock formed by the solidification of molten magma.
A kind of person.
example: I can't tolerate people of his ilk.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English ilke, from Old English ilca, conjectured as from Proto-Germanic *ilīkaz, a compound of *iz and *-līkaz from the noun *līką (“body”).

definition: Ignorance resulting from not reading.
example: Illiteracy is widespread in certain areas of the country.
etymology: From il- + literacy.

definition: Based on or having the nature of an illusion.
example: Illusive hopes of finding a better job.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French illusorie (modern French illusoire), derived from Latin illūsōrius (“mocking, ironical”).

definition: (followed by ‘with’) deeply filled or permeated.
example: Imbued with the spirit of the Reformation.

definition: Of no importance or relevance especially to a law case.
example: An objection that is immaterial after the fact.
etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English immaterial, inmateriall (“incorporeal;

definition: Not having reached maturity.
example: Emotional immaturity.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin immātūritātem.

definition: Impossible to measure.
example: Immeasurable suffering.
etymology: From Middle English inmesurable, ynmesurable; equivalent to im- + measurable.

definition: Lack of an intervening or mediating agency.
example: The immediacy of television coverage.
etymology: From immedi(ate) + -acy.

definition: Thrust or throw into.
example: Immerse yourself in hot water.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.

definition: Not capable of movement or of being moved.
etymology: From Old French immobile, from Latin immōbilis, equivalent to im- + mobile.

definition: The quality of not being in accord with standards of right or good conduct.
example: The immorality of basing the defense of the West on the threat of mutual assured destruction.

definition: Not able or intended to be moved.
example: The immovable hills.
etymology: From Middle English immevable, immoveable. Equivalent to im- + movable.

definition: Therapy designed to produce immunity to a disease or to enhance resistance by the immune system.
etymology: From immuno- + therapy.

definition: Not subject or susceptible to change or variation in form or quality or nature.
example: The view of that time was that all species were immutable, created by God.
etymology: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- + mutable.

definition: Make worse or less effective.
example: His vision was impaired.
etymology: From Middle English impairen, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, from Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from in- + Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from peiōrem (“worse”), comparative of malus (“bad”).

definition: An inclination to weigh both views or opinions equally.
etymology: From Middle French impartialité. By surface analysis, impartial + -ity = im- + partial + -ity.

definition: A situation in which no progress can be made or no advancement is possible.
example: Reached an impasse on the negotiations.

definition: Characterized by intense emotion.
example: An impassioned appeal.
etymology: From impassion + -ed.

definition: Made difficult or slow.
example: We blamed our impeded progress on lack of money.

definition: Preventing movement.
The state or an instance of being imperfect.
Not relating to or responsive to individual persons.
example: An impersonal corporation.
etymology: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.

definition: Assume or act the character of.
example: She impersonates Madonna.
etymology: From im- + person + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: A representation of a person that is exaggerated for comic effect.
etymology: From im- + person + -ation or impersonate + -ion.

definition: Not admitting of passage or capable of being affected.
example: A material impervious to water.
etymology: From Latin impervius (“that cannot be passed through”), from in- (“not”) + pervius (“letting things through”).

definition: Having a quality that provokes disbelief.
example: Gave the teacher an implausible excuse.
etymology: From im- + plausible.

definition: Bring into intimate and incriminating connection.
example: He is implicated in the scheme to defraud the government.
etymology: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined;

definition: Call upon in supplication; entreat.
A sudden inward collapse.
example: The implosion of a light bulb.
etymology: From im- + explosion.

definition: A technique used in behavior therapy; client is flooded with experiences of a particular kind until becoming either averse to them or numbed to them.
To a degree impossible of achievement.
example: Long thought to be an impossibly difficult operation.
etymology: From impossible + -ly.

definition: A person who makes deceitful pretenses.
etymology: Replacement of impostor -or with -er.

definition: A person who makes deceitful pretenses.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French imposteur, respelled in the Latin manner; ultimately from Latin impositor, agent form of Latin imponere (“to impose”).

definition: The quality of lacking strength or power; being weak and feeble.
etymology: From Middle French impotence, from Latin impotentia.

definition: Easily impressed or influenced.
example: An impressionable youngster.
etymology: From French impressionnable, equivalent to impression + -able. See also impressible.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of Impressionism.
example: Impressionist music.

definition: In an impressive manner.
example: The students progressed impressively fast.
etymology: From impressive + -ly.

definition: Lock up or confine, in or as in a jail.
example: The suspects were imprisoned without trial.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.

definition: An improper demeanor.
etymology: From French impropriété, from Latin improprietās. By surface analysis, improper + -iety or im- + propriety.

definition: Combined with extraneous elements.
example: The impure gemstone was not good enough to be made into a necklace, so it was thrown out.
etymology: From Middle French impur, from Latin impūrus.

definition: For life.
example: Desire happiness in perpetuity.

definition: The quality of being inaccurate and having errors.
etymology: Morphologically in- + accuracy.

definition: The process of rendering inactive.
example: The gene inactivation system.
etymology: From in- + activation or inactive + -ation.

definition: Lack of an adequate quantity or number.
example: The inadequacy of unemployment benefits.
etymology: From inadequate + -cy or in- + adequacy.

definition: Not deserving to be admitted.
example: Inadmissible evidence.
etymology: From French inadmissible, from Middle French inadmissible. Morphologically in- + admissible.

definition: Happening by chance or unexpectedly or unintentionally.
example: With an inadvertent gesture she swept the vase off the table.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inadvertēns.

definition: Impossible to hear; imperceptible by the ear.
example: An inaudible conversation.
etymology: From in- + audible.

definition: The act of mating closely related individuals.
example: Inbreeding can result in handicapped children.

definition: Electric lamp consisting of a transparent or translucent glass housing containing a wire filament (usually tungsten) that emits light when heated by electricity.
Lack of intellectual power.
etymology: From in- (“negative”) + capacity.

definition: Possessing or existing in bodily form.
example: An incarnate spirit.
etymology: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed;

definition: Enclose in, or as if in, a case.
etymology: From in- + case.

definition: Angered at something unjust or wrong.
example: Incensed at the judges' unfairness.
etymology: See incense.

definition: With unflagging resolve.
example: He jabbered incessantly and annoyed everyone.
etymology: From incessant + -ly.

definition: Having or demonstrating ability to recognize or draw fine distinctions.
example: Incisive comments.
etymology: Late Middle English (in the sense “cutting, penetrating”), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”, adjectival suffix). Compare Middle French incisif.

definition: An act of urging on or spurring on or rousing to action or instigating.
example: The incitement of mutiny.
etymology: From French incitement, from Latin incitāmentum (“incentive; incitement”), from incitō (“urge; quicken; incite”, verb). Equivalent to incite + -ment.

definition: (of weather or climate) severe.
example: Inclement weather.
etymology: From Latin inclēmēns (“unmerciful, severe”), from in- (“not”) + clēmēns (“mild, placid”).

definition: Such that comparison is impossible; unsuitable for comparison or lacking features that can be compared.
example: An incomparable week of rest and pleasure.
etymology: From Middle English incomparable, from Middle French incomparable, from Old French [Term?], from Latin incomparābilis. By surface analysis, in- + comparable.

definition: The relation between propositions that cannot both be true at the same time.
etymology: From incompatible + -ity.

definition: (obstetrics) uterine cervix that becomes dilated before term and without labor often resulting in miscarriage or premature birth.
Lacking worth or importance.
example: His work seems trivial and inconsequential.
etymology: From in- + consequential.

definition: Not prominent or readily noticeable.
example: He pushed the string through an inconspicuous hole.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin incōnspicuus. Equivalent to in- + conspicuous.

definition: Not disposed or willing to believe; unbelieving.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin incrēdulus (“unbelieving”).

definition: A process of becoming larger or longer or more numerous or more important.
example: The increase in unemployment.
etymology: From Middle English encrement, increment, from Latin incrēmentum, from incrēscō (whence increase), from in- + crēscō (“grow”). Equivalent to increase + -ment.

definition: Acquiring or coming into something (usually undesirable).
example: Incurring debts is easier than paying them.

definition: The act of entering some territory or domain (often in large numbers).
example: The incursion of television into the American living room.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French, from Latin incursiō.

definition: An obligation to pay money to another party.
etymology: From indebted + -ness.

definition: Doubt concerning two or more possible alternatives or courses of action.
example: His indecision was only momentary but the opportunity was lost.
etymology: From French indécision.

definition: Characterized by lack of decision and firmness.
example: An indecisive manager brought the enterprise to a standstill.
etymology: From in- + decisive.

definition: (of theories etc.) incapable of being defended or justified.
etymology: From in- + defensible.

definition: (grammar) a pronoun having no specific referent, such as someone, anybody, or nothing.
Cannot be removed or erased.
example: An indelible stain.
etymology: From Latin indēlēbilis (“indestructible”). By surface analysis, in- + delible.

definition: Ink that cannot be erased or washed away.
Protection against future loss.
etymology: From late Middle English indempnite, from Middle French indemnité, from Late Latin indemnitās (“security from damage”), from Latin indemnis (“undamaged”), from in- (“not”) + damnum (“damage”).

definition: Bound by contract.
example: Indentured servant.
etymology: From indenture + -ed.

definition: Defying expression or description.
example: Indescribable beauty.
etymology: From in- + describe + -able.

definition: Not precisely determined or established; not fixed or known in advance.
example: Of indeterminate age.

definition: Accuse formally of a crime.
example: A book that indicts modern values.

definition: A disorder of digestive function characterized by discomfort or heartburn or nausea.
etymology: From Middle English indigestioun, from Old French indigestion, from Late Latin indigestio, by surface analysis, in- + digestion.

definition: Angered at something unjust or wrong.
example: An indignant denial.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin indignāns, present participle of indignor (“to consider as unworthy, be angry or displeased at”), from in- (“privative”) + dignor (“to deem worthy”), from dignus (“worthy”).

definition: Small deep blue North American bunting.
In a random manner.
etymology: From indiscriminate + -ly.

definition: Not open to question; obviously true.
example: Indisputable evidence of a witness.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin indisputābilis. By surface analysis, in- + disputable.

definition: Impossible of undergoing division.
example: An indivisible union of states.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle French indivisible, from Late Latin indivisibilis. Equivalent to in- + divisible.

definition: Cannot be divided without leaving a remainder.
Teaching someone to accept doctrines uncritically.
example: Political indoctrination.
etymology: First attested in 1646; from indoctrinate + -ion.

definition: Impossible to subdue.
etymology: From Late Latin indomitābilis, from in- (“not”) + domitō, frequentative of domō (“to tame”). By surface analysis, in- + domitable.

definition: Arising from inductance.
example: Inductive reactance.
etymology: From Middle French inductif, from Late Latin inductivus.

definition: Reasoning from detailed facts to general principles.
Someone who manages or has significant financial interest in an industrial enterprise.
etymology: From industrial + -ist.

definition: Characterized by hard work and perseverance.
example: He was a very industrious student at school.
etymology: From Middle French industrieux, from Late Latin industriosus (“diligent, active, industrious”), from Latin industria (“diligence, industry”); see industry.

definition: Not producing an intended effect.
example: An ineffective teacher.
etymology: From in- + effectual.

definition: Unskillfulness resulting from a lack of efficiency.
etymology: From in- + efficiency.

definition: Of or relating to inertia.
etymology: From inertia + -al.

definition: A coordinate system in which Newton's first law of motion is valid.
A method of controlling the flight of a missile by devices that respond to inertial forces.
(physics) the mass of a body as determined by the second law of motion from the acceleration of the body when it is subjected to a force that is not due to gravity.
A method of controlling the flight of a missile by devices that respond to inertial forces.
Impossible to avoid or evade.
example: Inescapable conclusion.
etymology: From in- + escapable. Piecewise doublet of unescapable.

definition: The quality of being unavoidable.
Without excuse or justification.
etymology: From Middle French inexcusable, from Latin inexcusabilis.

definition: Lack of experience and the knowledge and understanding derived from experience.
example: Procedural inexperience created difficulties.
etymology: Borrowed from French inexpérience, from Late Latin inexperientia.

definition: In an inextricable manner.
example: Motives inspired by Mammon were often inextricably blended with things pertaining to Caesar and to God.
etymology: From inextricable + -ly.

definition: Indicating a lack of maturity.
example: Infantile behavior.
etymology: Mid-15th century, "pertaining to infants," from Latin infantilis (“pertaining to an infant”), equivalent to infant + -ile, from īnfāns. Sense of "infant-like" is from 1772.

definition: A rare but serious syndrome of childhood characterized by withdrawal and lack of social responsiveness or interest in others and serious linguistic deficits.
example: There is considerable dispute among specialists concerning infantile autism.

definition: Localized necrosis resulting from obstruction of the blood supply.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin infarctiō, equivalent to infarct + -ion.

definition: Marked by foolish or unreasoning fondness.
example: He was infatuated with her.
etymology: From infatuate + -ed.

definition: A foolish and usually extravagant passion or love or admiration.
A sense of personal inferiority arising from conflict between the desire to be noticed and the fear of being humiliated.
etymology: Calque of German Minderwertigkeitskomplex (literally “complex of lesser value”), coined in 1920 by Alfred Adler.

definition: A bomb that has a detonating mechanism that can be set to go off at a particular time.
Incapable of reproducing.
example: An infertile couple.
etymology: From Middle French infertile, from Late Latin infertilis, equivalent to in- + fertile.

definition: Conflict between members of the same organization (usually concealed from outsiders).
etymology: From in- + fighting. Compare Middle English infighten (“to attack”), Old English infiht (“infighting”).

definition: Associated with or tending to cause increases in inflation.
example: Inflationary prices.
etymology: From inflation + -ary.

definition: An episode of inflation in which prices and wages increase at an increasing rate and currency rapidly loses value.
A change in the form of a word (usually by adding a suffix) to indicate a change in its grammatical function.
example: In English, word order often does the work that inflection did in Latin.
etymology: From older inflexion, borrowed from Middle French inflexion, itself borrowed from Latin inflexiōnem (“alteration”, literally “bending”).

definition: Incapable of change.
example: A man of inflexible purpose.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inflexible, from Latin īnflexibilis. See also in- + flexible.

definition: The process of flowing in.
example: The inflow of air.
etymology: From Middle English inflowen, equivalent to in- + flow.

definition: A person who has a large following on one or more social media platform that works to generate interest in contemporary social issues and/or advertise consumer products.
One who reveals confidential information to the police or other authority.
example: Being an informer often meant living in fear.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English enformour, from Anglo-Norman enfourmour; equivalent to inform + -er.

definition: (in writing) at a later place.
example: Vide infra.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin infra (“below”).

definition: Beneath your dignity.
example: Considered helping with the dishes to be infra dig.
etymology: Shortened form of Latin infrā dignitātem (literally “beneath [one's] dignity”).

definition: A crime less serious than a felony.
example: Even stealing a pack of gum is an infraction in the eyes of the law.
etymology: From Middle French infraction, from Latin infractio, from infractum, past participle of infringere, from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

definition: Not frequent; not occurring regularly or at short intervals.
example: Infrequent outbursts of temper.
etymology: From in- + frequent.

definition: Go against, as of rules and laws.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnfringō, īnfringere (“to break off, break, bruise, weaken, destroy”), from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

definition: Marked by extreme anger.
example: Infuriated onlookers charged the police who were beating the boy.

definition: Serve oneself to, or consume regularly.
example: The plane's engine ingested a large bird and flamed out.
etymology: From Latin ingerō (“to carry in”).

definition: The process of taking food into the body through the mouth (as by eating).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ingestionem, accusative of ingestio (“a pouring in”), action noun of the perfect passive participle of ingerere (“pour in”), from in- (“in, into”) + gero (“to carry, to bear”).

definition: (astronomy) the disappearance of a celestial body prior to an eclipse.
example: All ingress was prohibited.
etymology: From Latin ingressus, from the verb ingredior.

definition: A person who inhabits a particular place.
etymology: From Middle English inhabitantes (n.

definition: General anesthesia achieved by administration of an inhalation anesthetic.
A gas that produces general anesthesia when inhaled.

A form of anthrax infection acquired by inhalation of dust containing Bacillus anthracis; initial symptoms (chill and cough and dyspnea and rapid pulse) are followed by extreme cardiovascular collapse.
A dispenser that produces a chemical vapor to be inhaled in order to relieve nasal congestion.
etymology: From inhale + -er.

definition: Having the legal right to inherit.
Restrictive of action.
example: An overly strict and inhibitory discipline.
etymology: From late 15th century (early modern English). Formed as inhibit + -ory or adapted from Medieval Latin inhibitōrius and Middle French inhibitoire.

definition: Unfavorable to life or growth.
example: The barren inhospitable desert.
etymology: From Middle French inhospitable, from Medieval Latin inhospitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + hospitable.

definition: A contrivance for injecting (e.g., water into the boiler of a steam engine or particles into an accelerator etc.).
etymology: From inject + -or.

definition: An eraser that removes ink marks.
A slight suggestion or vague understanding.
example: He had no inkling what was about to happen.
etymology: From Middle English ningkiling, nyngkiling (“hint, slight indication; mention, whisper”), and then either: * possibly a variant of nikking, nyckyng (“hint, slight indication;

definition: A jib between the outer jib and the fore staysail on a large square-rigged ship.
Being deepest within the self.
example: One's innermost feelings.
etymology: From Middle English innermost, innermest, in-nermast, alteration (due to Middle English inner, innere (“inner”)) of Old English innemest (“innermost”), equivalent to inner + -most.

definition: In a not unlawful manner.
example: He claimed to have purchased the contraband innocently.
etymology: From innocent + -ly.

definition: An indirect (and usually malicious) implication.
example: She made a devious innuendo about her opponent, who was embarrassed.
etymology: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).

definition: Not able to perform its normal function.
etymology: From in- + operable.

definition: Someone who asks a question.
etymology: From inquire + -er.

definition: Given to inquiry.
example: An inquiring mind.

definition: Showing curiosity.
example: If someone saw a man climbing a light post they might get inquisitive.
etymology: Late 14th century, from Old French inquisitif, from Late Latin inquisitivus, from Latin inquisitus, past participle of inquirere. See also inquire.

definition: A questioner who is excessively harsh.
example: During the meeting, Jake turned into an inquisitor, firing questions at the presenter non-stop.
etymology: From Old French inquisiteur, from Latin inquīsītor.

definition: A chemical substance that repels insects.
The act of sowing (of seeds in the ground or, figuratively, of germs in the body or ideas in the mind, etc.).
A small picture inserted within the bounds or a larger one.
example: A map of the whole state with city maps as insets.
etymology: From Middle English insetten, from Old English insettan (“to set in, institute, appoint”), equivalent to in- + set.

definition: Calculated to please or gain favor.
(of a substance) incapable of being dissolved.
example: Petroleum is largely insoluble in water.
etymology: From Middle English insolible, from Middle French insoluble, from Latin insolūbilis, from in- + solūbilis. Piecewise doublet of insolvable and unsolvable. By surface analysis, in- + soluble.

definition: Unable to meet or discharge financial obligations.
example: An insolvent person.
etymology: From in- + solvent.

definition: A body of inspectors.
etymology: From inspector + -ate (forms nouns denoting a rank or office, a body of people performing it, the concrete charge of it).

definition: In or of the present month.
example: Your letter of the 10th inst.

definition: Without any delay.
etymology: From instantaneous + -ly.

definition: Provoke or stir up.
example: To instigate a riot.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnstīgātus, perfect passive participle of īnstīgō (“to instigate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: An automatic instinctive unlearned reaction to a stimulus.
Serving to instruct or enlighten or inform.
example: Well, that was an instructive lesson.
etymology: From instruct + -ive.

definition: Unbearably arrogant or conceited.
example: Insufferable insolence.
etymology: From Late Middle English insufferable (“unbearably painful, intolerable”), and then either: * from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + sufferable, souffrable (“bearable, endurable, tolerable; allowable, permissible;

definition: To an insufficient degree.
example: He was insufficiently prepared.
etymology: From insufficient + -ly or in- + sufficiently.

definition: Protect from heat, cold, or noise by surrounding with insulating material.
example: We had his bedroom insulated before winter came.
etymology: From Latin īnsula (“isle, island”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or from Late Latin īnsulātus (“made an island”), see etymology at -ate. First attested in the 16th century;

definition: Combining and coordinating diverse elements into a whole.
example: An integrative approach.
etymology: From integrate + -ive.

definition: A measure of a person's intelligence as indicated by an intelligence test; the ratio of a person's mental age to their chronological age (multiplied by 100).
etymology: Calque of German Intelligenzquotient. Coined in 1912 by German psychologist William Stern.

definition: Capable of being apprehended or understood.
example: Italian and Spanish are partially mutually intelligible languages.
etymology: From Middle French intelligible, from Old French, from Latin intelligibilis.

definition: Action that makes something stronger or more extreme.
etymology: From intense + -ification.

definition: Increasing in strength or intensity.
In an intensive manner.
example: He studied the snake intensively.
etymology: From intensive + -ly.

definition: With strained or eager attention.
example: Listened intently.
etymology: From intent + -ly.

definition: A fast maneuverable fighter plane designed to intercept enemy aircraft.
etymology: From intercept + -or.

definition: A prayer to God on behalf of another person.
etymology: First attested in the early 15th Century.

definition: In an interchangeable manner.
example: These terms can be used interchangeably.
etymology: From interchangeable + -ly.

definition: A communication system linking different rooms within a building or ship etc.
example: Emergency intercom.
etymology: Clipping of intercommunicator.

definition: The loudspeaker on an intercom or public address system.
Involving persons of different religious faiths.
example: An interfaith marriage.
etymology: From inter- + faith.

definition: An antiviral protein produced by cells that have been invaded by a virus; inhibits replication of the virus.
etymology: From interfere + -on (suffix: chemical compound), from its role interfering with viral replication.

definition: Between or among galaxies.
example: Intergalactic space.
etymology: From inter- + galactic.

definition: The space between galaxies.
example: The Milky Way travels through intergalactic space.

definition: A person who specializes in interior decoration.
Contact by fitting together.
Clinical neurological syndrome characterized by muscular twitching and cramps and (when severe) seizures; associated with calcium deficiency (hypoparathyroidism) or vitamin D deficiency or alkalosis.
Clinical neurological syndrome characterized by muscular twitching and cramps and (when severe) seizures; associated with calcium deficiency (hypoparathyroidism) or vitamin D deficiency or alkalosis.
Either one of the two posterior openings at the back of the nasal cavity leading to the nasopharynx.
Confinement during wartime.
etymology: From intern + -ment.

definition: A camp for prisoners of war.
Between or among planets.
example: Interplanetary travel.
etymology: From inter- + planetary.

definition: Microscopic particles in the interplanetary medium.
A rarefied flow of gas and charged particles (plasma) that stream from the sun and form the solar wind.
Interplanetary space including forms of energy and gas and dust.
The part of outer space within the solar system.
A message (spoken or written) that is introduced or inserted.
example: With the help of his friend's interpolations his story was eventually told.
etymology: From French interpolation, from Latin interpolatio. Morphologically interpolate + -ion.

definition: Placed in a grave.
Transmit (a signal) for setting off an appropriate response, as in telecommunication.
example: The police interrogated the suspect at some length before they let him go.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin interrogō (“to inquire, interrogate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Crossed or intersected in the form of an X.
Of or relating to interstices.
example: The novel's interstitial chapters.
etymology: From Latin interstitiālis. By surface analysis, interstitium + -al.

definition: Liquid found between the cells of the body that provides much of the liquid environment of the body.
Tissue between the cells of a structure or part in plant or animal.
Linked or locked closely together as by dovetailing.
Rise and fall of the voice pitch.
example: Her intonation was false.
etymology: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.

definition: Intonations characteristic of questions and requests and statements.
Liquid contained inside the cell membranes (usually containing dissolved solutes).
Not tractable; difficult to manage or mold.
example: An intractable disposition.
etymology: From in- + tractable.

definition: An anesthetic that produces anesthesia when injected into the circulatory system.
The contemplation of your own thoughts and desires and conduct.
etymology: From Latin intrōspectiō, noun of action (with -iō) from past-participle (intrōspectus) stem of intrōspiciō (“to look into, look at, examine, observe attentively”), from intro- (“inward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look at”).

definition: Given to examining own sensory and perceptual experiences.
etymology: From Latin intro "inward, within" (see intro-) + Latin specere "look at".

definition: Fold inwards.
example: […] the Soul being straight, introverted […] into itself, and easily conforming to God's will and time […].
etymology: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

definition: Given to examining own sensory and perceptual experiences.
example: The introverted type is characterised by the fact that his libido is turned towards his own personality to a certain extent.
etymology: From introvert + -ed, q.v.

definition: Enter uninvited.
example: They intruded on our dinner party.
etymology: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).

definition: To intrude upon, infringe, encroach on, violate.
example: The neighbors intrude on your privacy.

definition: Someone who enters by force in order to conquer.
etymology: From invade + -er.

definition: Deprived of legal force.
The inverse function of the sine; the angle that has a sine equal to a given number.
The inverse function of the tangent; the angle that has a tangent equal to a given number.
In an inverse or contrary manner.
example: Inversely related.
etymology: From inverse + -ly.

definition: An electrical converter that converts direct current into alternating current.
etymology: From invert + -er.

definition: The quality of not being perceivable by the eye.
etymology: From Middle French invisibilité, from Latin invisibilitas.

definition: A prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service.
example: The invocation of papers or evidence into court.
etymology: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.

definition: Against one's will or done without conscious thought.
example: He was involuntarily held against his will.
etymology: From involuntary + -ly or in- + voluntarily.

definition: To or toward the inside of.
etymology: From in + -wards.
