definition: High-energy radiation capable of producing ionization in substances through which it passes.
A tiny or scarcely detectable amount.
example: As a Greek numeral, iota represents ten.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *yad- (“hand”). Doublet of jot and yodh.

definition: Feeling or showing extreme anger.
example: Irate protesters.
etymology: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

definition: Varying in color when seen in different lights or from different angles.
example: A dragonfly hovered, vibrating and iridescent.
etymology: Coined around 1800, from Latin iris, iridis (“rainbow”) + -escent.

definition: A chemical compound that is a constituent of steel and cast iron; very hard and brittle.
A cement resembling putty; made by mixing ferric oxide and boiled linseed oil; is acid resistant.
(of linens or clothes) smoothed with a hot iron.
At an uneven rate.
example: The patient is breathing irregularly.
etymology: From irregular + -ly.

definition: Impossible to repair, rectify, or amend.
example: Irreparable harm.
etymology: From Middle French irréparable, from Old French, from Latin irreparabilis, equivalent to ir- + reparable.

definition: Showing lack of due respect or veneration.
example: Irreverent scholars mocking sacred things.
etymology: From Latin irreverēns. By surface analysis, ir- + reverent.

definition: Incapable of being retracted or revoked.
example: Firm and irrevocable is my doom.
etymology: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.

definition: In an irrevocable manner.
etymology: From irrevocable + -ly.

definition: An irritable petulant feeling.
example: Irritability of temper.
etymology: From Latin irritabilitās, equivalent to irritable + -ity.

definition: Local anemia in a given body part sometimes resulting from vasoconstriction or thrombosis or embolism.
etymology: From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”).

definition: Relating to or affected by ischemia.
etymology: From ischemia + -ic. Compare French ischémique.

definition: The most common kind of stroke; caused by an interruption in the flow of blood to the brain (as from a clot blocking a blood vessel).
An inhabitant of an island.
A small island.
example: There is an islet on the other side of this body of water.
etymology: From Middle French islette. By surface analysis, is(le) + -let. Mostly displaced native Middle English eyt, eit and Middle English holm, holme (See eyot and holm for more).

definition: Related by an isometry.
example: Isometric exercise.
etymology: From iso- + -metric.

definition: Muscle-building exercises (or a system of musclebuilding exercises) involving muscular contractions against resistance without movement (the muscles contracts but the length of the muscle does not change).
A line connecting isometric points.
A thermodynamic process during which the volume of the closed system undergoing such a process remains constant.
A relatively narrow strip of land (with water on both sides) connecting two larger land areas.
etymology: Borrowing from Latin isthmus (“a strip of land between two seas”), from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck, narrow passage”), possibly from εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go”). Cognate to Old Norse eið (“isthmus”).

definition: Whitish mites that attack the skin of humans and other animals.
example: Itch mites cause scabies.

definition: Marked by iteration.
etymology: Borrowed from French itératif.

definition: The aspect of the verb that expresses the repetition of an action.
Traveling from place to place to work.
example: Itinerant labor.
etymology: From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

definition: White Arctic gull; migrates as far south as England and New Brunswick.

definition: Having one side lower or smaller or lighter than the other.
example: Carrying a heavy suitcase, he walked with a lopsided gait.
etymology: From lop (“to hang loosely”) + side + -ed.

definition: Fishes having large mouths with a wormlike filament attached for luring prey.
etymology: Borrowed from French lotte.

definition: Electro-acoustic transducer that converts electrical signals into sounds loud enough to be heard at a distance.
Electro-acoustic transducer that converts electrical signals into sounds loud enough to be heard at a distance.
A long narrow (nearly landlocked) cove in Ireland.
etymology: Borrowed from Irish loch (from Old Irish loch), from Proto-Celtic *loku (“lake, pool”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“pond, pool”). Doublet of lay, loch, and Looe.

definition: A man's soft jacket usually with a tie belt; worn at home.
A robe worn before dressing or while lounging.
Having characteristics that attract love or affection.
Restrained in style or quality.
example: A little masterpiece of low-keyed eloquence.

definition: (of a garment) having a low-cut neckline.
Relating to small (not capitalized) letters that were kept in the lower half of a compositor's type case.
example: Lowercase letters: a and b and c etc.
etymology: From the noun phrase lower case, which itself consists of an adjective modifying a noun;

definition: Of relatively low or level country.
etymology: From low + land.

definition: Lofty fir of the Pacific coast of northwestern America having long curving branches and deep green leaves.
The condition of having been made smooth or slippery by the application of a lubricant.
etymology: From lubricate + -ion.

definition: Important European leguminous forage plant with trifoliate leaves and blue-violet flowers grown widely as a pasture and hay crop.
etymology: Borrowed from French luzerne, from Occitan luzerno, of uncertain origin.

definition: A wrench with jaws that have projecting lugs to engage the object that is to be rotated.
One of four or five pairs of arteries that originate in the abdominal aorta and supply the lumbar vertebrae and the back muscles and abdominal wall.
Removal by centesis of fluid from the subarachnoid space of the lumbar region of the spinal cord for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.
The quality of being luminous; emitting or reflecting light.
example: Its luminosity is measured relative to that of our sun.
etymology: Borrowed from French luminosité or else a native formation from luminous + -ity.

definition: Like or containing small sticky lumps.
example: I don't know which was worse, the lumpy soup or the lumpy bed.
etymology: From lump + -y.

definition: The commonest and least severe form of actinomycosis; affects the face and neck regions.
Obsolete terms for legal insanity.
etymology: From lun(atic) + -acy.

definition: Silver nitrate fused into sticks and formerly used as a caustic.
etymology: From lunar (“[alchemical] silver”) + caustic.

definition: The act of moving forward suddenly.
etymology: From French allonge, from Old French alonge, from alongier, from Vulgar Latin *allongare, from ad + Late Latin longare, from Latin longus. Doublet of allonge.

definition: Any plant of the genus Lupinus; bearing erect spikes of usually purplish-blue flowers.
Walk as if unable to control one's movements.
etymology: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of unknown origin.

definition: A quality that outshines the usual.
example: Metallic luster.
etymology: From Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro, from Old Italian lustrare (“brighten”), from Latin lūstrō (“to purify, to brighten”), from Latin lūstrum (“purification ritual”).

definition: A surface coating for ceramics or porcelain.
etymology: From Middle French lustre. See luster (etymology 1).

definition: Vigorously passionate.
etymology: From Middle English lusty (“mirthful, pleasant, delicious, delightful”), equivalent to lust + -y.

definition: A substance for packing a joint or coating a porous surface to make it impervious to gas or liquid.
etymology: From Middle French lut (modern luth), from Old French leüt, probably from Old Occitan laüt, from Arabic اَلْعُود (al-ʕūd, “wood”) (probably representing an Andalusian Arabic or North African pronunciation).

definition: Elegant and sumptuous.
example: A deluxe car.
etymology: From French luxe, from Latin luxus. Cognate with English lock.

definition: The source of lymph and lymphocytes.
Of or relating to or produced by lymph.
etymology: From lymph + -atic.

definition: The interconnected system of spaces and vessels between body tissues and organs by which lymph circulates throughout the body.
Tissue making up the lymphatic system.
A vascular duct that carries lymph which is eventually added to the venous blood circulation.
In a lyrical manner.
example: She danced the part of the Black Swan very lyrically.
etymology: From lyrical + -ly.

definition: A person who writes the words for songs.
etymology: From lyric + -ist.

definition: Shockingly repellent; inspiring horror.
example: Macabre tales of war and plague in the Middle ages.
etymology: Borrowed from French macabre, whose etymology is uncertain. Possibly from the term danse macabre, most commonly believed to be from corruption of the biblical name Maccabees; compare Latin Chorea Machabaeorum.

definition: A craftsman skilled in operating machine tools.
etymology: From French machiniste, from machine (“machine, mechanical device”), from Latin māchina, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

definition: A lightweight waterproof (usually rubberized) fabric.
etymology: From Charles Macintosh (1766–1843), who patented a type of rubberized cloth in 1823. Former trademark. The letter k is a later addition.

definition: A diacritical mark (-) placed above a vowel to indicate a long sound.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μακρόν (makrón), neuter form of μακρός (makrós, “long”) (English macro-).

definition: Extremely annoying or displeasing.
example: The ceaseless tumult of the jukebox was maddening.

definition: Small silvery drumfish often mistaken for white perch; found along coasts of United States from New York to Mexico.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French mademoiselle.

definition: A white crystalline powder used chiefly in medicines.
A dipole with opposing magnetic poles.
The act of expanding something in apparent size.
Splendid or imposing in size or appearance.
etymology: From Middle English magnificence, from Old French magnificence, from Latin magnificentia.

definition: Wonderfully.
etymology: From Middle English magnyficently; equivalent to magnificent + -ly.

definition: Enlarged to an abnormal degree.
example: The image was magnified by a factor of eight.

definition: Increase in size, volume or significance.
example: Her terror was magnified in her mind.
etymology: From Middle English magnifien, from Middle French magnifier, from Latin magnificāre, from magnificus.

definition: Light microscope consisting of a single convex lens that is used to produce an enlarged image.
example: The magnifying glass was invented by Roger Bacon in 1250.

definition: A great work of art or literature.
example: The 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four is widely considered to be George Orwell's magnum opus.
etymology: From Latin magnum opus (“great work”).

definition: Long-tailed black-and-white crow that utters a raucous chattering call.
etymology: From Mag, a nickname for Margaret that was used to denote a chatterer, + archaic pie (“magpie”). Displaced native Old English agu (“magpie”) and Middle English aguster (“magpie”), whence English haggister.

definition: A person who mails something.
example: The cassette came in a brown paper mailer.
etymology: From mail + -er.

definition: A man who delivers the mail.
etymology: From mail + man.

definition: Having a part of the body crippled or disabled.
etymology: From Middle English maymed, ymaymed. By surface analysis, maim + -ed.

definition: A large digital computer serving 100-400 users and occupying a special air-conditioned room.
etymology: From main + frame.

definition: A large digital computer serving 100-400 users and occupying a special air-conditioned room.
Powerful mackerel shark of the Atlantic and Pacific.
etymology: Borrowed from Māori makō (“shark”), a Southern Maori dialect form of the more standard mangō (“shark”).

definition: Powerful mackerel shark of the Atlantic and Pacific.
etymology: Borrowed from Māori makō (“shark”), a Southern Māori dialect form of the more standard mangō (“shark”).

definition: Stem of the rattan palm used for making canes and umbrella handles.
A cane made from the stem of a rattan palm.
Physical discomfort (as mild sickness or depression).
etymology: From French malaise (“ill ease”), from mal- (“bad, badly”) + aise (“ease”). Compare ill at ease.

definition: A man who is an aristocrat.
Harmful or evil in intent or effect.
example: Maleficent influence.
etymology: From Latin *maleficēns, from male (“bad”) + -ficēns, combining form from faciēns, present participle of faciō (“to make or do”).

definition: Wishing or appearing to wish evil to others; arising from intense ill will or hatred.
example: A gossipy malevolent old woman.
etymology: From Middle English *malevolent (suggested by Middle English malevolence), from Old French malivolent and Latin malevolentem, from male (“badly, wrongly”) + volens (“willing, wishing”), from velle (“to wish”).

definition: A computer program designed to have undesirable or harmful effects.
Not performing or able to perform its regular function.
example: A malfunctioning valve.

definition: With malice; in a malicious manner.
example: She answered maliciously.
etymology: From Middle English maliciousli; equivalent to malicious + -ly.

definition: A chronic progressive anemia of older adults; thought to result from a lack of intrinsic factor (a substance secreted by the stomach that is responsible for the absorption of vitamin B12).
Any of several malignant neoplasms (usually of the skin) consisting of melanocytes.
Wild dabbling duck from which domestic ducks are descended; widely distributed.
etymology: From Middle English malard, mawlard, from Old French malard, malart, mallart (“male wild duck”), from Old French male, masle (“male”) + -ard, -art. Cognate with Medieval Latin maslardus, mallardus.

definition: Easily influenced.
example: My opinion on the subject is malleable.

definition: Not being provided with adequate nourishment.
etymology: From mal- + nourished.

definition: A Latin American dance similar in rhythm to the rumba.
etymology: From Haitian Creole manbo (“voodoo priestess”) (ultimately from Yoruba mambo (“to talk”)), in later senses via Cuban Spanish mambo (“dance”).

definition: Any of various geometric designs (usually circular) symbolizing the universe; used chiefly in Hinduism and Buddhism as an aid to meditation.
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit मण्डल (máṇḍala). Doublet of mandal.

definition: The jaw in vertebrates that is hinged to open the mouth.
etymology: From late Middle English, from Late Latin mandibula (“a jaw”), from mandō (“to chew, masticate”) + -bula (instrument noun suffix).

definition: A stringed instrument related to the lute, usually played with a plectrum.
etymology: From French mandoline, from Italian mandolino, diminutive of mandola, a large stringed instrument.

definition: A container (usually in a barn or stable) from which cattle or horses feed.
etymology: From Middle English manger, from Old French mangeoire, menjoere, from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger). Cognate with Galician manxadoira, Italian mangiatoia, Occitan manjadoira, French mangeoire.

definition: Having edges that are jagged from injury.
etymology: From mangle + -ed.

definition: A tropical tree or shrub bearing fruit that germinates while still on the tree and having numerous prop roots that eventually form an impenetrable mass and are important in land building.
etymology: A modification of earlier mangrowe (obsolete) by the influence of grove (“small forest”) through folk etymology.

definition: Trees and shrubs that usually form dense jungles along tropical seacoasts.
A hole (usually with a flush cover) through which a person can gain access to an underground structure.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:manhole.
etymology: From man + hole.

definition: A flush iron cover for a manhole (as in a street).
Trim carefully and neatly.
example: Manicure fingernails.
etymology: From French manucure.

definition: A set of implements used to manicure.
An agent that operates some apparatus or machine.
etymology: From manipulate + -or.

definition: Hardened sugary exudation of various trees.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old English, from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מן (mān, “'manna”).

definition: Southern Mediterranean ash having fragrant white flowers in dense panicles and yielding manna.
Any of several moisture-loving grasses of the genus Glyceria having sweet flavor or odor.
Tall tree yielding a false manna.
A blanket that is used as a cloak or shawl.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish manta (“blanket”).

definition: Extremely large pelagic tropical ray that feeds on plankton and small fishes; usually harmless but its size make it dangerous if harpooned.
etymology: From Spanish mantarraya, itself a compound from manta and raya; according to Jorge Juan y Santacilia and Antonio de Ulloa, so called “for being broad and long like a quilt”.

definition: Shelf that projects from wall above fireplace.
etymology: A variant of mantle (“cloak, robe”) now distinguished in sense.

definition: Someone who works with their hands; someone engaged in manual labor.
example: I hired a manual laborer to re-shingle my roof.

definition: The (prehensile) extremity of the superior limb.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin manus (“hand”). Doublet of mano.

definition: A spread made chiefly from vegetable oils and used as a substitute for butter.
etymology: Borrowed from French margarine, from acide margarique (“margaric acid”), from Ancient Greek μάργαρον (márgaron, “pearl”), in allusion to its pearly lustre, with the suffix -ine, influenced by glycérine (“glycerine”).

definition: A grunt with a red mouth that is found from Florida to Brazil.
A group of street musicians in Mexico.
etymology: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish mariachi. The origin of the Spanish word is unclear.

definition: Any of various tropical American plants of the genus Tagetes widely cultivated for their showy yellow or orange flowers.
etymology: From Middle English marigolde, marygoldye, from Mary (referring to the Virgin Mary) + Middle English golde (“marigold”).

definition: Mixtures of vinegar or wine and oil with various spices and seasonings; used for soaking foods before cooking.
example: I like to use a lemon marinade with chicken.
etymology: Borrowed from French marinade. By surface analysis, marine + -ade.

definition: The archeology of underwater sites.
Someone who promotes or exchanges goods or services for money.
etymology: From market + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (agent noun suffix).

definition: A man skilled in shooting.
etymology: From mark + -s- + man.

definition: A preserve made of the pulp and rind of citrus fruits.
example: Lime marmalade.

definition: Tree of the West Indies and northern South America bearing succulent edible orange-sized fruit.
Evergreen South American shrub having showy trumpet-shaped orange flowers; grown as an ornamental or houseplant.
Any of various common orange trees yielding sour or bitter fruit; used as grafting stock.
Brown oval fruit flesh makes excellent sherbet.
Tropical American tree having wood like mahogany and sweet edible egg-shaped fruit; in some classifications placed in the genus Calocarpum.
Nobleman (in various countries) ranking above a count.
example: Anne Boleyn was created Marquess of Pembroke in 1532.
etymology: See marquis for etymology. Note also that marquess is very unusual in the English language in that it ends in -ess but is a masculine term. The title is granted only to males (the female equivalent is marchioness).

definition: A very sweet white spread resembling marshmallow candy.
etymology: From a US brand name.

definition: (Islam) a Muslim place of worship.
example: Any masjid where the practices are devoted absolutely to The God ALONE.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid), from the root س ج د (s j d). Doublet of mosque.

definition: Spectroscope for obtaining a mass spectrum by deflecting ions into a thin slit and measuring the ion current with an electrometer.
Relating to or involving mass spectroscopy.
Someone who arranges (or tries to arrange) marriages for others.
etymology: From match + maker.

definition: Marked by materialism.
etymology: From material + -istic.

definition: Come into being; become reality.
example: Her dream really materialized.
etymology: From material + -ize.

definition: Equipment and supplies of a military force.
etymology: Borrowed from French matériel. Doublet of material.

definition: A theatrical performance held during the daytime (especially in the afternoon).
etymology: From French matinée.

definition: Someone who is adored blindly and excessively.
Of or relating to the state of marriage.
example: Matrimonial bliss.
etymology: From Middle French matrimonial, also matrimony + -al.

definition: That branch of jurisprudence that studies the laws governing matrimony.
Any of various shrubs or vines of the genus Lycium with showy flowers and bright berries.
Tangled in a dense mass.
example: Tried to push through the matted undergrowth.

definition: Coming to full development; becoming mature.
etymology: From Middle English maturacioun, from Middle French maturation, from Latin maturatio. By surface analysis, mature + -ation.

definition: Split (wood) with a maul and wedges.
example: The bear mauled him in a terrible way.
etymology: From Middle English malle (“mace, maul”), from Anglo-Norman mail, from Old French mail, from Latin malleus (“hammer”). Doublet of malleus.

definition: Medium-sized evergreen of southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico with oblong leathery often spiny-edged leaves.
A large burial chamber, usually above ground.
Someone who is dazzlingly skilled in any field.
etymology: From Yiddish מבֿין (meyvn, “connoisseur, expert, know-it-all”), from Hebrew מֵבִין (mevín, “one who understands, connoisseur, expert”), from הֵבִין (hevín, “to understand”).

definition: Common Old World thrush noted for its song.
etymology: From Middle English mavys, from Anglo-Norman mauvis, from Old French mauvis (“song thrush”).

definition: Low-growing evergreen shrub of eastern North America with leathery leaves and clusters of fragrant pink or white flowers.
etymology: From May + flower.

definition: One millionth (1/1,000,000) gram.
North American bulbous plant.
Deficient in amount or quality or extent.
etymology: From Middle French maigre.

definition: Of a path e.g.
example: Meandering streams.

definition: In a meaningful manner; so as to be meaningful.
example: He glanced at her meaningfully.
etymology: From meaningful + -ly.

definition: Ground meat formed into a ball and fried or simmered in broth.
A baked loaf of ground meat.
etymology: Compound of meat + loaf.

definition: Relating to or concerned with machinery or tools.
example: Mechanical arts.

definition: Equipped with machinery.
example: A mechanized factory.

definition: An armored unit of a modern army equipped with motor vehicles.
Intrude in other people's affairs or business; interfere unwantedly.
example: Don't meddle in my affairs!
etymology: From Middle English medlen, from Anglo-Norman medler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin misceō (“to mix”).

definition: Relating to or belonging to the Middle Ages.
Deeply or seriously thoughtful.
example: Yoga is a meditative practice.
etymology: From Middle French méditatif.

definition: A cone-shaped acoustic device held to the mouth to intensify and direct the human voice.
etymology: From mega- + -phone.

definition: Characterized by or causing or expressing sadness.
example: Growing more melancholy every hour.
etymology: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”).

definition: Insoluble pigments that account for the color of e.g. skin and scales and feathers.
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem of μέλας (mélas, “black”) + -in; by surface analysis, melan- + -in.

definition: Hormone secreted by the pineal gland.
etymology: From mela- + tone + -in, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black, dark”).

definition: Having the excitement and emotional appeal of melodrama.
example: A melodramatic account of two perilous days at sea.
etymology: From melodrama + -tic. Modelled after dramatic.

definition: The 13th letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
etymology: From Phoenician 𐤌𐤌 (mm /⁠mem⁠/, “water”), from Proto-Semitic *maʾ- (“*maʾ-/*may-”). Doublet of mu.

definition: A reminder of past events.
A collection of live animals for study or display.
etymology: From French ménagerie, derived from ménager (“to keep house”), household. Housekeeping used to include taking care of domestic animals.

definition: Garments that must be repaired.
Used of unskilled work (especially domestic work).
example: A menial wretch.
etymology: From Middle English meyneal, from Anglo-Norman mesnal, from maisnee (“household”), from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō (“house”).

definition: (anatomy) a disk of cartilage that serves as a cushion between the ends of bones that meet at a joint.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μηνίσκος (mēnískos, “crescent”), from μήνη (mḗnē, “moon”). Piecewise doublet of moonish.

definition: The monthly discharge of blood from the uterus of nonpregnant women from puberty to menopause.
example: The women were sickly and subject to excessive menstruation.
etymology: From menstruum + -ation, modelled after Late Latin menstruatio. The word is a cognate with French menstruation, Spanish menstruación, which displaced Old English mōnaþblōd (literally “monthblood”).

definition: Any abnormality of mental function.
Intelligence as revealed by an ability to give correct responses without delay.
Lack of normal development of intellectual capacities.
A crystalline compound that has the cool and minty taste and odor that occurs naturally in peppermint oil; used as a flavoring and in medicine to relieve itching, pain, and nasal congestion.
etymology: From Latin mentha (“mint”) + -ol.

definition: Without pity; in a merciless manner.
example: He was mercilessly trounced by his opponent in the House.
etymology: From merciless + -ly.

definition: Relating to or containing or caused by mercury.
example: Mercurial preparations.
etymology: Noun sense 1 (“(obsolete) plant known as mercury”) is from Middle English mercurial (“a plant, probably the goosefoot (Chenopodium);

definition: Sweet topping especially for pies made of beaten egg whites and sugar.
example: The key to a good baked Alaska is the meringue topping.
etymology: Borrowed from French meringue.

definition: A kiss made of sugar and egg white and baked slowly.
White sheep originating in Spain and producing a heavy fleece of exceptional quality.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish merino.

definition: White sheep originating in Spain and producing a heavy fleece of exceptional quality.
Deserving reward or praise.
example: A lifetime of meritorious service.
etymology: From Middle English meritorious, borrowed between 1375 and 1425 from Latin meritōrius (“earning money”), from meritus, past participle of mereō (“to earn”).

definition: In a joyous manner.
example: Go merrily along.
etymology: From Middle English myriely, from Old English myriġlīċe; equivalent to merry + -ly.

definition: Having your attention fixated as though by a spell.
etymology: Derived from mesmerism, a pseudoscientific theory and practiced originating with and named after Franz Anton Mesmer and also known as animal magnetism.

definition: Attracting and holding interest as if by a spell.
example: She had a warm mesmeric charm.

definition: Of or relating to a messiah promising deliverance.
example: Messianic cult.
etymology: From Messiah + -n- + -ic.

definition: Any substance involved in metabolism (either as a product of metabolism or as necessary for metabolism).
etymology: From metabolism + -ite.

definition: Of or relating to metallurgy.
example: Metallurgical engineer.
etymology: From metallurgy + -ical.

definition: An engineer trained in the extraction and refining and alloying and fabrication of metals.
The science and technology of metals.
etymology: From French métallurgie, from Ancient Greek μεταλλουργός (metallourgós, “miner”).

definition: In a metaphorical manner.
example: She expressed herself metaphorically.
etymology: From metaphorical + -ly.

definition: The spreading of a disease (especially cancer) to another part of the body.
A tumor that is malignant and tends to spread to other parts of the body.
A specialist who studies processes in the earth's atmosphere that cause weather conditions.
etymology: From meteorology + -ist.

definition: An amphetamine derivative (trade name Methedrine) used in the form of a crystalline hydrochloride; used as a stimulant to the nervous system and as an appetite suppressant.
etymology: From meth- + amphetamine; 1945–1950.

definition: A light volatile flammable poisonous liquid alcohol; used as an antifreeze and solvent and fuel and as a denaturant for ethyl alcohol.
etymology: From methane + -ol.

definition: In a methodical manner.
example: She worked methodically.
etymology: From methodical + -ly.

definition: First or lowest balcony.
example: On our way to the top floor, we stopped at the mezzanine.
etymology: PIE word *médʰyos The noun is borrowed from French mezzanine, and from its etymon Italian mezzanino, from mezzano (“(adjective) middle; (noun) go-between”) + -ino (diminutive suffix).

definition: Intermediate floor just above the ground floor.

Any of various minerals consisting of hydrous silicates of aluminum or potassium etc. that crystallize in forms that allow perfect cleavage into very thin leaves; used as dielectrics because of their resistance to electricity.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mīca (“grain, crumb”).

definition: Electronic equipment consisting of a small crystal of a silicon semiconductor fabricated to carry out a number of electronic functions in an integrated circuit.
example: By the early 2020s, the strategic priority level of microchip fabrication prowess and capacity had only grown.
etymology: From micro- + chip.

definition: A miniature model of something.
etymology: From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”), equivalent to micro- + -cosm.

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one millionth of a meter.
etymology: From French micron, from Ancient Greek μικρόν (mikrón), neuter of μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

definition: Integrated circuit semiconductor chip that performs the bulk of the processing and controls the parts of a system.
example: A microprocessor functions as the central processing unit of a microcomputer.
etymology: From micro- + processor.

definition: Electronic equipment consisting of a small crystal of a silicon semiconductor fabricated to carry out a number of electronic functions in an integrated circuit.
A man who buys large quantities of goods and resells to merchants rather than to the ultimate customers.
example: Act as a middleman.
etymology: From Middle English myddil man, equivalent to middle + man.

definition: Lacking exceptional quality or ability.
example: The performance was middling at best.
etymology: The noun is probably from middle (noun) + -ing; the adjective is most likely derived from the noun, and the adverb from the adjective.

definition: Minute two-winged mosquito-like fly lacking biting mouthparts; appear in dancing swarms especially near water.
etymology: From Middle English mydge, migge, from Old English myġġ, myċġ (“midge, gnat, mosquito”), from Proto-West Germanic *muggju, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mu-, *mew- (“fly, midge”).

definition: A point equidistant from the ends of a line or the extremities of a figure.
etymology: From mid + point.

definition: The middle of a week.
example: This Wednesday is churchwide midweek; men's is the next one.
etymology: From mid- + week. Compare Saterland Frisian Midwiek (“Wednesday”, literally “midweek”), German Low German Middeweek (“Wednesday”, literally “midweek”), German Mittwoch (“Wednesday”, literally “midweek”).

definition: The branch of medicine dealing with childbirth and care of the mother.
etymology: From Middle English medewifry; equivalent to midwife + -ery.

definition: Powerfully or vigorously.
example: He strove mightily to achieve a better position in life.
etymology: From Middle English mightili (“with might, powerfully, strongly; forcefully, violently; greatly;

definition: Serious pest of grain-growing and range areas of central and western United States.
Old World locust that travels in vast swarms stripping large areas of vegetation.
The typical Old World quail.
The process of becoming mildewed.
etymology: From Middle English myldew, from Old English mildēaw, meledēaw, from Proto-West Germanic *milidauw, from *mili (“honey”) + *dauw (“dew”). Compare West Frisian moaldau, Dutch meeldauw, German Mehltau. More at dew.

definition: The environmental condition.
etymology: PIE word *me Borrowed from French milieu (“physical or social environment;

definition: A political orientation of a people or a government to maintain a strong military force and to be prepared to use it aggressively to defend or promote national interests.
(of grains especially rice) having the husk or outer layers removed.
example: Coarsely milled maize is termed cornmeal, but when finely milled and sifted it is called corn flour.

Thrush-like American songbird able to mimic other birdsongs.

definition: Oriented toward the north.

definition: Causing numbness or insensitivity.
example: The numbing effect of grief.

definition: Partial or total lack of sensation in a part of the body; a symptom of nerve damage or dysfunction.
etymology: From numb + -ness.

definition: A symbol used to represent a number.
example: He learned to write the numerals before he went to school.
etymology: As an adjective, from Middle English numeral, numerall, from Latin numerālis (“pertaining to a number”), from numerus (“a number”). As a noun, via Middle French numeral.

definition: In number; with regard to numbers.
example: Our forces are numerically inferior to those of the enemy.
etymology: From numerical + -ly.

definition: A buoy resembling a cone.
A registered nurse who has received special training and can perform many of the duties of a physician.
A compound lever used to crack nuts open.
etymology: From nut + cracker.

definition: Hickory of southern United States and Mexico having hard nutmeg-shaped nuts.
A muskmelon vine with fruit that has a thin reticulated rind and sweet green flesh.
Any culture medium that uses agar as the gelling agent.
A specialist in the study of nutrition.
etymology: From nutrition + -ist (“person”).

definition: (classical mythology) a minor nature goddess usually depicted as a beautiful maiden.
example: The ancient Greeks believed that nymphs inhabited forests and bodies of water.
etymology: From Middle English nimphe, from Old English nymphē and Old French nimphe, both from Latin nympha (“nymph, bride”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young maiden”). Doublet of nympha.

definition: An implement used to propel or steer a boat.
example: He is a good oar.
etymology: From Middle English ore (“oar”), from Old English ār, from Proto-West Germanic *airu, from Proto-Germanic *airō (“oar”). Cognate with Old Norse ár.

definition: Annual grass of Europe and North Africa; grains used as food and fodder (referred to primarily in the plural: ‘oats’).
example: The oat stalks made good straw.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English ote, from Old English āte, from Proto-West Germanic *aitā, from Proto-Germanic *aitǭ (“swelling; gland; nodule”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyd- (“to swell”). See English atter (“poison”).

definition: A stone pillar having a rectangular cross section tapering towards a pyramidal top.
etymology: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”). Compare obelus.

definition: A bandage in which successive turns proceed obliquely up or down a limb.
Having oblique angles.
Mark for deletion, rub off, or erase.
example: The rainclouds obliterated the sun as they swept across the sky.
etymology: PIE word *h₁epi (start of 17th century) From earlier obliterat, learned borrowing from Latin obliterātus, oblitterātus (“having been blotted out, effaced, erased;

definition: (of a leaf shape) having a somewhat elongated form with approximately parallel sides.
etymology: From Middle English oblong, oblonge, borrowed from Latin oblongus.

definition: A simple leaf that is rounded at each end with parallel sides.
Haunt like a ghost; pursue.
example: Some people are obsessed with sports.
etymology: From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc.; compare assess, possess.

definition: In a compulsive manner.
etymology: From obsessive + -ly.

definition: Acid or granitic glass formed by the rapid cooling of lava without crystallization; usually dark, but transparent in thin pieces.
etymology: From Latin obsidianus; named after Obsidius, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

definition: Shut off to passage or view or hindered from action.
example: A partially obstructed passageway.

definition: Preventing movement.
example: I wanted to see his report on me, but my manager was being obstructive.
etymology: From obstruct + -ive.

definition: Shock caused by obstruction of blood flow.
A triangle that contains an obtuse interior angle.
Denoting or characteristic of countries of Europe and the western hemisphere.
example: Occidental civilization.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French occidental, from Latin occidentalis, equivalent to occident + -al.

definition: Closure or blockage (as of a blood vessel).
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin occlūsiō, occlūsiōnis (“occluding, obstruction”), from the Classical Latin occlūdō (“to shut up or close up; to restrain”), from ob + claudō (“to shut or close”).

definition: Common along northeastern coast of North America.
An eight-sided polygon.
etymology: From Latin octagōnon, octōgōnon (“octagon”), and from its etymon Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon, “octagon”), probably from Koine Greek ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “having eight corners”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns).

definition: Of or relating to or resembling the eye.
example: Ocular muscles.
etymology: Derived from the Latin oculāris (“of the eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

definition: A leather or steel helmet similar to a nasal helmet but with a convex nasal and frontal head stripe that forms an ocular, popular in medieval Scandinavia.
One of the small muscles of the eye that serve to rotate the eyeball.
A person with an unusual or odd personality.
etymology: Compound of odd + ball. First used in late 1930s, describing an extra ball played as a bonus in pin-ball type games. Well-attested since the 1940s, with the adjective appearing earlier than the noun.

definition: Eccentricity that is not easily explained.
etymology: From odd + -ity.

definition: Unequivocally detestable.
example: Consequences odious to those you govern.
etymology: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

definition: The sensation that results when olfactory receptors in the nose are stimulated by particular chemicals in gaseous form.
The total output of a writer or artist (or a substantial part of it).
example: He studied the entire Wagnerian oeuvre.
etymology: From French œuvre, from Old French uevre, from Latin opera (plural of Latin opus), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”). Doublet of opera, opus, and ure.

definition: (informal) strikingly unconventional.
example: He has such an offbeat sense of humor that hardly anyone finds his jokes amusing.
etymology: From off- + beat; not following the beat (e.g., of a drum that sounds out cadence).

definition: A member of a legation.
Transfer to a peripheral device, of computer data.
example: The driver of the car carrier offloaded the cars at the dealership.
etymology: From off- + load.

definition: A minimum credit balance that a bank may require a borrower to keep on deposit as a condition for granting a loan; a common requirement for establishing a line of credit at a bank.
A natural consequence of development.
example: The offshoots of a tree.
etymology: From off- + shoot.

definition: Semisolid preparation (usually containing a medicine) applied externally as a remedy or for soothing an irritation.
example: The doctor prescribed an antibiotic ointment for the wound.

definition: Leaf or strip from a leaf of the talipot palm used in India for writing paper.
An elderly man.
Relating to time long past.
example: Olden days.
etymology: From Middle English olden, probably originally an inflected plural form of old (compare Old English ealdum, dative plural of eald (“old”)), but later reanalysed as equivalent to old + -en (“made of”).

definition: One of two enlargements at the terminus of the olfactory nerve at the base of the brain just above the nasal cavities.
A disorder in the sense of smell.
The sensation that results when olfactory receptors in the nose are stimulated by particular chemicals in gaseous form.
A political system governed by a few people.
example: One of his cardinal convictions was that Britain was not run as a democracy but as an oligarchy.
etymology: Borrowed from French oligarchie, from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

definition: A dull greyish to yellowish or light olive brown.
Of a light brownish green color.
Small large-eyed semiaquatic salamander of the United States Northwest.
Beaten eggs or an egg mixture cooked until just set; may be folded around e.g. ham or cheese or jelly.
etymology: First attested in 1611; borrowed from French omelette, see which for further etymology.

definition: Pan for cooking omelets.
Having unlimited power.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

definition: Being present everywhere at once.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.

definition: A specialist in oncology.
etymology: From oncology + -ist or onco- + -logist.

definition: Having a single ear.
One part in a hundred equal parts.
example: Ten and two one-hundredths percent = 10.02%.

definition: One part in a million equal parts.
The quality of being united into one.
etymology: From Middle English oonnesse, onnesse, from Old English ānnes (“oneness, unity, agreement, covenant, solitude”), from Proto-West Germanic *ainnassī (“oneness”), equivalent to one + -ness.

definition: Not easily borne; wearing.
example: My duties weren't onerous: I only had to greet the guests.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English onerous, borrowed from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, a learned borrowing from Latin onerosus, from onus (“burden”) + -ōsus. Compare exonerate.

definition: Fungus causing a downy mildew on onions.
Smut fungus causing blackish blisters on scales and leaves of onions; especially destructive to seedlings.
(of winds) coming from the sea toward the land.
example: An onshore gale.
etymology: From on + shore.

definition: Not offside; being within the prescribed area of play.
example: The goal was allowed because the attacker was onside.
etymology: From on + side.

definition: (computer science) a rigorous and exhaustive organization of some knowledge domain that is usually hierarchical and contains all the relevant entities and their relations.
etymology: Popularized as a philosophical term by German philosopher Christian Wolff (1679–1754).

definition: An onerous or difficult concern.
example: The onus is on the landlord to make sure the walls are protected from mildew.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin onus (literally “burden”).

definition: A chalcedony with alternating black and white bands; used in making cameos.
etymology: From Middle English onix (c. 1300), earlier oniche (c. 1250), from Old French oniche or onix, from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux, “onyx”). Doublet of unguis.

definition: A hard compact kind of calcite.
Any thick, viscous matter.
etymology: * (Noun) Middle English wose (“sap”), from Old English wōs (“sap, froth”), from Proto-Germanic *wōsą, from Proto-Indo-European *wóseh₂ (“sap”) (cf. Sanskrit वसा (vásā, “fat”)).

definition: A very soft leather made from the skins of calves and having a suede finish on the flesh side.
Release (a liquid) in drops or small quantities.
Run slowly and gradually.
example: Blood oozed through the bandage.

definition: Leaking out slowly.
The phenomenon of not permitting the passage of electromagnetic radiation.
example: We could not see the sandbar due to the opacity of the muddy water.
etymology: From opaque + -ity, from French opacité, from Latin opācitās, from opācus.

definition: Of a shirt; not buttoned at the neck.
example: Dressed casually in shorts and an open-collared shirt.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of opera.
example: The politician's address was so flamboyant as to be operatic.
etymology: From opera + -ic, probably influenced by dramatic.

definition: Singer of lead role in an opera.
The branch of medicine concerned with the eye and its diseases.
etymology: From ophthalmo- + -logy.

definition: Obstinate in your opinions.
example: Her dad is so opinionated that when he's around it is hard to simply relax and have a light conversation.

definition: A male who is older than the speaker, especially used by Korean female.
example: Sign #2- Changing your phone's, laptop's etc. wallpaper/lockscreen with your oppa's photo.
etymology: Borrowed from Korean 오빠 (oppa, “elder brother or close elder male friend (of a female)”).

definition: Taking immediate advantage, often unethically, of any circumstance of possible benefit.
etymology: From French opportuniste, equivalent to opportune + -ist.

definition: Come down on or keep down by unjust use of one's authority.
example: The government oppresses political activists.

definition: An optical phenomenon resulting from the failure of a lens or mirror to produce a good image.
Lens used to concentrate light on an object.
Opacity to light.
In an optimal and most desirable way.
etymology: From optimal + -ly.

definition: In an optional manner.
example: This rule is applied optionally.
etymology: From optional + -ly.

definition: Ostentatiously rich and superior in quality.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin opulēns, opulentus, from ops (“wealth, power, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op- (“to work; produce in abundance”).

definition: The opening through which food is taken in and vocalizations emerge.
Liqueur flavored with orange.
Marmalade made from oranges.
The rind of an orange.
Having orange flowers.
A person who delivers a speech or oration.
etymology: From Middle English oratour, from Anglo-Norman oratour, from Latin ōrātor.

definition: Addressing an audience formally (usually a long and rhetorical address and often pompous).
example: He loved the sound of his own oratory.
etymology: From Middle English oratorie, from Anglo-Norman oratorie, Middle French oratoire, and their source, Late Latin ōrātōrium. Doublet of oratorio. Displaced native Old English bēdhūs.

definition: Predatory black-and-white toothed whale with large dorsal fin; common in cold seas.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin orca (“tun, cask; whale”), see there for more. Although the origin is obscure, the sometimes-cited association with orcus (“underworld”) is folk-etymology. Doublet of orc.

definition: Appoint to a clerical posts.
etymology: Partly inherited from Middle English ordinat(e) (adjective and participle), partly directly borrowed from Latin ōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of ōrdinō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Doublet of ordain.

definition: Chocolate cookie with white cream filling.
etymology: Genericized use of Oreo, q.v.

definition: Chocolate cookie with white cream filling.
A fertilizer that is derived from animal or vegetable matter.
A person who plays an organ.
etymology: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

definition: Adjusted or located in relation to surroundings or circumstances; sometimes used in combination.
example: The house had its large windows oriented toward the ocean view.

definition: The Japanese art of folding paper into shapes representing objects (e.g., flowers or birds).
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 折(お)り紙(がみ) (origami), from 折(お)り (ori, “to fold”) + 紙(かみ) (kami, “paper”).

definition: Someone who creates new things.
etymology: From originate + -or.

definition: Not pertinent to the matter under consideration.
etymology: From Middle French orthogonal, in turn from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis and Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρθογώνιος (orthogṓnios, “rectangular”).

definition: The relation of opposition between things at right angles.
Of or relating to orthopedics.
example: Orthopedic shoes.

definition: Having periodic vibrations.
The process of oscillating between states.
etymology: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.

definition: Generator that produces sonic oscillations or alternating current.
etymology: From oscillate + -or.

definition: Large harmless hawk found worldwide that feeds on fish and builds a bulky nest often occupied for years.
example: 1594, George Peele (attributed), The Battle of Alcazar I will provide thee of a princely osprey.
etymology: From Late Middle English ospray, from Anglo-Norman ospriet, from Medieval Latin avis praedae (“bird of prey”), a generic term apparently confused with this specific bird in Old French on its similarity to ossifrage.

definition: Chronic breakdown of cartilage in the joints; the most common form of arthritis occurring usually after middle age.
etymology: From osteo- + arthritis.

definition: Abnormal loss of bony tissue resulting in fragile porous bones attributable to a lack of calcium; most common in postmenopausal women.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”) + Ancient Greek πώρωσις (pṓrōsis, “petrification, callousness”), from Ancient Greek πῶρος (pôros, “tuff, a porous type of rock”). By surface analysis, osteo- + pore + -osis.

definition: Tall fern of northern temperate regions having graceful arched fronds and sporophylls resembling ostrich plumes.
Perennial aromatic herb of eastern North America having variously colored tubular flowers in dense showy heads.
Existing outside of or not in accordance with nature.
etymology: From other world (“a world beyond death; a world other than the everyday world”) + -ly (suffix meaning having the likeness of, resembling forming adjectives).

definition: Remove from a position or office.
example: The chairman was ousted after he misappropriated funds.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman ouster, oustier, from Old French oster (modern French ôter), from post-classical Latin obstare (“to remove”), classical obstāre (“to obstruct, stand in the way of”). Not related to out.

definition: Surpass someone in cruelty or evil.
A motorboat with an outboard motor.
Internal-combustion engine that mounts at stern of small boat.
The part of a rock formation that appears above the surface of the surrounding land.
etymology: From out- + crop.

definition: Second outermost triangular sail at the front of the large square-rigged ship.
Furnished with essential equipment for a particular occupation or undertaking occupation.
example: A well outfitted expedition to the South Pole.

definition: A person who comes from a foreign country; someone who does not owe allegiance to your country.
etymology: From outland + -er. In certain uses, influenced by or a calque of the Dutch uitlander or Afrikaans uitlander. Also cognate with German Ausländer, Swedish utlänning and Danish udlænding. Doublet of uitlander.

definition: Live longer than.
example: The tool outlasted its need.
etymology: From out- + last.

definition: The act of spending or disbursing money.
example: Without too much outlay, you could buy a second-hand car.
etymology: From out- + lay.

definition: A person who lives away from their place of work.
Be larger in number.
example: Women outnumbered men by two to one.
etymology: From out- + number.

definition: A natural flow of ground water.
etymology: From out- + pouring.

definition: The concluding section of a piece of music.
example: So, you said that you had an outro that you've been practicing?
etymology: Blend of out + intro, an analogy using out as the opposite of in. First attested in the title of the song The Intro and the Outro (1967), by the Bonzo Dog Doo-Dah Band, and written by Vivian Stanshall.

definition: Run faster than.
example: In this race, I managed to outrun everybody else.
etymology: From out- + run.

definition: Obtain goods or services from an outside supplier; to contract work out.
example: Many companies outsource and hire consultants in order to maintain a flexible workforce.
etymology: From out- + source.

definition: Fully extended especially in length.
example: A kitten with one paw outstretched.

definition: Toward the outside.
example: Move the needle further outward!
etymology: From Middle English outwardes, from Old English ūtweardes; equivalent to outward + -s or out + -wards. Cognate with German auswärts.

definition: A cystic tumor (usually benign) of the ovary.
The organ that bears the ovules of a flower.
etymology: From New Latin ovarium, from Medieval Latin ovaria (“bird ovary”), from Latin ovum (“egg”). Doublet of ovarium.

definition: Expecting unquestioning obedience.
example: Insufferably overbearing behavior toward the waiter.
etymology: From overbear (“to bear down (on)”) + -ing.

definition: Puffed up with vanity.
example: Overblown oratory.

definition: A heavy coat worn over clothes in winter.
example: Wait 24 hours before applying an overcoat.
etymology: From over- + coat.

definition: Do something to an excessive degree.
example: He overdid it last night when he did 100 pushups.
etymology: From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + do.

definition: Represented as greater than is true or reasonable.
etymology: From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + done.

definition: A draft in excess of the credit balance.
example: I have an overdraft of £1234.
etymology: From over- + draft.

definition: Credit provided by a bank in honoring a customer's overdrafts.
An appraisal that is too high.
etymology: From over- + estimate.

definition: Project over.
etymology: From Old English oferhangan, corresponding to over- + hang.

definition: Heated beyond a safe or desirable point.
example: The child became overheated.

definition: Extremely joyful.
example: Fans were overjoyed at / by the sight of their team handing the visitors such a decisive defeat.

definition: Bridge formed by the upper level of a crossing of two highways at different levels.
example: The homeless man had built a little shelter, complete with cook-stove, beneath a concrete overpass.
etymology: From over- + pass.

definition: Overcome by superior force.
example: We overpowered the opposing army within a couple of hours.
etymology: From over- + power.

definition: So strong as to be irresistible.
example: An overpowering need for solitude.

definition: Show an exaggerated response to something.
example: Don't overreact to the bad news — take it easy.
etymology: From over- + react.

definition: An excessive reaction; a reaction with inappropriate emotional behavior.
example: She had every right to dump you, but cutting up all your clothes after she did so was an overreaction.
etymology: From over- + reaction.

definition: A person who directs and manages an organization.
Represented as greater than is true or reasonable.
The expulsion of an ovum from the ovary (usually midway in the menstrual cycle).
etymology: From ovulate + -ion.

definition: Natural family planning in which the fertile period is inferred from changes in the character and quantity of cervical mucus; ovulation is marked by an increase in mucus that becomes sticky and then clearer and slippery.
Combined with or having undergone a chemical reaction with oxygen.
example: The oxidized form of iodine.

definition: Hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland (trade name Pitocin); stimulates contractions of the uterus and ejection of milk.
etymology: From oxytocic, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “swift”) + τόκος (tókos, “childbirth”, from τίκτω (tíktō, “I give birth”)).

definition: A leading instance in its field.
example: Natural pacemaker.
etymology: From pace + maker.

definition: Of or relating to the medical care of children.
Any of various religions other than Christianity or Judaism or Islamism.
example: Most people in that region practise their own form of paganism.
etymology: From Latin pāgānismus (“heathenism”), from pāgānus (“peasant, rural, rustic”). The term was used pejoratively by local Orthodox Christian Demonyms to belittle what remained of alternative native ideas and ideals.

definition: Calling out the name of a person (especially by a loudspeaker system).
example: The public address system in the hospital was used for paging.

definition: An Asian temple; usually a pyramidal tower with an upward curving roof.
example: I, in about two hours, notwithstanding the utmost caution, found myself minus upwards of six hundred pagodas […] .

definition: Tall sparingly branched conical tree having large fragrant yellow flowers with white centers.
etymology: (source of wealth): See pagoda (“a kind of gold coin”).

definition: A roughly cylindrical vessel that is open at the top.
Emotionally hurt or upset or annoyed.
example: Face had a pained and puzzled expression.

definition: A medicine used to relieve pain.
Characterized by extreme care and great effort.
example: Painstaking research.
etymology: From pains + taking; see take pains. The /ˈpeɪnˌsteɪkɪŋ/ pronunciation which dominates in the United States suggests a reanalysis of the word as pain + staking.

definition: In a fastidious and painstaking manner.
example: Painstakingly learn the routines of selling.
etymology: From painstaking + -ly.

definition: A pair of loose trousers tied by a drawstring around the waist; worn by men and women in some Asian countries.
example: We were greeted by an old, pajama-clad man.

definition: Someone who fights for a cause.
etymology: Borrowed from French paladin, from Italian paladino, from Late Latin palātīnus (“palace officer”), derived from palātium (“palace”). Doublet of palatine.

definition: Relating to or lying near the palate.
example: Palatal index.
etymology: From late Middle English palatyne, from Old French palatin, from Medieval Latin palātīnus (“relating to the palace”), from palātium (“palace”) + -īnus (“-ine”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of paladin.

definition: Either of two irregularly shaped bones that form the back of the hard palate and helps to form the nasal cavity and the floor of the orbits.
A vein that drains the region of the palate and empties into the facial vein.
Become less interesting or attractive.
example: The liquor palls.
etymology: From Middle English pal, palle, from Old English pæl, pæll, from Old French paile and Latin pallium (“cloak;

definition: A 17th century game; a wooden ball was driven along an alley with a mallet.
Large shrub of tropical Africa and Asia having large palmate leaves and spiny capsules containing seeds that are the source of castor oil and ricin; widely naturalized throughout the tropics.
Large shrub of tropical Africa and Asia having large palmate leaves and spiny capsules containing seeds that are the source of castor oil and ricin; widely naturalized throughout the tropics.
Not worth considering.
example: He considered the prize too paltry for the lives it must cost.
etymology: From Middle Low German paltrig (“ragged, rubbishy, worthless”), from palter, palte (“cloth, rag, shred”), from Old Saxon *paltro, *palto (“cloth, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *paltrô, *paltô (“scrap, rag, patch”).

definition: Treat with excessive indulgence.
example: Grandparents often pamper the children.

definition: Hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists.
example: A monorail will be a panacea for our traffic woes.
etymology: From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

definition: A village council in India or southern Pakistan.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi पंचायत (pañcāyat, “panchayat (originally a council of five)”).

definition: The most common hereditary disease; the child's lungs and intestines and pancreas become clogged with thick mucus; caused by defect in a single gene; no cure is known.
A relatively narrow strip of land projecting from some larger area.
example: Wheeling is located in the northern panhandle of West Virginia.
etymology: From pan + handle.

definition: Communicate by hooting and panting, as of primates.
Breathing heavily (as after exertion).
A home appliance in which trousers can be hung and the wrinkles pressed out.
Short underpants for women or children.
A woman's tights consisting of underpants and stockings.
etymology: From panty + hose.

definition: An armored vehicle or tank.
etymology: First attested in 1940. Borrowed from German Panzer, from Middle High German Panzer (“armour”), from Old French panciere (“coat of mail”), from Latin pantex (“paunch”).

definition: Tropical American shrub or small tree having huge deeply palmately cleft leaves and large oblong yellow fruit.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish papaya, from Lokono papáia. Doublet of pawpaw.

definition: Trees native to tropical America and Africa with milky juice and large palmately lobed leaves.
Juice from papayas.
Tropical American shrub or small tree having huge deeply palmately cleft leaves and large oblong yellow fruit.
Chromatography that uses selective adsorption on a strip of paper.
Cephalopod mollusk of warm seas whose females have delicate papery spiral shells.
Plant bearing large mild thick-walled usually bell-shaped fruits; the principal salad peppers.
etymology: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar, from Proto-Slavic *pьpьrь, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from Indo-Aryan;

definition: Veloute sauce with sauteed chopped onion and paprika and cream.
Paper made from the papyrus plant by cutting it in strips and pressing it flat; used by ancient Egyptians and Greeks and Romans.
etymology: From Middle English papirus, borrowed from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros), of unknown origin. Doublet of papyros.

definition: Resembling or expressed by parables.
etymology: From Ancient Greek παραβολικός (parabolikós).

definition: (mathematics) geometry based on Euclid's axioms.
A parabolic reflector for light radiation.
Seemingly contradictory but nonetheless possibly true.
example: It is paradoxical that standing is more tiring than walking.
