etymology: From Middle English porke despyne, from Old French porc-espin, from Latin porcus (“pig”) + spinus (“spine”), hence also spine pig. Cognate with Spanish puercoespín, Italian porcospino, Portuguese porco-espinho.

definition: Meat patties rolled in rice and simmered in a tomato sauce.
Spines become erect when the body is inflated; worldwide in warm waters.
A measure undertaken by a corporation to discourage unwanted takeover attempts.
An aperture or hole that opens into a bodily cavity.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin porta (“a gate”). See port.

definition: The quality of being light enough to be carried.
etymology: From portable + -ity.

definition: Pantropical tree of usually seacoasts sometimes cultivated as an ornamental for its rounded heart-shaped leaves and showy yellow and purple flowers; yields valuable pink to dark red close-grained wood and oil from its seeds.
A word picture of a person's appearance and character.
etymology: From Middle English portraiture, portrature, purtraiture, pourtreture, from Old French portraiture, pourtraiture and Anglo-Norman purtraiture.

definition: Put (something somewhere) firmly.
example: She posited her hand on his shoulder.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin positus, perfect participle of pōnō (“put, place”). Noun sense 3 (type of number format) was coined by American computer scientist and businessman John Gustafson in 2017.

definition: A numeration system in which a real number is represented by an ordered set of characters where the value of a character depends on its position.
A pronoun indicating possession, for example mine, yours, hers, theirs.
Relatively tall deciduous water oak of southeastern United States often cultivated as a shade tree; thrives in wet soil.
(phonetics) Any sound articulated with the tongue near or touching the back of the alveolar ridge.
etymology: From post- + alveolar.

definition: The posterior lobe of the pituitary body; primarily glandular in nature.
All of the offspring of a given progenitor.
example: We must secure the benefits of freedom for ourselves and our posterity.
etymology: Late 14th century, from Middle French posterité, from Latin posteritas, from posterus (“following, coming after”), from post (“after”) (English post-).

definition: Birth of a child after the father has died.
Occurring immediately after birth.
etymology: 1844, from Latin post (“after”) + partum (“giving birth”), form of partus, from pariō (“to give birth”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forth”).

definition: A note appended to a letter after the signature.
etymology: From New Latin postscriptum, from Latin, neuter of postscriptus, past participle of postscrībō (“write after”), from post (“after”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, post- + script.

definition: Adopting a vain conceited posture.
Suitable for drinking.
example: Potable water.

definition: A potassium compound often used in agriculture and industry.
etymology: From pot + ash, because the substance was originally obtained by leaching ash in water and then boiling down the resulting solution in a pot. Compare Dutch potas, German Pottasche.

definition: A potassium compound often used in agriculture and industry.
A blight of potatoes.
Fungous disease causing dark warty spongy excrescences in the eyes of potato tubers.
Resistors connected in series across a voltage source; used to obtain a desired fraction of the voltage.
Of plants; planted or grown in a pot.
example: Potted geraniums.
etymology: From pot + -ed. Adjective meaning "prepared in advance" by analogy with potted meat (canned meat), first used in a published work by L.

definition: The act of pouncing.
etymology: From French ponce, from Latin pūmex. Doublet of pumice.

definition: (used only in combination) something weighing a given number of pounds.
example: The fisherman caught a 10-pounder.
etymology: From pound (“verb”) + -er (“agent suffix”).

definition: A disdainful grimace.
etymology: From Middle English pouten, probably from Scandinavian (compare Norwegian pute (“pillow, cushion”), dial.

definition: The metallurgy of powdered metals; how to produce solid metal objects from powdered metal by compaction and sintering.
Consisting of fine particles.
example: Powdered cellulose.

definition: Of a moderate to pale blue or purplish blue.
Usable for a specific purpose.
example: A practicable solution.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prācticābilis, partly modelled on Middle French praticable. By surface analysis, practice (verb) + -able.

definition: Concerned with actual use rather than theoretical possibilities.
etymology: From practical + -ity.

definition: (philosophy) the doctrine that practical consequences are the criteria of knowledge and meaning and value.
etymology: From Ancient Greek stem of πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “act”) + -ism.

definition: Violet-flowered perennial aster of central United States having solitary heads.
Brown mottled North American grouse of western prairies.
Small hard green-and-white inedible fruit of the prairie gourd plant.
Widely distributed between the Mississippi and the Rockies.
A large wagon with broad wheels and an arched canvas top; used by the United States pioneers to cross the prairies in the 19th century.
etymology: From the sail-like appearance of the wagons' covers when traversing tall grass.

definition: A small vehicle with four wheels in which a baby or child is pushed around.
etymology: From Dutch praam (“a flat-bottomed boat”), from Middle Dutch praem, from Middle Low German prām, from Old Czech *prám, from Proto-Slavic *pormъ.

definition: Translating an idea into action.
example: Differences between theory and praxis of communism.
etymology: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

definition: To a preeminent degree; with superiority or distinction above others; in a preeminent manner.
example: A wide variety of pre-eminently contemporary scenes.

definition: A preliminary introduction to a statute or constitution (usually explaining its purpose).
example: High winds are often a preamble to a winter storm.
etymology: From Middle English preamble, from Old French preambule (French préambule), from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from praeambulō (“to walk before”).

definition: Taken in advance to protect against possible danger or failure.
example: Gave precautionary advice.
etymology: From precaution + -ary.

definition: Be earlier in time; go back further.
example: Stone tools precede bronze tools.
etymology: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.

definition: A very steep cliff.
example: To stand on a precipice.
etymology: First attested in 1598, from Middle French precipice, from Latin praecipitium (“a steep place”), from praeceps (“steep”), from prae + caput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“head”).

definition: Bring about abruptly.
example: The crisis precipitated by Russia's revolution.
etymology: From Latin praecipitātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

definition: Characterized by or characteristic of exceptionally early development or maturity (especially in mental aptitude).
example: A precocious child.
etymology: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”).

definition: (of an idea or opinion) formed beforehand; especially without evidence or through prejudice.
example: Certain preconceived notions.

definition: An opinion formed beforehand without adequate evidence.
example: He did not even try to confirm his preconceptions.

definition: An opinion formed beforehand without adequate evidence.
example: He did not even try to confirm his preconceptions.

definition: An opinion formed beforehand without adequate evidence.
example: He did not even try to confirm his preconceptions.

definition: An act of plundering and pillaging and marauding.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praedātiō, praedātiōnis, from praedor (“pillage, plunder”), from praeda (“plunder, spoils”).

definition: Make the (grammatical) predicate in a proposition.
example: The predicate ‘dog’ is predicated of the subject ‘Fido’ in the sentence ‘Fido is a dog’.

definition: A system of symbolic logic that represents individuals and predicates and quantification over individuals (as well as the relations between propositions).
The quality of being predictable.
etymology: From predict + -ability.

definition: Made susceptible.
example: Because of conditions in the mine, miners are predisposed to lung disease.
etymology: From pre- + disposed.

definition: Susceptibility to a pathogen.
etymology: From pre- + disposition.

definition: Greatest in importance or degree or significance or achievement.
example: A preeminent archeologist.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.

definition: Designed or having the power to deter or prevent an anticipated situation or occurrence.
example: A preemptive business offer.
etymology: From preempt + -ive.

definition: A high bid that is intended to prevent the opposing players from bidding.
The right granting to shareholders the first opportunity to buy a new issue of stock; provides protection against dilution of the shareholder's ownership interest.
Existing previously or before something.
Anterior to a frontal structure.
example: A prefrontal bone.
etymology: From pre- + frontal.

definition: The anterior part of the frontal lobe.
Heat beforehand.
example: Preheat the oven!
etymology: From pre- + heat.

definition: The time during the development of human culture before the appearance of the written word.
Characterized by deliberate purpose and some degree of planning.
example: A premeditated crime.

definition: An idea that preoccupies the mind and holds the attention.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French préoccupation, from Latin praeoccupātiō. By surface analysis, pre- + occupation or preoccupy + -ation.

definition: Building reserved for the officiating clergy.
Pertaining to giving directives or rules.
example: Prescriptive grammar is concerned with norms of or rules for correct usage.
etymology: From Latin praescriptivus (“relating to a legal exception”), from praescript- (“directed in writing”), from the verb praescribere.

definition: A grammar that is produced by prescriptive linguistics.
Fit to be seen.
example: Presentable clothes.
etymology: From Middle French presentable, from Old French, as if present + -able.

definition: Set in advance.
example: A preset plan of action.
etymology: From pre- + set.

definition: Act as president.
example: Preside over companies and corporations.
etymology: From Old French presider, from Latin praesidēre (“preside”), from pre- (“before”) + sedere (“to sit”). Displaced Old English foresittan, which might have been a calque of the Latin.

definition: Suddenly.
example: Presto! begone! 'tis here again.
etymology: From Italian presto (“quickly”).

definition: Having a reasonable basis for belief or acceptance.
example: The presumptive heir (or heir apparent).
etymology: PIE word *upó From pre- + Latin sūmptus + -ive, from Late Middle English presumptif, presumptijf (“based on presumption”), from Anglo-Norman presumptif and Middle French presumptif, présomptif (“based on presumption;

definition: Excessively forward.
example: The duchess would not put up with presumptuous servants.
etymology: From Middle English presumptuous, borrowed from Old French presumpcieus, presumptieus, presumptuos and its etymon Medieval Latin praesūmptuōsus.

definition: A person who makes deceitful pretenses.
etymology: From pretend + -er.

definition: An infant that is born prior to 37 weeks of gestation.
Glazed and salted cracker typically in the shape of a loose knot.
etymology: From dialectal German Pretzel, a variant of standard Brezel, from Old High German brēzitella, from Vulgar Latin *brāchiātellus, diminutive of Latin brāchium, bracchium (“arm”); named for the appearance of folded arms.

definition: The winds from the west that occur in the temperate zones of the Earth.
European annual wild lettuce having prickly stems; a troublesome weed in parts of United States.
Cacti having spiny flat joints and oval fruit that is edible in some species; often used as food for stock.
etymology: From prickly + pear, from the nature of the plant's fruit, which, like the cactus it grows on, has spines on its surface.

definition: A small two-needled upland pine of the eastern United States (Appalachians) having dark brown flaking bark and thorn-tipped cone scales.
Any plant of the genus Argemone having large white or yellow flowers and prickly leaves and stems and pods; chiefly of tropical America.
Associated with the priesthood or priests.
example: Priestly (or sacerdotal) vestments.
etymology: From Middle English prestly; equivalent to priest + -ly.

definition: Assume a prim appearance.
example: They mince and prim.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. In the verb sense, first appeared in Thomas D'Urfey's A Fool's Preferment in the year 1688.

definition: Dress primly.
Dress primly.
A leading female ballet dancer.
etymology: From Italian.

definition: The act of making something ready.
The first or preliminary coat of paint or size applied to a surface.
The best of its kind.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian primo (“first”). Doublet of prime and primus.

definition: Any of numerous short-stemmed plants of the genus Primula having tufted basal leaves and showy flowers clustered in umbels or heads.
etymology: From Middle English primerose, from Old French primerose, from Medieval Latin prima (“first”) + rosa (“rose”).

definition: A dicotyledonous family of the order Primulales with a regular flower; widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere.
Evergreen rambling yellow-flowered shrub of western China.
A life of ease and pleasure.
etymology: Coined by William Shakespeare in 1609 in The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, act 1, scene 3: "Himself the primrose path of dalliance treads".

definition: Ostentatiously rich and superior in quality.
example: A princely sum.
etymology: From prince + -ly (adverbial suffix).

definition: Territory ruled by a prince.
etymology: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.

definition: Fit for publication because free of material that is morally or legally objectionable.
example: Printable language.
etymology: From print + -able.

definition: Assign a priority to.
example: We have too many things to do and must prioritize.
etymology: From priority + -ise.

definition: Of or relating to or resembling or constituting a prism.
example: Prismatic form.
etymology: Borrowed from French prismatique. Equivalent to prism + -atic.

definition: Done or produced as a formality only.
example: A one-candidate pro forma election.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prō fōrmā.

definition: For the time being.
example: He is the president pro tem.
etymology: Clipping of pro tempore, from Latin prō tempore (literally “for a time”).

definition: Of or relating to the Roman Catholic philosophy of probabilism.
etymology: From probabil(ity) + -istic and probabil(ism) + -istic.

definition: A thinker who focuses on the problem as stated and tries to synthesize information and knowledge to achieve a solution.
The act of procrastinating; putting off or delaying or deferring an action to a later time.
Recklessly wasteful.
example: Prodigal in their expenditures.

definition: So great in size or force or extent as to elicit awe.
example: A prodigious storm.
etymology: * Middle French prodigieux (“portentous”) (modern French prodigieux)

definition: Practice as a profession, teach, or claim to be knowledgeable about.
example: She professes organic chemistry.
etymology: From Old French professer, and its source, the participle stem of Latin profitērī, from pro- + fatērī (“to confess, acknowledge”).

definition: In an abundant manner.
example: He thanked her profusely.
etymology: From profuse + -ly.

definition: An ancestor in the direct line.
example: Abraham, alias Ibrahim, is the presumed progenitor of both the Jewish and Arab peoples.

definition: Tending to discourage (especially of prices).
example: The price was prohibitive.
etymology: From Middle English prohibitif, prohibityve, from Medieval Latin prohibitīvus, from prohibit-, past-participle stem of Latin prohibēre. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ive.

definition: Belonging to or characteristic of the proletariat.
etymology: From Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”).

definition: Not selective of a single class or person.
example: Clinton was criticized for his promiscuous solicitation of campaign money.

definition: Formally made public.
A pointed projection.
example: A pitchfork with four prongs.

definition: A chain-link collar with blunted open ends turned towards the dog's neck.
Having prongs or tines; usually used in combination.
example: A three-pronged fork.
etymology: From prong + -ed.

definition: In a punctual manner.
example: I need to finish this assignment pronto.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish pronto, from Latin prōmptus. Doublet of prompt.

definition: Tending to or capable of propelling.
example: Propellant fuel for submarines.
etymology: From propel + -ant.

definition: An explosive that is used to propel projectiles from guns or to propel rockets and missiles or to launch torpedos and depth charges.
Tending to or capable of propelling.
example: Propellant fuel for submarines.

definition: To a proportionate degree.
example: Your salary will rise proportionately to your workload.
etymology: From proportional + -ly.

definition: The act of propping up with shores.
Correct or appropriate behavior.
etymology: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.

definition: Corrective consisting of a replacement for a part of the body.
The branch of medicine dealing with the production and use of artificial body parts.
etymology: By surface analysis, prosth- + -etic + -s.

definition: Any enzyme that catalyzes the splitting of proteins into smaller peptide fractions and amino acids by a process known as proteolysis.
etymology: From prote(in) + -ase.

definition: The policy of imposing duties or quotas on imports in order to protect home industries from overseas competition.
etymology: Borrowed from French protectionnisme, equivalent to protection + -ism.

definition: An advocate of protectionism.
etymology: Borrowed from French protectionniste, equivalent to protection + -ist.

definition: Coloration making an organism less visible or attractive to predators.
A state or territory partly controlled by (but not a possession of) a stronger state but autonomous in internal affairs; protectorates are established by treaty.
example: Egypt became a British protectorate in 1914.
etymology: From protector + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a system ruled by people of such office).

definition: Temporarily and conditionally.
example: They have agreed provisionally.
etymology: From provisional + -ly.

definition: Move about in or as if in a predatory manner.
example: The suspicious stranger prowls the streets of the town.
etymology: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin.

definition: A car in which policemen cruise the streets; equipped with radiotelephonic communications to headquarters.
Cultivate, tend, and cut back the growth of.
example: A good grape grower will prune the vines once a year.
etymology: From Middle English prunen, prounen, proinen, from Old French proignier (“to trim the feathers with the beak”), earlier prooignier.

definition: Moist cake containing prunes that have been made into a puree.
Dessert made of prune puree and whipped cream.
Affecting the mind or mood or other mental processes.
example: Psychoactive drugs.
etymology: From psycho- + active.

definition: A drug that can produce mood changes and distorted perceptions.
A drug that can produce mood changes and distorted perceptions.
Of or relating to or incorporating the methods and theory of psychiatric treatment originated by Sigmund Freud.
example: Freud's psychoanalytical theories.
etymology: From psycho- + analytic.

definition: A process that is assumed to occur in psychoanalytic theory.
Suffering from an undiagnosed mental disorder.
example: A psychopathic killer is on the loose.
etymology: From psycho- + -pathic.

definition: Any easement enjoyed by the public in general (as the public's right to use public streets).
A toilet that is available to the public.
Make public.
etymology: From public + -ize.

definition: Gathered for protruding fullness.
example: The dress had puffed sleeves.
etymology: From puff + -ed.

definition: Puffy rice kernels.
Puffy wheat berries.
Blowing tobacco smoke out into the air.
example: They smoked up the room with their ceaseless puffing.

definition: Having a blunt nose.
example: A pug-nosed boy with freckles.

definition: The reflex act of ejecting the contents of the stomach through the mouth.
A simple machine consisting of a wheel with a groove in which a rope can run to change the direction or point of application of a force applied to the rope.

(electronics) a sharp transient wave in the normal electrical state (or a series of such transients).
Spending money raised by borrowing; used by governments to stimulate their economy.
Punch consisting of pliers for perforating paper or leather.
The point of a joke or humorous story.
Acting or arriving or performed exactly at the time appointed.
example: She expected guests to be punctual at meals.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis (adjective suffix).

definition: A theory of evolution holding that evolutionary change in the fossil record came in fits and starts rather than in a steady process of slow change.
Having a hole cut through.
example: A punctured balloon.

definition: Strong and sharp.
example: The pungent taste of radishes.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pungens (stem pungent-), present participle of pungo (“to sting”). Doublet of poignant.

definition: Inferior in strength or significance.
example: A puny physique.

definition: Food prepared by cooking and straining or processed in a blender.
example: Tomato sauce is generally a puree.
etymology: Borrowed from French purée.

definition: An act of removing by cleansing; ridding of sediment or other undesired elements.
etymology: From Middle English purgynge; equivalent to purge + -ing.

definition: Serving to purge or rid of sin.
Small hybrid apricot of Asia and Asia Minor having purplish twigs and white flowers following by inferior purple fruit.
Having purple flowers.
Believed or reputed to be the case.
etymology: From purported + -ly.

definition: Make a soft swishing sound.
example: The car engine purred.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: The range of interest or activity that can be anticipated.
One who intrudes or pushes themself forward.
etymology: From push + -er.

definition: A person who is regarded as easygoing and agreeable.
Purported; commonly put forth or accepted as true on inconclusive grounds.
example: The foundling's putative father.
etymology: First attested c. 1432, from Middle French putatif, from Latin putātīvus (“supposed, purported”), from putātus (“thought”), from putō (“to think, to consider, to reckon”).

definition: Work lightly.
etymology: Alteration of potter.

definition: Move around aimlessly.
A dough-like mixture of whiting and boiled linseed oil; used especially to patch woodwork or secure panes of glass.
etymology: Borrowed from French potée (“polishing powder", originally "the contents of a pot, potful”), from French pot (“pot”). More at English pot.

definition: A spatula used to mix or apply putty.
European evergreen carpeting perennial.
Child's word for a duck.
A four-sided polygon.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English quadrangle, borrowed from Old French quadrangle, from Late Latin quadrangulum.

definition: An equation in which the highest power of an unknown quantity is a square.
A soft wet area of low-lying land that sinks underfoot.
example: That quagmire regularly ‘swallows’ caught-up hikers’ boots.
etymology: Recorded since 1579, from quag + mire. The sense “perilous, mixed up and troubled situation” has been recorded since 1775. Alternatively, the word may apparently be a variation of the earlier quakemire, from quake + mire.

definition: A limitation imposed on the variables of a proposition (as by the quantifiers ‘some’ or ‘all’ or ‘no’).
etymology: Coined by Scottish philosopher Sir William Hamilton: "quantification of the predicate".

definition: Under forced isolation especially for health reasons.
example: A quarantined animal.

definition: One of the four competitions in an elimination tournament whose winners go on to play in the semifinals.
etymology: From quarter + final.

definition: An oscillator that produces electrical oscillations at a frequency determined by the physical characteristics of a piezoelectric quartz crystal.
Put down by force or intimidation.
example: The government quashes any attempt of an uprising.

definition: Consisting of or especially arranged in sets of four.
example: Quaternate leaves.
etymology: Derived from Latin quaternārius (“containing or consisting of four”), from quaternī (“four each”, “four at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary); compare the French quaternaire.

definition: The widow of a king.
Satisfy (thirst).
example: The cold water quenched his thirst.
etymology: From Middle English quenchen, from Old English cwenċan, from Proto-Germanic *kwankijaną.

definition: Condition of heightened watchfulness or preparation for action.
etymology: Borrowed from French qui vive.

definition: Having keen hearing.
Mentally nimble and resourceful.

definition: Hurried repair.

definition: Skillful performance or ability without difficulty.
example: His quick adeptness was a product of good design.
etymology: From Middle English quiknes, qwiknes, quyknesse, cwicnesse, equivalent to quick + -ness.

definition: Liable to sudden unpredictable change.
example: A quicksilver character, cool and willful at one moment, utterly fragile the next.
etymology: From Middle English quyk silver, quyksilver, quikselver, from Old English cwicseolfor (“quicksilver”, literally “living silver”) (see Latin argentum vīvum) from its ability to move. See quick in the sense of "living".

definition: Made of layers of fabric held together by patterned stitching.
example: A brand of quilted toilet paper.

definition: Small Asian tree with pinkish flowers and pear-shaped fruit; widely cultivated.
example: Quince dress.
etymology: Clipping of quinceañera.

definition: Small Asian tree with pinkish flowers and pear-shaped fruit; widely cultivated.
A musical composition for five performers.
example: The composer wrote a string quintet in his early twenties.
etymology: From French quintette, from Italian quintetto, diminutive of quinto (“fifth”), itself from Latin quintus, related to quīnque (“five”).

definition: Beading formed with a narrow groove separating it from the surface it decorates.
A molding having a small groove in it.
An almost pleasurable sensation of fright.
example: He's got lots of sales pitches in his quiver.
etymology: From Middle English quiver, cwiver, from Old English *cwifer, probably related to cwic (“alive”).

definition: An improper and unacceptable kind of compromise verdict.

A canal for a current of water.

definition: Full of zest or vigor.

definition: The absence of symmetry about an axis.
Of or relating to automobile tires that have a strip under the tread and relatively little stiffening in the sidewalls.
example: Radial-ply tires.

definition: Send out rays or waves.
example: The sun radiates heat.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus, perfect passive participle of radiō (“to radiate, furnish with spokes, give out rays, radiate, shine”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from radius (“a spoke, ray”).

definition: Grating that admits cooling air to car's radiator.
Surgical removal of the uterus and the ovaries and oviducts and cervix and related lymph nodes.
The political orientation of those who favor revolutionary change in government and society.
etymology: From radical + -ism.

definition: Opacity to X-rays or other radiation.
The spontaneous emission of a stream of particles or electromagnetic rays in nuclear decay.
etymology: From radioactive + -ity or radio- + activity.

definition: A measure of radioactivity.
A radioactive isotope of carbon.
etymology: From radio- + carbon.

definition: A chemical analysis used to determine the age of organic materials based on their content of the radioisotope carbon 14; believed to be reliable up to 40,000 years.
Of or relating to radiology.
etymology: From radiology + -ical.

definition: Pungent fleshy edible root.
A cruciferous plant of the genus Raphanus having a pungent edible root.
An intensely radioactive metallic element that occurs in minute amounts in uranium ores.
etymology: Borrowed from French radium, from rad(ioactif) (“radioactive”) + -ium (suffix used to form the names of metallic elements).

definition: The use of radium in radiation therapy.
A radioactive gaseous element formed by the disintegration of radium; the heaviest of the inert gasses; occurs naturally (especially in areas over granite) and is considered a hazard to health.

definition: A large number or amount.

Fringed orchid of the eastern United States having a greenish flower with the lip deeply lacerated.
A laborer who splits logs to build split-rail fences.
Common smelt of eastern North America and Alaska.
A bridge partner who increases the partner's bid.
example: She is a raiser of gerbils.
etymology: From raise + -er.

definition: Bran flakes with raisins.
Cookie containing raisins.
Moth whose larvae attack dried fruits and cereal products.
Continue talking or writing in a desultory manner.
example: This novel rambles on and jogs.

definition: Continue talking or writing in a desultory manner.
example: This novel rambles on and jogs.

definition: Shrubby plant with aromatic greyish-green leaves used as a cooking herb.
An embankment built around a space for defensive purposes.
example: They stormed the ramparts of the city.

definition: (used of decomposing oils or fats) having a rank smell or taste usually due to a chemical change or decomposition.
example: Rancid butter.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin rancidus (“stinking, rank, rancid, offensive”).

definition: (thermodynamics) a thermodynamic quantity representing the amount of energy in a system that is no longer available for doing mechanical work.
example: There was no randomness in the teacher's selection of the class representative.
etymology: From random + -ness.

definition: (the feminine of raja) a Hindu princess or the wife of a raja.
etymology: From Hindustani رانی (rānī) / रानी (rānī), from Sanskrit राज्ञी (rā́jñī, “queen, princess”). Doublet of Regina.

definition: Wrongfully emptied or stripped of anything of value.
A recorder appointed by a committee to prepare reports of the meetings.
A screwdriver with a ratchet (so the blade turns in only one direction) and a spiral in the handle (so the blade rotates) with downward pressure on the handle.
Approve and express assent, responsibility, or obligation.
example: All parties ratified the peace treaty.
etymology: From Middle English ratifien, from Old French ratifier, from Medieval Latin ratifico, from Latin ratus (“reckoned”).

definition: Defend, explain, clear away, or make excuses for by reasoning.
example: Rationalize the child's seemingly crazy behavior.
etymology: From French rationaliser. By surface analysis, rational + -ize.

definition: Substitute a natural for a supernatural explanation of.
example: You can rationalize away all the strange noises you hear — there is no poltergeist in the house!

definition: Pit viper with horny segments at the end of the tail that rattle when shaken.
etymology: From rattle + snake.

definition: Coarse prickly perennial eryngo of United States thought to cure rattlesnake bite.
etymology: The plant was reputed to cure rattlesnake bites.

definition: Herb of central and southern Europe having purple florets.
A hawkweed with a rosette of purple-veined basal leaves; Canada to northern Georgia and Kentucky.
Unpleasantly loud and harsh.
example: At night, raucous ruckus took place in the swamp.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin raucus (“hoarse, husky, raucous”).

definition: Extremely hungry.
example: A ravenous boy.
etymology: From Middle English ravenous, ravynous, from Old French ravineus. By surface analysis, ravin + -ous.

definition: Small circular or square cases of dough with savory fillings.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian ravioli.

definition: A medium to dark tan color.
A synthetic silklike fabric.
etymology: Name chosen by the National Retail Dry Goods Association of America, probably from French rayon (“a beam of light, ray”) and so called because it is shiny;

definition: Women's stockings made from a sheer material (nylon or rayon or silk).
Torn down and broken up.
(of angles) pointing inward.
example: A polygon with re-entrant angles.

definition: Responsive to stimulation.
etymology: From reactive + -ity.

definition: The quality of written language that makes it easy to read and understand.
example: The book had a clever plot, but lacked readability.
etymology: From readable + -ity or read + -ability.

definition: Affirm once again.
example: He reaffirmed his faith in the church.
etymology: From re- + affirm.

definition: A chemical agent for use in chemical reactions.
etymology: Possibly from Latin reagō. Compare with Norwegian Bokmål reagens.

definition: An edge tool for cutting grass or crops; has a curved blade and a short handle.
Revise or renew one's assessment.
etymology: From re- + assess.

definition: Assignment to a different duty.
etymology: From re- + assignment.

definition: Cast again, in a different role.
example: He was recast as Iago.
etymology: From re- + cast.

definition: A slow or gradual disappearance.
Awaiting payment.
example: Accounts receivable.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English receyvable; by surface analysis, receive + -able.

definition: A container that is used to put or keep things in.
etymology: From Middle English receptacle, from Anglo-Norman receptacle and Middle French receptacle (“organ containing a fluid; gathering place;

definition: Having a sunken area.
example: 1809-1812, Maria Edgeworth, "Manoeuvring", in Tales of Fashionable Life comfortably recessed from curious impertinents.

definition: Of or pertaining to a recession.
etymology: From Latin recēdō + -ive, or directly from New Latin recessīvus.

definition: Gene that produces its characteristic phenotype only when its allele is identical.
example: The recessive gene for blue eyes.

definition: Capable of being recharged.
example: A rechargeable battery.
etymology: From recharge + -able.

definition: A pronoun or pronominal phrase (as ‘each other’) that expresses a mutual action or relationship between the individuals indicated in the plural subject.
example: The sentence ‘They cared for each other’ contains a reciprocal pronoun.

definition: Act, feel, or give mutually or in return.
example: We always invite the neighbors and they never reciprocate!

definition: Written matter that is recited from memory.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French récitation, from Latin recitatio, equivalent to recite + -ation.

definition: In a reckless manner.
etymology: From Middle English reklesly, from Old English rēcelēaslīce; equivalent to reckless + -ly.

definition: The trait of giving little thought to danger.
example: His recklessness repeatedly put him in danger.
etymology: From Middle English reklesnes, reklesnesse, rekelesnesse (also assibilated as rechelesnes, reccheleesnesse), from Old English rēcelēasnes (“recklessness, carelessness, negligence”), equivalent to reckless + -ness.

definition: The act of assuming or maintaining a reclining position.
An armchair whose back can be lowered and foot can be raised to allow the sitter to recline in it.
Withdrawn from society; seeking solitude.

etymology: From Old French reclus, past participle of reclure, from Latin reclūdere (“to disclose, to open”), from re- + claudō (“close”).

definition: Withdrawn from society; seeking solitude.
example: Lived an unsocial reclusive life.
etymology: From recluse + -ive.

definition: Capable of being recognized.
etymology: From recognise + -able.

definition: Of or relating to recombinant DNA.
A protein derived from recombinant DNA.
(physics) a combining of charges or transfer of electrons in a gas that results in the neutralization of ions; important for ions arising from the passage of high-energy particles.
etymology: From re- + combination.

definition: Tending to reconcile or accommodate; bringing into harmony.
Helping to restore to good condition.
example: Reconstructive surgery.
etymology: From reconstruct + -ive.

Surgery concerned with therapeutic or cosmetic reformation of tissue.
An act of narration.
example: His endless recounting of the incident eventually became unbearable.

definition: Reimburse or compensate (someone), as for a loss.

etymology: From French recouper (“cut short”).

definition: Capable of being recovered or regained.

definition: One of the arteries supplying the rectal area.
Having been put right.
An official residence provided by a church for its parson or vicar or rector.
etymology: From Middle French rectorie, from Medieval Latin rectoria. See rector.

definition: Of or relating to a recursion.
(mathematics) a definition of a function from which values of the function can be calculated in a finite number of steps.
A routine that can call itself.
Large tree of Pacific coast of North America having hard red wood much used for furniture.
A shrub buckeye of southern United States.
Brightly colored tropical fishes with chin barbels.
An Irish breed with a chestnut-brown or mahogany-red coat.
Atmospheric electricity (lasting 10 msec) appearing as globular flashes of red (pink to blood-red) light rising to heights of 60 miles (sometimes seen together with elves).
Having red flowers.
Rimmed with red.
example: Your red-rimmed eyes reveal that you have been crying.

definition: Having red stripes.
Recoverable upon payment or fulfilling a condition.
example: Redeemable goods in a pawnshop.
etymology: From redeem + -able.

definition: Discover again.
example: I rediscovered the books that I enjoyed as a child.
etymology: From re- + discover.

definition: Distribute anew.
example: Redistribute the troops more strategically.
etymology: From re- + distribute.

definition: Having population and industries relocated from urban to outlying areas.

definition: A response of body tissues to injury or irritation; characterized by pain and swelling and redness and heat.
example: Nancy Reagan is famous for the redness of her wardrobe.
etymology: From Middle English reednes, rednesse, from Old English rēadnes (“redness”), equivalent to red + -ness.

definition: A reversible chemical reaction in which one reaction is an oxidation and the reverse is a reduction.

definition: Characterized by or causing diminution or curtailment.

definition: Have an element suggestive (of something).

definition: The act of umpiring.

definition: The change in direction of a propagating wave (light or sound) when passing from one medium to another.
Of or relating to or capable of refraction.

Not responding to treatment.

definition: (neurology) the time after a neuron fires or a muscle fiber contracts during which a stimulus will not evoke a response.
A small porous bowl made of bone ash used in assaying to separate precious metals from e.g. lead.
(of furnaces) lined with material that has a high melting point.

definition: A course that reviews and updates a topic for those who have not kept abreast of developments.
Snacks and drinks served as a light meal.

definition: In a regional manner.

etymology: From regional + -ly.

definition: (of taxes) adjusted so that the rate decreases as the amount of income increases.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin regressīvus, equivalent to regress + -ive.

definition: Deserving regret.
example: Regrettable remarks.
etymology: From regret + -able.

definition: By bad luck.

etymology: From regrettable + -ly.

definition: A hexagon with six sides of equal length.
Engage in a rehearsal (of).
example: There’s no need to rehearse the same old argument; we’ve heard it before, and we all agree.
etymology: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).

definition: Install again.
example: She reinstalled the washer after it had been repaired.
etymology: From re- + install.

definition: The condition of being reinstated.
example: Her reinstatement to her former office followed quickly.
etymology: From reinstate + -ment.

definition: Sharing the risk by insurance companies; part or all of the insurer's risk is assumed by other companies in return for part of the premium paid by the insured.
example: Reinsurance enables a client to get coverage that would be too great for any one company to assume.
etymology: From re- + insurance.

definition: A second or subsequent investment in the same thing.
etymology: From re- + investment.

definition: A feeling of great happiness.
example: There was much rejoicing when the good news finally arrived.

definition: The phenomenon of vitality and freshness being restored.
example: The annual rejuvenation of the landscape.
etymology: From rejuvenate + -ion, cf. Latin reiuvenatiō.

definition: An adjective that classifies its noun (e.g., ‘a nervous disease’ or ‘a musical instrument’).
Relating or subject to the special or the general theory of relativity.

etymology: From relativist + -ic or relative + -istic.

definition: (physics) the mass of a body in motion relative to the observer: it is equal to the rest mass multiplied by a factor that is greater than 1 and that increases as the magnitude of the velocity increases.
That has been withdrawn or retreated from.
A recurrence of a prior experience.
example: The reliving of a strong emotion can be therapeutic.

definition: Creation that is created again or anew.
example: It is a remake of an old film.

definition: Refer (a matter or legal case) to another committee or authority or court for decision.

definition: Recall the past.

definition: Do over, as of (part of) a house.

definition: A solvent that removes a substance (usually from a surface).

etymology: From remove + -er.

definition: Someone who pays rent to use land or a building or a car that is owned by someone else.
etymology: From rent + -er.

definition: The imposition of a new organization; organizing differently (often involving extensive and drastic changes).
example: A committee was appointed to oversee the reorganization of the curriculum.

etymology: From re- + organize.

definition: A person who repeats.

etymology: From repeat + -er.

definition: Serving or tending to repel.
example: I find his obsequiousness repellent.
etymology: From Latin repellēns. Equivalent to repel + -ent.

definition: A storehouse where a stock of things is kept.
A theatrical company that performs plays from a repertoire.
Express the same message in different words.
example: Make sure to rephrase your thesis in your conclusion.
etymology: From re- + phrase.

definition: Capable of being replaced.
example: A replaceable battery replaceable parts.
etymology: From replace + -able.

definition: Filled to satisfaction with food or drink.
example: A kitchen replete with all the ultimate appliances.
etymology: From Middle English replete (adjective) and repleten (verb), from Old French replet, from Latin repletus.

definition: Put or confide something in a person or thing.
example: These philosophers reposed the law in the people.

definition: Use as a basis for theories and claims.
Bringing or deserving severe rebuke or censure.
example: Adultery is as reprehensible for a husband as for a wife.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendo; equivalent to reprehend + -ible.

definition: Put down by force or intimidation.
example: To repress rebellion or sedition.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin repressus, the perfect passive participle of reprimō (“to repress”).

definition: A (temporary) relief from harm or discomfort.
example: The prisoner was saved from execution; the governor had requested a reprieve.
etymology: First use appears c. 1513 in the writings of Robert Fabyan.

definition: Rebuke formally.
etymology: From French réprimande, from réprimer (“to repress”).

definition: A retaliatory action against an enemy in wartime.
Repeat an earlier theme of a composition.
example: The aging actress played the role she played in her youth, as if to reprise it.
etymology: From Middle English reprise (noun) and reprisen (verb), from Old French reprise, from reprendre. In some senses borrowed anew from Modern French reprise.

definition: A mild rebuke or criticism.
example: Words of reproach.

definition: Of or relating to the class Reptilia.
etymology: From reptile + -ian, replacing earlier reptilious and adjectival reptile.

definition: The act of purchasing back something previously sold.
etymology: From re- + purchase.

definition: Broadcast again, as of a film.
example: They're still rerunning The Flintstones on this channel.
etymology: From re- + run.

definition: Assign a new time and place for an event.
example: We had to reschedule the doctor's appointment.
etymology: From re- + schedule.

definition: Sell (something) again after having bought it.

definition: Full of or marked by resentment or indignant ill will.
example: Resentful at the way he was treated.

definition: Shape anew or differently.

definition: A redistribution of something.

definition: Honorableness by virtue of being respectable and having a good reputation.

Someone who responds.

definition: Affording physical or mental rest.
example: She spent a restful night at home.
etymology: From Middle English restful, restfulle, equivalent to rest + -ful.

definition: A spore of certain algae or fungi that lies dormant; may germinate after a prolonged period.
The quality of being ceaselessly moving or active.
example: The restlessness of the wind.
etymology: From restless + -ness.

definition: Stock again.
example: He restocked his land with pheasants.
etymology: From re- + stock.

definition: Tending to impart new life and vigor to.
etymology: From Middle English restoratif, restoratyve, from Old French restoratif, restauratif and Medieval Latin restaurātīvus. Equivalent to restore + -ative.

definition: The act of reviving a person and returning them to consciousness.
example: Although he was apparently drowned, resuscitation was accomplished by artificial respiration.
etymology: From Middle English resuscitacion, from Old French ressuscitacion and Latin resuscitātio. Equivalent to resuscitate + -ion.

definition: Of or relating to or having the nature of retribution.
example: The hostile forces were at an impasse; neither could attack with enough force and still defend against the retaliatory counterattack.
etymology: From retaliate + -ory.

definition: Tariff imposed on a foreign commercial entity as a form of reprisal.

etymology: retaliatory + tariff

definition: Visual impairment resulting from the retina becoming separated from the choroid in the back of the eye; treated by photocoagulation.
Someone who has retired from active working.

etymology: From retire + -ee.

definition: A quick reply to a question or remark (especially a witty or critical one).
example: He countered her insult with a clever retort.

definition: Capable of being retracted.

definition: A disavowal or taking back of a previous assertion.

definition: Descriptive of any event or stimulus or process that has an effect on the effects of events or stimuli or process that occurred previously.

definition: After the fact.

Tending to return to an earlier state.

definition: Bringing again into activity and prominence.
etymology: From revitalize + -ation.

definition: Restore strength.

definition: Change radically.

etymology: From revolution + -ize.

definition: To watch a show or television one more time.

etymology: From re- + watch.

definition: Use again in altered form.
example: You'll have to rework the crank assembly to incorporate the changes.
etymology: From re- + work.

definition: Any of various large chiefly tropical beetles having horns on the head; pest on coconuts.

The 17th letter of the Greek alphabet.

definition: A glancing rebound.

definition: The natural outer covering of food (usually removed before eating).

definition: Desire for sensual pleasures.
example: Pure sensuality.
etymology: Derived from Middle French sensualité, derived from Late Latin sēnsuālitātem (“sensibility, capacity for sensation”). By surface analysis, sensual + -ity.

definition: Taking delight in beauty.
example: The sensuous joy from all things fair.
etymology: From Latin sensus (“sense”) + English -ous.

definition: Falsely emotional in a maudlin way.
etymology: From sentimental + -ity. The music sense is a calque of German Empfindsamkeit.

definition: An apparatus that uses centrifugal force to separate particles from a suspension.
A shade of brown with a tinge of red.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin sēpia (“cuttlefish”), from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía). Cognate with Italian seppia, Portuguese siba, and Spanish sepia.

definition: (anatomy) a dividing partition between two tissues or cavities.
example: Look, I got a new septum!
etymology: Borrowed from Latin sēptum (“enclosure, wall, fence”).

definition: In a sequential manner.
etymology: From sequential + -ly.

definition: The act of segregating or sequestering.
example: Sequestration of the jury.
etymology: From Middle French sequestration, from Late Latin sequestrātiō, from Latin sequestrō (“sequester”).

definition: Wood of either of two huge coniferous California trees that reach a height of 300 feet; sometimes placed in the Taxodiaceae.
A musical composition in several movements; has no fixed form.
example: “Eine kleine Nachtmusik” is a well-known serenade written by Mozart.
etymology: Borrowed from French sérénade, from Italian serenata, from the past participle of serenare, from Latin serenare, from serenus (“calm”), of uncertain origin (see there).

definition: The trait of being serious.
example: A lack of solemnity is not necessarily a lack of seriousness.

definition: Notched like a saw with teeth pointing toward the apex.
example: That knife has a serrated blade.
etymology: Past participle of serrate.

definition: Ready for service or able to give long service.
example: Serviceable equipment.
etymology: From Middle English servisable, from Old French servisable, from servise. By surface analysis, service + -able.

definition: Of or involving servomechanisms.
etymology: Clipping of servomotor.

definition: Set fire to; cause to start burning.
example: Lightning set the forest afire.

definition: Narrow chisel made of steel; used to cut stone or bricks.
One who sets written material into type.
The act of severing.
Fastened with stitches.
Waste matter carried away in sewers or drains.
example: They put off paedophiles by spraying the child with eight litres of pressurized sewerage.
etymology: From sewer + -age.

definition: Chromatin found only in female cells.
example: The presence or absence of sex chromatin in cells obtained by amniocentesis makes it possible to determine the sex of a fetus.

definition: Bony flesh of herring-like fish usually caught during their migration to fresh water for spawning; especially of Atlantic coast.
etymology: From Middle English shadde, from Old English sċeadd, of uncertain origin. Compare Low German Schade (“shad, herring”), Scottish Gaelic sgadan (“herring”), Welsh ysgadan.

definition: Annual weed of Europe and North America having a rosette of basal leaves and tiny flowers followed by oblong seed capsules.
Filled with shade.
example: The surface of the pond is dark and shadowed.

definition: The act of following someone secretly.
etymology: From shadow (verb) + -ing (suffix forming nouns denoting the act of doing something, an action, or the embodiment of an action; or forming present participles of verbs).

definition: A rug with long pile.
Without shame.
example: He unashamedly abandoned the project when he realized he would not gain from it.
etymology: From shameless + -ly.

definition: Creeping European clover having white to pink flowers and bright green leaves; naturalized in United States; widely grown for forage.
Trailing trifoliate Asiatic and African herb having cobalt blue flowers.
A measure undertaken by a corporation to discourage unwanted takeover attempts.
Having keen hearing.
Hybrid garden flower derived from Chrysanthemum maximum and Chrysanthemum lacustre having large white flower heads resembling oxeye daisies; often placed in the genus Chrysanthemum.
Having the beard or hair cut off close to the skin.
An adult male who shaves.
etymology: From Middle English schaver; equivalent to shave + -er.

definition: A workman who uses shears to cut leather or metal or textiles.
etymology: From shear + -er.

definition: Removing by cutting off or clipping.
example: The whole shearing of a flock; the shearings from cloth.
etymology: From Middle English scherynge; equivalent to shear + -ing.

definition: Large scissors with strong blades.
example: The shears of a lathe or planer.

definition: Characterized by insincerity or deceit; evasive.
example: Shifty eyes.
etymology: From shift + -y. Cognate with Dutch schiftig (“loose-fitting, open-textured”).

definition: Shine with a weak or fitful light.
example: Beech leaves shimmered in the moonlight.
etymology: From Middle English schimeren, from Old English sċymrian, sċimrian, sċimerian, from Proto-Germanic *skimarōną. Cognate with Dutch schemeren, German schimmern.

definition: Building material used as siding or roofing.
etymology: From dialectal French chingler (“to strap, whip”), from Latin cingula (“girt, belt”), from cingere (“to girt”).

definition: Small deciduous tree of eastern and central United States having leaves that shine like laurel; wood is used in western states for shingles.
East Indian timber tree with hard durable wood used especially for tea boxes.
A sandbank in a stretch of water that is visible at low tide.
example: Shoals of tourists.

definition: Having the capacity to absorb the energy of an impact.
example: The material absorbs shock and is used for shock-absorbent insoles.

definition: A hereditary military dictator of Japan; the shoguns ruled Japan until the revolution of 1867-68.
etymology: From Japanese 将軍 (shōgun), itself the short form of 征夷大将軍 (seii taishōgun, literally “general who overcomes the barbarians”), ultimately from Middle Chinese. Doublet of jiangjun.

definition: Drive away by crying ‘shoo!’.
example: Don't just shoo away mosquitoes, kill them!
etymology: From Middle English schew, schowe, show, showe, scou (“shoo!”, interjection).

definition: Drive away by crying ‘shoo!’.
etymology: From shoo + away.

definition: Coarse South American herb grown for its blue-and-white flowers followed by a bladderlike fruit enclosing a dry berry.
Drive away by crying ‘shoo!’.
An easy victory.
example: She's very popular and good with numbers, so I expect she'll be a shoo-in for treasurer.
etymology: From a sense of the verb shoo, where racehorses would fall back and allow a chosen rider to win a fixed race. See 1910 quotation.

definition: Play a game of craps.
A merchant who owns or manages a shop.
etymology: From shop + keeper.

definition: The act of stealing goods that are on display in a store.
example: Shrinkage is the retail trade's euphemism for shoplifting.
etymology: By surface analysis, shoplift + -ing. The noun sense (from 1690) predates the verb.

definition: The portion of the loin from which porterhouse steaks are cut.
Having short ears.
Breathing laboriously or convulsively.
The property of being of short spatial extent.
example: The shortness of the Channel crossing.
etymology: From Middle English schortnesse, from Old English sċortnes, sċeortnys, equivalent to short + -ness.

definition: An athlete who competes in the shot put.
The bony arch formed by the collarbones and shoulder blades in humans.
A vise with jaws that are padded in order to hold lumber without denting it.
Having shoulders or shoulders as specified; usually used as a combining form.
example: Stoop-shouldered.

definition: An arch consisting of a horizontal lintel supported at each end by corbels that project into the aperture.
A male sponsor who books and stages public entertainments.
example: A consummate showman.
etymology: From show + -man.

definition: Plant having branching leafy stems each branch with an especially showy solitary flower head with many narrow pink or lavender or white rays; northwestern United States mountains.
A device that shreds documents (usually in order to prevent the wrong people from reading them).
etymology: From shred + -er.

definition: Sharp piercing cry.
Sharp piercing cry.
etymology: From shriek + -ing.

definition: Process or result of becoming less or smaller.
example: The material lost 2 inches per yard in shrinkage.
etymology: From shrink + -age.

definition: A passage by which a bodily fluid (especially blood) is diverted from one channel to another.
example: An arteriovenus shunt.
etymology: From Middle English schonten, schunten (“to jerk, swerve; to dodge, escape”), either: * possibly a back-formation from Middle English schonen (“to avoid, refuse, hate, fear”), from Old English sċunian, sċyniġan; see shun.

definition: A closed circuit in which the current divides into two or more paths before recombining to complete the circuit.
Silence (someone) by uttering ‘shush!’.
example: He wouldn't shush so I kicked him.
etymology: Imitative. Compare shh and hush.

definition: A feeling of fear of embarrassment.
example: Her shyness kept her from asking him to the prom.
etymology: From shy + -ness.

definition: An inlet with two or more couplings to which a hose can be attached so that fire engines can pump water into the sprinkler system of a building.
An inlet with two or more couplings to which a hose can be attached so that fire engines can pump water into the sprinkler system of a building.
Confined to bed (by illness).
Facial hair that has grown down the side of a man's face in front of the ears (especially when the rest of the beard is shaved off).
A removable board fitted on the side of a wagon to increase its capacity.
etymology: From side + board.

definition: A subordinate incident of little importance relative to the main event.
example: Instruction is not an educational sideshow.
etymology: From side + show.

definition: An earth color containing ferric oxides; used as a pigment.
etymology: From Italian terra di Siena (“earth of Siena”), Siena being the most notable Renaissance location of the clay.

definition: Tube formed by cells joined end-to-end through which nutrients flow in flowering plants and brown algae.
The act of separating grain from chaff.
etymology: From Middle English syftynge; equivalent to sift + -ing.

definition: Someone who signs and is bound by a document.
example: John Hancock is famous for being the first signatory to the American Declaration of Independence, and for writing his name large.
etymology: From Latin signatorius.

definition: The meaning of a word or expression; the way in which a word or expression or situation can be interpreted.
example: The signifier is linked to the signified.

definition: Used as an Italian courtesy title; can be prefixed to the name or used separately.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian signor, apocopic form of signore. Doublet of senior and señor.

definition: An extremely hard blue-black crystalline compound (SiC) used as an abrasive and a heat refractory material; crystals of silicon carbide can be used as semiconductors.
The brightly colored garments of a jockey; emblematic of the stable.
Australian breed of toy dogs having a silky blue coat.
A ludicrous folly.
etymology: From silly + -ness.

definition: Mud or clay or small rocks deposited by a river or lake.
etymology: PIE word *sḗh₂l From Middle English silte, cilte, cylte, perhaps from Middle English silen ("to filter; strain";

definition: Become chocked with silt.
example: The river silted up.

definition: Having a silver-colored body.
Of grey resembling silver.
Of grey resembling silver.
Cooking in a liquid that has been brought to a boil.
A lack of penetration or subtlety.
example: They took advantage of her simplicity.

definition: Allowing communication in only one direction at a time, or in telegraphy allowing only one message over a line at a time.
example: Simplex system.
etymology: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin simplex (“plain, simple; single”). The first part, sim-, comes from Proto-Indo-European *sem-, *sm̥- (“one; together”).

definition: A method for solving problems in linear programming that tests adjacent vertices of the feasible set in sequence so that at each new vertex the objective function improves or is unchanged.
A textile machine that transforms the drawn sliver into roving.
example: Simplex machines give the attenuated sliver a small amount of twist to ensure the required strength of the roving.

definition: A method for solving problems in linear programming that tests adjacent vertices of the feasible set in sequence so that at each new vertex the objective function improves or is unchanged.
An explanation that omits superfluous details and reduces complexity.
etymology: From the French simplification.

definition: Characterized by one unified purpose.
etymology: From single-minded + -ness.

definition: In a singular manner or to a singular degree.
example: He behaved most singularly when we met him last night.
etymology: From Middle English singulerly; equivalent to singular + -ly.

definition: A depression in the ground communicating with a subterranean passage (especially in limestone) and formed by solution or by collapse of a cavern roof.
etymology: From Middle English sinkehole, sinkeholl, equivalent to sink + hole.

definition: A tube running from the liquid in a vessel to a lower level outside the vessel so that gravity forces the liquid through the tube.
etymology: From Middle French siphon, from Old French sifon, from Latin sīphō, from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of uncertain origin;

definition: Convey, draw off, or empty by or as if by a siphon.
The kinship relation between a female offspring and the siblings.
etymology: From Middle English susterhede; equivalent to sister + -hood (with a modification in the suffix).

definition: Make a sound like frying fat.
example: I sizzled the bacon for a few minutes in the pan.
etymology: Probably a derivative of Middle English sissen (“to hiss; buzz; hum”), equivalent to siss + -le (frequentative suffix); Ultimately imitative.

definition: Someone who habitually doubts accepted beliefs.
A book containing sheets of paper on which sketches can be drawn.
etymology: From sketch + book.

definition: An arch whose jambs are not at right angles with the face.
Any correlation in which the rates of change of the variables is not constant.
Having eyes that look in different directions.
Turned or twisted toward one side.
example: His wig was, as the British say, skew-whiff.
etymology: From skew + weft. The expression 'skew weft' dates at least from the 18th century as a term used by handloom weavers, typically in northern England.

definition: Having or showing knowledge and skill and aptitude.
A male worker who has acquired special skills.
With skill.
example: Fragments of a nearly complete jug, skillfully restored at the institute of archaeology.
etymology: From Middle English skilfully, skylfully, skilfulliche, equivalent to skillful + -ly.

definition: Used of milk and milk products from which the cream has been removed.
example: She can drink skimmed milk but should avoid butter.

definition: Milk from which the cream has been skimmed.
example: We like to drink skimmed milk instead so as to consume fewer calories.

definition: Containing little excess.
example: A skimpy allowance.
etymology: From skimp + -y.

definition: Being all around the edges; enclosing.
example: The room's skirting board needs painting.

definition: A molding covering the joint formed by a wall and the floor.
A bowling game that is played by rolling a bowling ball down a bowling alley at a target of nine wooden pins.
Deciduous perennial low-growing fetid swamp plant of eastern North America having minute flowers enclosed in a mottled greenish or purple cowl-shaped spathe.
etymology: From skunk + cabbage, from the strong odor produced when the leaves are broken or torn.

definition: A window in a roof to admit daylight.
etymology: From sky + light.

definition: Propels bright light high in the sky, or used to propel a lifesaving line or harpoon.
etymology: From sky + rocket.

definition: A person who shirks their work or duty (especially one who tries to evade military service in wartime).
etymology: From slack + -er; compare especially slack off.

definition: The evasion of work or duty.
(used in the plural) pants for casual wear.
Having an oblique or slanted direction.
example: The news report was slanted in favor of the nationalists.

definition: A boisterous comedy with chases and collisions and practical jokes.
etymology: From slap + stick, calque of Italian batacchio. The pair of sticks was used by the comic character Harlequin in the commedia dell'arte.

definition: Someone who slashes another person.
etymology: From slash + -er.

definition: A building where animals are butchered.
etymology: From slaughter + house.

definition: A heavy long-handled hammer used to drive stakes or wedges.
etymology: Compound of sledge + hammer.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Malvaviscus having brilliant bell-shaped drooping flowers like incompletely opened hibiscus flowers.
An occasion of spending a night away from home or having a guest spend the night in your home (especially as a party for children).
etymology: From sleep + over.

definition: Made with sleeves or sleeves especially as specified; often used in combination.
example: Sleeved garments.
etymology: From Middle English *sleved, *isleved, from Old English ġeslīefed (“sleeved”), equivalent to sleeve + -ed.

definition: Having no sleeves.
example: Sleeveless summer dresses.
etymology: From Middle English slevelees, sleveles, from Old English slīeflēas (“sleeveless”), equivalent to sleeve + -less.

definition: A vehicle mounted on runners and pulled by horses or dogs; for transportation over snow.
example: Santa travels in a sleigh.
etymology: From Modern Dutch slee, from Middle Dutch slede, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slidô. Doublet of sled and further related to slide.

definition: A bed with solid headboard and footboard that roll outward at the top.
A bell attached to a sleigh, or to the harness of a horse that is pulling a sleigh.
Adroitness in using the hands.
etymology: From Middle English sleighte, sleyght, sleythe, from Old Norse slœgð (“cunning”), from Proto-Germanic *slōgiþō, from *slōgiz (“cunning”) (whence English sly). Doublet of sly and slöjd/sloyd.

definition: Throwing with a wide motion (as if with a sling).
A plaything consisting of a Y-shaped stick with elastic between the arms; used to propel small stones.
etymology: From sling + shot.

definition: A loop formed in a cord or rope by means of a slipknot; it binds tighter as the cord or rope is pulled.
Any of several chiefly American wildflowers having an inflated pouchlike lip; difficult or impossible to cultivate in the garden.
Divide into slivers or splinters.
example: To sliver wood.
etymology: From Middle English slivere, sliver from Middle English sliven (“to cut, cleave, split”), from Old English slīfan (as in tōslīfan (“to split, split up”)).

definition: Work doggedly or persistently.
example: It was like being slogged by a heavyweight boxer.
etymology: Probably a variation of slug (“to hit very hard”) or slough. Possibly related to slag, seen in the North Germanic languages, in association with the third verb and second noun definition.

definition: A sailing vessel with a single mast set about one third of the boat's length aft of the bow.
Having an oblique or slanted direction.
Sloping channel through which things can descend.
Retarded in intellectual development.
(baseball) a ballplayer who is batting.
example: That will bring up the slugger, Jones.
etymology: From slug + -er.

definition: A suspension of insoluble particles (as plaster of Paris or lime or clay etc.) usually in water.
etymology: Unclear; probably related to Middle English sloor (“thin or fluid mud”); compare slur. From mid-15th c.

definition: Make a splashing sound.
etymology: May be a variant of sludge or imitative like slosh. Perhaps a confluence of both influences.

definition: Spill or splash copiously or clumsily.
A fund for buying votes or bribing public officials.
example: He is said to have used his party’s slush fund to buy votes in the election.
etymology: Originally in reference to money for miscellaneous uses that sailors made by selling slush (“a soft mixture of grease and other ingredients”).

definition: Having small ears.
Consisting of fine particles.
In a clever manner.
example: A smartly managed business.
etymology: From Middle English smertly; equivalent to smart + -ly.

definition: Small cold-water silvery fish; migrate between salt and fresh water.
etymology: From Middle English smelt, from Old English smelt, from Proto-West Germanic *smelt, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaz.

definition: An industrial plant for smelting.
example: He works as a smelter.
etymology: From smelt + -er.

definition: Haddock usually baked but sometimes broiled with lots of butter.
Showing scarcely suppressed anger.
example: Her tone was … conversational although … her eyes were smoldering.

definition: Common shrub of the eastern United States with smooth bark.
A variety of aster (Symphyotrichum laeve).
Closely shaved recently.
Made smooth by ironing.
A texture without roughness; smooth to the touch.
example: Admiring the slim smoothness of her thighs.
etymology: From Middle English smothenesse; equivalent to smooth + -ness. Compare Old English smēþnes (“smoothness, a smooth place, a level surface”).

definition: Envelop completely.
example: Smother the meat in gravy.
etymology: From Middle English smother, smorther (“a suffocating vapour, dense smoke”), from Old English smorþor (“smoke”, literally “that which suffocates”), from smorian (“to suffocate, choke”) + -þor (instrumental suffix).

definition: A smoky fire to drive away insects.
example: There was a smudge on the paper.
etymology: Derived from the verb (see below). Doublet of smutch.

definition: Someone who imports or exports without paying duties.
etymology: From smuggle + -er.

definition: A black colloidal substance consisting wholly or principally of amorphous carbon and used to make pigments and ink.
etymology: From Middle English smutten (“to defile, debase”), related to German Schmutz (“filth, dirt, smut”) and schmutzen (“to make dirty, stain”). Doublet of schmutz. Compare also Old English smitta (“smear; blot; mark; stain;

definition: Any fungus of the order Ustilaginales.
etymology: From smut (“soot, black smoke”) + fungus.

definition: Grass native to West Indies but common in southern United States having tufted wiry stems often infested with a dark fungus.
Disdainfully or ironically humorous; scornful and mocking.
etymology: From snark + -y; 1906, as “irritable”, from snark (“to snort”), by onomatopoeia (1866). Compare Low German snarken (“to snore”), North Frisian snarke, Swedish snarka.

definition: A small piece of anything (especially a piece that has been snipped off).
example: That wholesale auction lot was a snip at $10.
etymology: From Dutch snippen (“to snip; shred”) or Low German snippen (“to snip; shred”), of imitative origin. Compare snap.

definition: Sever or remove by pinching or snipping.
A person regarded as arrogant and annoying.
Sleeping for a short period of time (usually not in bed).
example: The cat enjoys taking a snooze on a sunny windowsill.
etymology: Unknown, attested since 18th century. Compare Dutch snoezelen (“to snooze”) or Swedish snusa (“to snore lightly”). Compare also Ancient Greek νυστάζω (nustázō, “to doze, drowse”) and Russian сон (son, “sleep, dream”).

definition: The rattling noise produced when snoring.
etymology: From Middle English snoren, fnoren (“to snore loudly; snort”), from Middle English snore, *fnore (“snore; snort”, noun), from Old English fnora (“snort;

definition: An act of forcible exhalation.
Small weevil having a prolonged snout; destructive to e.g. grains and nuts.
A machine that removes snow by scooping it up and throwing it forcefully through a chute.
Tracked vehicle for travel on snow having skis in front.
etymology: From snow + -mobile.

definition: A storm with widespread snowfall accompanied by strong winds.
etymology: From earlier snow-storm, snow storm, equivalent to snow + storm.

definition: Small New World egret.
An instance of driving away or warding off.
example: I hope the people we couldn't invite don't see it as a snub.
etymology: From Middle English snubben, snibben (noun), either from an undocumented Old English [Term?] or from Old Norse snubba (“to curse, chide, snub, scold, reprove, rebuff, infringe”), from Proto-Germanic *snūbaną, *snūpaną.

definition: Resembling or having the qualities of soap.
example: A soapy consistency.
etymology: From soap + -y. Compare German Low German sepig (“soapy”), German seifig (“soapy”), Swedish såpig (“soapy”).

definition: Tending to make sober or more serious.
example: The news had a sobering effect.

definition: Inclined to or conducive to companionship with others.
example: A sociable occasion.
etymology: From Middle French sociable, from Latin sociābilis.

definition: The condition of being arranged in social strata or classes within a group.
A socially prominent person.
etymology: From social (“pertaining to high society”) + -ite, perhaps as a play on social light, in imitation of words in -ite.

definition: Under group or government control.
example: Socialized ownership.

definition: The act of meeting for social purposes.
example: There was too much socialization with the enlisted men.

definition: A strongly alkaline caustic used in manufacturing soap and paper and aluminum and various sodium compounds.
Any location known for vice and corruption.
A pretzel made of soft bread.
(of especially persons) lacking sense or understanding or judgment.
The property of giving little resistance to pressure and being easily cut or molded.
etymology: From Middle English softnesse, from Old English sōftnes, alteration of earlier sēftnes. Equivalent to soft + -ness.

definition: Soiled or likely to soil with dirt or grime.
A temporary stay (e.g., as a guest).
The angle subtended by the mean equatorial radius of the Earth at a distance of one astronomical unit.
A large plexus of sympathetic nerves in the abdomen behind the stomach.
Fastening firmly together.
Flux applied to surfaces that are to be joined by soldering; flux cleans the surfaces and results in a better bond.
A hand tool with a heatable tip; used to melt and apply solder.
Make solid or more solid; cause to solidify.
etymology: From French solidifier. By surface analysis, solid + -ify.

definition: The quantity of a particular substance that can dissolve in a particular solvent (yielding a saturated solution).
A thinker who focuses on the problem as stated and tries to synthesize information and knowledge to achieve a solution.
example: The first successful solver of the puzzle will win a prize.
etymology: From solve + -er.

definition: Affecting or characteristic of the body as opposed to the mind or spirit.
example: A somatic symptom or somatic illness.
etymology: From Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

definition: Any of the cells of a plant or animal except the reproductive cells; a cell that does not participate in the production of gametes.
example: Somatic cells are produced from preexisting cells.

definition: A delusion concerning the body image or parts of the body.
The perception of tactual or proprioceptive or gut sensations.
The faculty of bodily perception; sensory systems associated with the body; includes skin senses and proprioception and the internal organs.
Lacking brightness or color; dull.
example: A sombre situation.
etymology: Borrowed from French sombre (“dark”), from Old French sombre, from a verb *sombrer or Latin sub- + umbra. Compare Spanish sombra (“shade; dark part of a picture; ghost”).

definition: Common Old World thrush noted for its song.
Praise in a sonnet.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French sonnet, from Italian sonetto, from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).

definition: Take in, also metaphorically.
A woman sorcerer.
etymology: From Middle English sorceresse, from Anglo-Norman sorceresse.

definition: Morally degraded.
example: The sordid details of his orgies stank under his very nostrils.
etymology: From Middle English sordide, from Latin sordidus.

definition: Economically important Old World tropical cereal grass.
etymology: From New Latin genus name Sorghum, from Italian sorgo, from Vulgar Latin *syricum (“Syrian”), from Sȳricus. Doublet of the synonyms sorgho (via French) and sorgo (via Italian).

definition: A former French coin of low denomination; often used of any small amount of money.
example: He hasn't a sou to his name.
etymology: Borrowed from French sou. Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solid, solidus, and xu.

definition: Lacking sensitivity or the capacity for deep feeling.
etymology: From Middle English soulelez; equivalent to soul + -less. Compare Old English sāwollēas; the Middle English word likely is a re-formation.

definition: Deeply or completely.
example: Slept soundly through the storm.
etymology: From Middle English soundly, soundely, from Old English ġesundlīċe (“safely, prosperously, gladly”), equivalent to sound + -ly. Originally meaning "safely", the present sense came in the 16ᵗʰ century.

definition: Australian tree having an agreeably acid fruit that resembles a gourd.
A leaven of dough in which fermentation is active; used by pioneers for making bread.
example: The troops went for those fresh tomatoes like sourdoughs going for gold in the Klondike.
etymology: From Middle English sour dogh, equivalent to sour + dough.

definition: Made with a starter of a small amount of dough in which fermentation is active.
Having turned bad.
Artificially soured light cream.
Situated in or oriented toward the south.
example: A southern exposure.
etymology: From souther + -ly.
