definition: A sharp hand gesture (resembling a blow).
example: He made a thrusting motion with his fist.

definition: Make a dull sound.
example: The knocker thudded against the front door.

definition: Move rhythmically.
example: The cat thumped its tail in irritation.
etymology: Mid 16th century, probably imitative.

definition: Beat out a rhythm.
(mythology) the spirit of thunder and lightning believed by some Native Americans to take the shape of a great bird.
etymology: From thunder + bird.

definition: Sounding like thunder.
example: The thundering herd.
etymology: From Middle English thonderynge, þoundryng, equivalent to thunder + -ing.

definition: Loud enough to cause (temporary) hearing loss.
etymology: From thunder + -ous.

definition: A jeweled headdress worn by women on formal occasions.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

definition: The inner and thicker of the two bones of the human leg between the knee and ankle.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tībia (“shin bone, leg”).

definition: Exciting by touching lightly so as to cause laughter or twitching movements.
example: A tickling sensation.

definition: Information about recent and important events.
Overtime play in order to break a tie; e.g. tennis and soccer.
etymology: From tie + breaker.

definition: Having irregularly cross-banded back; of arid foothills and canyons of southern Arizona and Mexico.
Widely distributed brown or black North American salamander with vertical yellowish blotches.
A state occasioned by scarcity of money and a shortage of credit.
etymology: From tight + -ness.

definition: The application of tiles to cover a surface.
example: All the tiling in the bathroom must be removed because of water damage to the wood under it.

definition: A shoot that sprouts from the base of a grass.
etymology: From Middle English tilier; equivalent to till + -er.

definition: Widely distributed in rugged ground of eastern United States.
A slight but appreciable amount.
etymology: The verb is derived from Latin tingere, present active infinitive of tingō (“to dip; to moisten; to colour, dye, tinge”). The noun is derived from the verb.

definition: An almost pleasurable sensation of fright.
example: Get/give tingles.
etymology: From Middle English tinglen, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English tingen (“to tink”) + -len, equivalent to ting + -le.

definition: A ringing or booming sensation in one or both ears; a symptom of an ear infection or Meniere's disease.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin tinnītus (“a jingling, ringing”).

definition: A trifle soaked in wine and decorated with almonds and candied fruit.
A speech of violent denunciation.
example: Come out with a tirade.
etymology: Borrowed from French tirade (“monologue, speech, tirade”).

definition: Temporary loss of strength and energy resulting from hard physical or mental work.
etymology: From Middle English tiredness, terednesse, equivalent to tired + -ness.

definition: Exact a tithe from.
example: The church was tithed.

definition: Barn originally built to hold tithes paid in kind and common in England.
Of or relating to a legal title to something.
example: Titulary rights.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French titulaire, from Latin titulāris, from titulus (“title”).

definition: Fungus causing a downy mildew on growing tobacco.
Having a toe or toes of a specified kind; often used in combination.
example: A three-toed sloth.
etymology: From toe (“digit of a foot”) + -ed.

definition: Caramelized sugar cooled in thin sheets.
example: What a load of old toffee!
etymology: An alteration of taffy.

definition: An apple that is covered with a candy-like substance (usually caramelized sugar).
example: Toffee apples and fairy floss are often sold as fairground snacks.
etymology: The weapon is named after the food item, having a similar shape, i.e. a sphere with attached stick or handle.

definition: Affectionate closeness.
example: Togetherness is the new wonder ingredient in marriage.
etymology: From together + -ness.

definition: Cut with a tomahawk.
example: Not satisfied with tomahawking our colleagues in the country, they ask the scanty remnant in the House to join in the scalp dance.
etymology: From an Eastern Algonquian word, most likely Powhatan tumahák; compare also Malecite-Passamaquoddy tomhikon (“axe”), Abenaki temahigan, demahigan (“axe”).

definition: A disease of tomato plants.
A girl who behaves in a boyish manner.
example: His sister, his dearest and only playmate, is a tomboy at heart.
etymology: From tom + boy. First attested in Ralph Roister Doister (published 1567, written circa 1552), where it is used to describe a boisterous girl;

definition: An inability to distinguish differences in pitch.
Any of various devices for taking hold of objects; usually have two hinged legs with handles above and pointed hooks below.
etymology: From Middle English tonges, equivalent to tong (“tool for manipulating things in a fire”) + -s.

definition: A tax imposed on ships that enter the US; based on the tonnage of the ship.
etymology: From Old French tonnage. Equivalent to tonne + -age.

definition: A tax imposed on ships that enter the US; based on the tonnage of the ship.
A box or chest or cabinet for holding hand tools.
etymology: From tool + box.

definition: An ache localized in or around a tooth.
example: I often have toothache.
etymology: From Middle English toth-ake, from Old English tōþeċe (“toothache”). By surface analysis, tooth + ache.

definition: Small deciduous aromatic shrub (or tree) having spiny branches and yellowish flowers; eastern North America.
Any of several whales having simple conical teeth and feeding on fish etc.
etymology: Calque of translingual Odontoceti. By surface analysis, toothed + whale.

definition: Lacking teeth.
example: Most birds are toothless.
etymology: From Middle English tothles, from Old English tōþlēas, from Proto-Germanic *tanþlausaz (“toothless”), equivalent to tooth + -less.

definition: A yellow quartz.
etymology: From Old French topace (compare French topaze), from Ancient Greek τόπαζος (tópazos).

definition: Anesthetic that numbs a particular area of the body.
Anesthetic that numbs a particular area of the body.
The study of anatomy based on regions or divisions of the body and emphasizing the relations between various structures (muscles and nerves and arteries etc.) in that region.
Concerned with topography.
example: A topographical engineer.

definition: Of or relating to topology.
example: Topological group.
etymology: From topology + -ical.

definition: (mathematics) any set of points that satisfy a set of postulates of some kind.
example: Assume that the topological space is finite dimensional.

definition: Fall down, as if collapsing.
example: The massed crowds toppled the statue of the former dictator.
etymology: From top + -le (frequentative verb suffix).

definition: Relating to or resulting from the action of a torrent.
example: Torrential erosion.
etymology: From torrent + -ial.

definition: A tortuous and twisted shape or position.
etymology: From Middle English torcion, from Middle French torsion, from Late Latin torsiōnem, from Latin tortiō, from torqueō (“twist, turn”). See torture, -tort.

definition: The angle between two planes.
Measuring instrument designed to measure small forces by the torsion they exert on a thin wire.
A metal bar acting as a torsional spring, used in the suspensions of some motor vehicles.
example: Over-rotating the torsion bars can cause the suspension to hit the bump-stop prematurely, causing a harsh ride.

definition: The Calvinist doctrine that everyone is born in a state of corruption as a result of original sin.
Surgical removal of the uterus and cervix.
A form of government in which the ruler is an absolute dictator (not restricted by a constitution or laws or opposition etc.).
etymology: 1938, from totalitarian + -ism, modeled after Italian totalitarismo (1923, by Giovanni Amendola) and German terms such as Totalstaat (1927, The Concept of the Political, by Carl Schmitt).

definition: Used of automobiles; completely demolished.
example: The insurance adjuster declared the automobile totaled.

definition: The faculty by which external objects or forces are perceived through contact with the body (especially the hands).
example: Only sight and touch enable us to locate objects in the space around us.

definition: A basis for comparison; a reference point against which other things can be evaluated.
etymology: From touch + stone.

definition: The people living in a municipality smaller than a city.
etymology: From town + -s- + people.

definition: A very small spaniel.
(usually followed by ‘to’) able to be traced to.
example: A failure traceable to lack of energy.

definition: Traditional jazz as revived in the 1950s.
etymology: Shortening of traditional.

definition: Stubbornly conservative and narrow-minded.
etymology: From traditional + -ist.

definition: Trailing plant having crowded clusters of 3 brilliant deep pink flowers resembling a single flower blooming near the ground; found in dry gravelly or sandy soil; southwestern United States and Mexico.
A commercial steamer for hire; one having no regular schedule.
Tread or stomp heavily or roughly.
example: The soldiers trampled across the fields.
etymology: From Middle English tramplen, trampelen (“to walk heavily”), equivalent to tramp + -le.

definition: A conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers.
An untroubled state; free from disturbances.
example: The garden offers a sense of tranquillity away from the busy city.
etymology: From tranquil + -ity, from Middle English tranquillite, from Old French tranquillite, tranquilité, from Latin tranquillitas.

definition: A broader form of use immunity that also protects the witness from any prosecution brought about relating to transactions to which they gave testimony.
Exceeding or surpassing usual limits especially in excellence.
etymology: From transcend + -ent, or borrowed from Latin trānscendēns.

definition: Spanning or crossing or on the farther side of a continent.
example: Transcontinental railway.
etymology: From trans- + continental.

definition: An electrical device that converts one form of energy into another.
etymology: 1924, Latin trānsdūcō + -er. By surface analysis, transduce + -er.

definition: The act of transgressing; the violation of a law or a duty or moral principle.
example: The boy was punished for the transgressions of his father.
etymology: From Middle English transgressioun, from Old French transgression, from Late Latin trānsgressiō, from Latin trānsgressus (perfect active participle of trānsgredior (“to step across”)) + -iō.

definition: Designating a verb that requires a direct object to complete the meaning.
example: The English verb "to notice" is a transitive verb, because we say things like "She noticed a problem".
etymology: From Latin trānsitīvus, from trānsitus, from trāns (“across”) + itus, from eō (“to go”).

definition: A paired dural sinus; terminates in the sigmoid sinus.
Someone who sets traps for animals (usually to obtain their furs).
etymology: From trap + -er, compare french trappeur.

definition: (usually plural) accessory wearing apparel.
example: He went through his belongings, gradually shedding the trappings of youth.
etymology: From trapping.

definition: A guidebook for travelers.
Soiled from travel.
example: Travel-soiled clothes.

definition: A stroke that keeps the head above water by thrashing the legs and arms.
Any of various small insectivorous birds of the Northern Hemisphere that climb up a tree trunk supporting themselves on stiff tail feathers and their feet.
Insectivorous arboreal mammal of southeast Asia that resembles a squirrel with large eyes and long sharp snout.
Someone who popularizes a new fashion.
Sorting and allocating aid on the basis of need for or likely benefit from medical treatment or food.
etymology: Borrowed from French triage, from trier (“to sort”).

definition: Verbal misrepresentation intended to take advantage of you in some way.
etymology: From trick + -ery, first recorded in 1719.

definition: Someone who plays practical jokes on others.
example: A skilled trickster knows how to outsmart their enemies with ease.
etymology: From trick + -ster.

definition: A vehicle with three wheels that is moved by foot pedals.
etymology: From French tricycle. By surface analysis, tri- + cycle.

definition: One (as a judge) who examines and settles a case.
etymology: From Middle English triour, from Anglo-Norman triour and Middle English trien (equivalent to try + -er).

definition: A cold pudding made of layers of sponge cake spread with fruit or jelly; may be decorated with nuts, cream, or chocolate.
etymology: From Middle English trifle, trifel, triful, trefle, truyfle, trufful, from Old French trufle (“mockery”), a byform of trufe, truffe (“deception”), of uncertain origin.

definition: Spend wastefully.
The mathematics of triangles and trigonometric functions.
example: Historically, trigonometry has been applied in areas such as geodesy, surveying, celestial mechanics and navigation.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to trigono- + -metry.

definition: A worker who thins out and trims trees and shrubs.
example: My new electric shaver has a beard trimmer attachment.
etymology: From trim + -er. Figurative sense of “person who changes views with prevailing opinions” from 1680s, from nautical sense of “adjust sails with the wind”.

definition: An arch built between trimmers in a floor (to support the weight of a hearth).
Capacitor having variable capacitance; used for making fine adjustments.
The accessories that normally accompany (something or some activity).
example: He bought a Christmas tree and trimmings to decorate it.

definition: Involving three parties or elements.
example: A tripartite treaty.
etymology: From Latin tripartītus.

definition: Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
example: His remarks were trite and commonplace.
etymology: From Latin trītus (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of terō (“to wear away, wear out”).

definition: Tropical marine gastropods having beautifully colored spiral shells.
etymology: From trit- + -on. From tritium, from Ancient Greek τρίτος (trítos, “third”).

definition: A brass instrument consisting of a long tube whose length can be varied by a U-shaped slide.
example: Jim plays the trombone very well.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian trombone, from tromba (“trumpet”) + -one (augmentative), literally “large trumpet”. The telecommunications sense alludes to the shape of the musical instrument.

definition: A musician who plays the trombone.
Relating to or situated in or characteristic of the tropics (the region on either side of the equator).
example: Tropical islands.
etymology: From Late Latin tropicus (“of or pertaining to the solstice, as a noun, one of the tropics”), from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic;

definition: Mostly white web-footed tropical seabird often found far from land.
Edible tropical and warm-water prawn.
Foot of a pig or sheep especially one used as food.
example: Grange cookbook recipes for trotters.
etymology: From Middle English trottere, equivalent to trot + -er.

definition: A horse trained to trot; especially a horse trained for harness racing.
A garment (or part of a garment) designed for or relating to trousers.
example: In his trouser's pocket.
etymology: Back-formation from trousers.

definition: A clip worn around a cyclist's ankles that keeps trousers from becoming caught in the bicycle chain.
A cuff on the bottoms of trouser legs.
The leg of a pair of trousers.
A home appliance in which trousers can be hung and the wrinkles pressed out.
Erect shrub having racemes of tawny yellow flowers; the dried leaves are used medicinally as a cathartic; sometimes placed in genus Cassia.
Small active brownish or greyish Old World birds.
Concocted with intent to deceive.
example: Trumped-up charges.
etymology: From the past participle form of the phrasal verb trump up.

definition: A North American woody vine having pinnate leaves and large red trumpet-shaped flowers.
A frustum formed from a cone.
A frustum formed from a pyramid.
Trying something to find out about it.
etymology: Deverbal from try out.

definition: The lowest brass wind instrument.
etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French tuba (“tuba”), German Tuba (“tuba”), originally Baß-Tuba (literally “bass tuba”), or Italian tuba (“tuba”), from Latin tuba (“tube, trumpet, military trumpet”).

definition: Woody vine having bright green leaves and racemes of rose-tinted white flowers; the swollen roots contain rotenone.
Hard volcanic rock composed of compacted volcanic ash.
etymology: From French tuffe, tuf, from Italian tufo, from Latin tōfus. Doublet of tufa.

definition: Mexican epiphytic orchid with glaucous grey-green leaves and lemon- to golden-yellow flowers appearing only partially opened; sometimes placed in genus Cattleya.
Tall North American deciduous timber tree having large tulip-shaped greenish yellow flowers and conelike fruit; yields soft white woods used especially for cabinet work.
A clothes dryer that spins wet clothes inside a cylinder with heated air.
A gymnast who performs rolls and somersaults and twists etc.
example: Rock tumbler.
etymology: From tumble + -er.

definition: A sudden violent disturbance.
An electronic receiver that detects and demodulates and amplifies transmitted signals.
etymology: From tune (verb) + -er.

definition: A traditional Muslim headdress consisting of a long scarf wrapped around the head.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband), also the root of tulip.

definition: Squash plants bearing hard-shelled fruit shaped somewhat like a turban with a rounded central portion protruding from the end opposite the stem.
etymology: From its resemblance to the headgear.

definition: The act of trying to make something hopelessly weak and unattractive appear strong and appealing.
A New World vulture that is common in South America and Central America and the southern United States.
Perennial herb of northeastern United States having a thick knotted yellow rootstock and large rounded leaves.
Widely cultivated plant having a large fleshy edible white or yellow root.
etymology: From Middle English turnepe, probably from turn + Middle English nepe, from Old English nǣp, from Latin nāpus.

definition: A bed in which turnips are growing.
A cruciferous plant with a thick bulbous edible yellow root.
Tender leaves of young white turnips.
Any of several widely cultivated plants having edible roots.
Shaped in the form of a turnip.
A circular horizontal platform that rotates a phonograph record while it is being played.
etymology: From turn + table.

definition: A hard smooth ivory colored dentine that makes up most of the tusks of elephants and walruses.
example: Until the CITES sales ban, elephant tusks were the 'backbone' of the legal ivory trade.

definition: Any of various seashore mollusks having a tapering tubular shell open at each end and a foot pointed like a spade for burrowing.
Utter ‘tsk,’ ‘tut,’ or ‘tut-tut,’ as in disapproval.
etymology: Shortening of tutorial.

definition: Teaching pupils individually (usually by a tutor hired privately).
example: The king's right of seigniory and tutelage.
etymology: From Latin tūtēla (“a watching, guardianship, protection”) + -age, from tuērī (“to watch, guard”). See tuition.

definition: Semiformal evening dress for men.
A disease of the ends of twigs of woody plants.
Spin, wind, or twist together.
example: Intertwine the ribbons.
etymology: From Middle English twinen, twynen, from Old English *twīnian (“to twine, thread”), from Proto-Germanic *twiznōną (“to thread”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwisnós (“double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”).

definition: Shining intermittently with a sparkling light.
example: Twinkling stars.
etymology: From Middle English twynkelynge, equivalent to twinkle + -ing.

definition: A sudden muscle spasm; especially one caused by a nervous condition.
Having two ears.
The ordinal number of two hundred in counting order.
etymology: From two hundred + -th.

definition: Having two lips.
etymology: From two + lipped.

definition: Having two prongs.
etymology: From two + pronged.

definition: Having two toes.
Having more than one decidedly dissimilar aspects or qualities.
example: The office of a clergyman is twofold; public preaching and private influence.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English twofold, from Old English twēofeald. Equivalent to two + -fold; cognate to Icelandic tvöfalt and Dutch tweevoudig.

definition: A specific size and style of type within a type family.
etymology: From type + face.

definition: Serious infection marked by intestinal inflammation and ulceration; caused by Salmonella typhosa ingested with food or water.
etymology: From typhus + -oid.

definition: Serious infection marked by intestinal inflammation and ulceration; caused by Salmonella typhosa ingested with food or water.
Rickettsial disease transmitted by body lice and characterized by skin rash and high fever.
etymology: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-, extended form of *dʰew- (“scatter like dust”).

definition: Rickettsial disease transmitted by body lice and characterized by skin rash and high fever.
Relating to or occurring or used in typography.
example: The typographic art.
etymology: From New Latin typographicus + -al.

definition: A mistake in printed matter resulting from mechanical failures of some kind.
Marked by unjust severity or arbitrary behavior.
example: A tyrannical parent.
etymology: From Latin tyrannicus + -al; ultimately from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos) (absolute ruler, despot).

definition: An amino acid found in most proteins; a precursor of several hormones.
etymology: From Ancient Greek τῡρός (tūrós, “cheese”) + -ine (since first discovered in cheese); surface analysis is approximately tyro- + -ine.

definition: Qualities of appearance that do not give pleasure to the senses.
example: There was some ugliness at the council meeting.
etymology: From ugly + -ness.

definition: In or of the month preceding the present one.
example: Your letter received on the 29th ult.
etymology: Clipping of ultimate.

definition: Lying beyond what is openly revealed or avowed (especially being kept in the background or deliberately concealed).
example: Looked too closely for an ulterior purpose in all knowledge.
etymology: From Latin ulterior (“further, more distant”), from ulter (“that is beyond”) + -ior (“more”).

definition: The last syllable in a word.
etymology: From the Latin feminine of ultimus (“last”).

definition: A game between two teams whose players try to toss a Frisbee to one another until they cross the opponents goal; possession changes hands when the Frisbee is intercepted or touches the ground or goes out of bounds.
Membranous duct connecting the fetus with the placenta.
etymology: From umbilical + cord. Largely displaced native navel-string. First attested in 1753.

definition: A vein in the umbilical cord; returns nutrient blood from the placenta to the fetus.
Being without an escort.
etymology: From un- + accompanied.

definition: Not affiliated.
etymology: From un- + affiliate + -ed.

definition: Remaining in an original state.
example: Persisting unaltered through time.
etymology: From un- + altered.

definition: Having or exhibiting a single clearly defined meaning.
example: As a horror, apartheid … is absolutely unambiguous.
etymology: From un- + ambiguous.

definition: Unwilling to make or express an apology.
example: An unapologetic believer.
etymology: From un- + apologetic.

definition: Not arrogant or presuming.
example: Unassuming to a fault, skeptical about the value of his work.
etymology: From un- + assuming.

definition: Impossible to achieve.
example: An unattainable goal.
etymology: From un- + attain + -able.

definition: (usually used with ‘to’) occurring or existing without the knowledge of.
example: A crisis unbeknown to me.
etymology: Variant of unbeknown with excrescent -st.

definition: Not secured within a cover.
example: An unbound book.

definition: Not restrained or controlled.
example: Unbridled rage.
etymology: From un- + bridled.

definition: Not required or requested.
example: Uncalled-for suggestions.
etymology: From un- + called for.

definition: Not bound by shackles and chains.
etymology: From un- + chained.

definition: Generally agreed upon; not subject to dispute.
example: Many of his crazy ideas remained unchallenged.
etymology: From un- + challenged.

definition: Not claimed or called for by an owner or assignee.
example: Unclaimed luggage.
etymology: From un- + claimed.

definition: Not subject to a security classification.
etymology: From un- + classified.

definition: Lacking complexity.
example: Small and uncomplicated cars for those really interested in motoring.
etymology: From un- + complicated.

definition: Not joined or linked together.
example: The light wouldn't work because the cable was unconnected.
etymology: From un- + connected.

definition: Lacking a conscience.
example: An unconscionable liar.
etymology: From un- + conscionable.

definition: Not disputed and not made the object of contention or competition.
example: Uncontested authority.
etymology: From un- + contested.

definition: In an uncontrolled manner.
example: She laughed uncontrollably.

definition: (spoken slang) unfashionable and boring.
etymology: From un- + cool.

definition: Not harmed or spoiled; sound.
etymology: From un- + damaged.

definition: Not in agreement with or according to democratic doctrine or practice or ideals.
example: The union broke with its past undemocratic procedures.
etymology: From un- + democratic.

definition: Relating to societies in which capital needed to industrialize is in short supply.
A university student who has not yet received a first degree.
etymology: Clipping of undergraduate.

definition: Give extra weight to (a communication).
example: Underline the important words in the text.
etymology: From under- + line.

definition: An undergarment that covers the body from the waist no further than to the thighs; usually worn next to the skin.
Lacking the rights and advantages of other members of society.
etymology: From under- + privileged.

definition: Give extra weight to (a communication).
example: I wish to underscore the importance of proper formatting.
etymology: From under- + score.

definition: Beneath the surface of the sea.
etymology: From under- + sea.

definition: A secretary immediately subordinate to the head of a department of government.
etymology: From under- + secretary.

definition: An actor able to replace a regular performer when required.
etymology: From under- + study.

definition: Being very thin.
example: He's so underweight he's had to buy smaller clothes.
etymology: From under- + weight.

definition: Not easily seen.
example: Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U).
etymology: From un- + detectable.

definition: Not yet having been ascertained or determined.
example: Of undetermined species.
etymology: From un- + determined.

definition: Eluding diagnosis.
example: Undiagnosed disease.
etymology: From un- + diagnosed.

definition: Women's underwear.
etymology: und(erwear) + -ies.

definition: Untroubled by interference or disturbance.
example: He could pursue his studies undisturbed.
etymology: From un- + disturbed.

definition: Get undressed.
example: Please don't undress in front of everybody!
etymology: From Middle English undressen, equivalent to un- + dress. Compare Old English unsċrȳdan (“to undress”, literally “un-shroud”).

definition: Of lumber or stone or hides; not finished or dressed.
example: Undressed granite.
etymology: From un- + dressed.

definition: To an undue degree.
example: She was unduly pessimistic about her future.
etymology: From undue + -ly or un- + duly.

definition: Physical discomfort (as mild sickness or depression).
etymology: From Middle English unese, equivalent to un- + ease. Compare disease.

definition: Not changed by editing.
etymology: From un- + edited.

definition: Continuing forever or indefinitely.
example: The unending bliss of heaven.
etymology: From un- + ending.

definition: Admitting of no doubt or misunderstanding; having only one meaning or interpretation and leading to only one conclusion.
example: Unequivocal evidence.
etymology: From un- + equivocal.

definition: Marked by no noteworthy or significant events.
example: An uneventful life.
etymology: From un- + eventful.

definition: Not yet discovered.
etymology: From un- + explored.

definition: Partiality that is not fair or equitable.
etymology: From unfair + -ness.

definition: Of depth; not capable of being sounded or measured.
example: The sheer number of warriors the enemy attacked with was unfathomable.
etymology: From un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + fathom (“to measure the depth of (water); (figurative) to deeply understand (someone or something)”) + -able (suffix forming adjectives denoting things not able or fit to be done).

definition: Not encouraging or approving or pleasing.
example: Unfavorable conditions.
etymology: From un- + favourable.

definition: Not bound by shackles and chains.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Showing or representing unfavorably.
example: An unflattering portrait.
etymology: From un- + flattering.

definition: Unwilling or unable to forgive or show mercy.
example: A surly unforgiving old woman.

Perennial of western North America.
Masked or pale-faced chimpanzees of western Africa; distantly related to the eastern and central chimpanzees; possibly a distinct species.
Tall evergreen of western North America; commercially important timber tree.
Male sheep especially a castrated one.
etymology: From Middle English wether, wethir, wedyr, from Old English weþer (“a wether, ram”), from Proto-West Germanic *weþru, from Proto-Germanic *weþruz (“wether”), from Proto-Indo-European *wet- (“year”).

definition: A chemical agent capable of reducing the surface tension of a liquid in which it is dissolved.
etymology: From wet + -er.

definition: The act of making something wet.
A chemical agent capable of reducing the surface tension of a liquid in which it is dissolved.
Tall-growing pine of eastern North America; bark is brown with longitudinal fissures when mature; valued as a timber tree.
(British informal) exhausted or worn out.
example: After that all-night party, we were all whacked.

definition: Strike hard.
etymology: Onomatopoeic, representing the sound of an object being slammed against something.

definition: A serious or devastating setback.
etymology: From wham + -y.

definition: A disease of the heads of wheat plants.
A lathe for turning railway-car and locomotive wheels.
Relating to breathing with a whistling sound.
The cause or intention underlying an action or situation, especially in the phrase ‘the whys and wherefores’.
etymology: From Middle English wherfor, wherfore, hwarfore, equivalent to where- (“what”) + for.

definition: Habitually complaining.
example: A whiny child.
etymology: From whine + -y.

definition: Turn in a twisting or spinning motion.
example: The dancer whirled across the stage, stopped, and whirled around to face the audience.

definition: Fly around.
example: Rising smoke whirled in the air.

definition: A powerful circular current of water (usually the result of conflicting tides).
etymology: From earlier whirlpoole, whirlpole, apparently from Middle English *whirlpole, potentially coalescing Old English hwierfel (“whirlpool”) and Old English hwierfepōl (“whirlpool”). Equivalent to whirl + pool.

definition: A small short-handled broom used to brush clothes.
Chiefly tropical clump-forming plants of skeletal appearance resembling whisk brooms; lacking roots.
The hair growing on the lower part of a man's face.
One who speaks in a whisper.
example: Dog whisperer.
etymology: From whisper + -er. The extended senses were popularized by the film The Horse Whisperer (1998).

definition: A buoy that makes a whistling noise.
A buoy that makes a whistling noise.
Tree of western United States.
A small to medium-sized tree growing in brackish water especially along the shores of the southwestern Pacific.
Silvery mullet of Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
Large light-grey African rhinoceros having two horns; endangered; sometimes placed in genus Diceros.
etymology: White of unknown origin, perhaps simply from the color (compare black rhinoceros), or perhaps from Dutch wijd (“wide”). See White Rhinoceros#Naming.

definition: The common stork of Europe; white with black wing feathers and a red bill.
etymology: From white and stork.

definition: Widely cultivated plant having a large fleshy edible white or yellow root.
A colorless water-soluble powder; used as a mordant or to preserve wood or for the electrodeposition of zinc.
(of plants) having white flowers.
Having white lips from fear or terror.
Having white ribs.
Having white streaks.
Changing to a lighter color.
Coated with whitewash.
example: Miles of whitewashed fences.
etymology: From whitewash + -ed.

definition: Frothy water as in rapids or waterfalls.
Resembling milk in color; not clear.
etymology: From Middle English whitisch, whytyssh, equivalent to white + -ish.

definition: Cut small bits or pare shavings from.
example: Whittle a piece of wood.
etymology: From Middle English whytel, from Old English hwītel (“cloak, blanket”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwītil, from Proto-Germanic *hwītilaz, equivalent to white + -le;

definition: Cut away in small pieces.
Cut away in small pieces.
Someone whose career progresses rapidly.
Someone who buys large quantities of goods and resells to merchants rather than to the ultimate customers.
etymology: From wholesale + -er.

definition: Move with a sibilant sound.
example: He whooshed the doors open.
etymology: Of imitative origin.

definition: Morally objectionable behavior.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English wikkednesse, wikkednes, equivalent to wicked + -ness.

definition: A basket made of wickerwork.
Something unspecified whose name is either forgotten or not known.
example: Suppose we have a widget factory that produces 100 units per year...
etymology: Coined by American playwright George S. Kaufman in 1924 in his play Beggar on Horseback (1924). The preface to the 1924 play credits an earlier German work from 1911 where there is an actor Elisabeth Wigge.

definition: Low-growing shrub with spreading branches and flowers in loose heads; desert regions of western United States (California to Utah).
Eurasian sage with blue flowers and foliage like verbena; naturalized in United States.
North American perennial having a slender bulb and whitish flowers.
Bedstraw with sweetish roots.
Common in meadows and pastures.
A common and long cultivated European herb from which most common garden pansies are derived.
Eurasian weed having yellow or mauve or white flowers and podlike fruits.
North American perennial herb; leaves are used medicinally; sometimes placed in genus Cassia.
Done by design.
etymology: From Middle English wilful; equivalent to will + -ful.

definition: A variety of aster (Symphyotrichum praealtum).
Marked by skill in deception.
example: A wily old attorney.
etymology: From Middle English wily, wiley, wyly. By surface analysis, wil(e) + -y.

definition: Mechanical device attached to an elevated structure; rotates freely to show the direction of the wind.
Breathing laboriously or convulsively.
example: She felt winded from her long run.

definition: Fruit that has fallen from the tree.
example: They couldn't reach the branches, so they ate the windfalls.
etymology: From Middle English windfal, wyndfall, equivalent to wind + fall. Cognate with Middle High German wintval, wintfal, German Windfall.

definition: Profit that occurs unexpectedly as a consequence of some event not controlled by those who profit from it.
Someone who decorates shop windows.
Transparent screen (as of glass) to protect occupants of a vehicle.
example: Oh no! A vandal has just smashed our windscreen! Susan, can you go and call the insurance company?
etymology: From wind + screen.

definition: The direction from which the wind is coming.
etymology: From wind + -ward.

definition: The side toward the wind.
A barrel that holds wine.
A male pilot who positions his aircraft outside and behind (on the wing of) the leader of a flying formation.
etymology: From wing + -man.

definition: Linear distance between the extremities of an airfoil.
example: The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird.
etymology: From wing + span.

definition: Closing the eyes intermittently and rapidly.
Flesh of American flounder; important in the winter.
Erect perennial subshrub having pink or white flowers and leathery leaves with a flavor of thyme; southern Europe.
Resinous leaves used in stews and stuffings and meat loaf.
A worker who wipes.
etymology: From wipe + -er.

definition: Contact consisting of a conducting arm that rotates over a series of fixed contacts and comes to rest on an outlet.
A mechanical device that cleans the windshield.
Electric motor that moves the windshield wiper.
A person who escapes into a world of fantasy.

Any of several deciduous low-growing shrubs of the genus Fothergilla having showy brushlike spikes of white flowers in spring and fiery red and orange autumn color; grows from Alabama to the Allegheny Mountains.
Lean and wrinkled by shrinkage as from age or illness.
example: A lanky scarecrow of a man with withered face and lantern jaws.

definition: Wreaking or capable of wreaking complete destruction.
example: The guns opened a withering fire.
etymology: From wither + -ing.

definition: The highest part of the back at the base of the neck of various animals especially draft animals.
etymology: From dialectal English wither (“against”) (compare wither-) + -s; see with. So-named because it is the part of the horse that pushes against a load.

definition: In an unfortunate or deplorable manner.
example: It was woefully inadequate.
etymology: From Middle English wofully, equivalent to woeful + -ly.

definition: Pan with a convex bottom; used for frying in Chinese cooking.
etymology: Borrowed from Cantonese 鑊 /镬 (wok⁶).

definition: Turned or twisted toward one side.
etymology: From English dialectal wanky, alteration of Middle English wankel (“unstable, shaky”), from Old English wancol (“unstable”), from Proto-West Germanic *wankul (“swaying, shaky, unstable”).

definition: Any of several asters of eastern North America usually growing in woods.
A chisel for working wood; it is either struck with a mallet or pushed by hand.
Any of several Old World birds of the genus Ibis.
A deity or nymph of the woods.
Any of several Old World birds of the genus Ibis.
Large thrush common in eastern American woodlands; noted for its melodious song.
A vise with jaws that are padded in order to hold lumber without denting it.
Small bright-colored American songbird with a weak unmusical song.
Any of numerous South American and Central American birds with a curved bill and stiffened tail feathers that climb and feed like woodpeckers.
Game bird of the sandpiper family that resembles a snipe.
etymology: From Middle English wodecocke, wode-koc, wodekok, from Old English wudecocc, wuducoc, equivalent to wood + cock.

definition: Any of several large caribou living in coniferous forests of southern Canada; in some classifications included in the species Rangifer tarandus.
A man who lives in the woods.
etymology: From Middle English woodeman, wodeman, from Old English wudemann, wudumann (“woodman”), equivalent to wood + -man.

definition: Bird with strong claws and a stiff tail adapted for climbing and a hard chisel-like bill for boring into wood for insects.
etymology: From wood + pecker. Compare Middle English wod spek (“woodpecker”), Middle English wodehake (“woodpecker”), Middle English wodewale (“woodpecker”). Displaced speight.

definition: Old World fragrant stoloniferous perennial having small white flowers and narrow leaves used as flavoring and in sachets; widely cultivated as a ground cover; in some classifications placed in genus Asperula.
etymology: From Old English wudurofe, from wudu (“wood”) + rofe, of uncertain meaning and origin.

definition: A man's courting of a woman; seeking the affections of a woman (usually with the hope of marriage).
Tiny grey woolly tufted annual with small golden-yellow flower heads; southeastern California to northwestern Arizona and southwestern Utah; sometimes placed in genus Eriophyllum.
Very hairy mammoth common in colder portions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Any plant of the genus Eriophyllum.
Biennial Eurasian white hairy thistle having pale purple flowers; naturalized in North America.
Covered with dense often matted or curly hairs.
example: Woolly lambs.

definition: Having a woolly stem.
An impairment in understanding spoken language that is not attributable to hearing loss.
A humorous play on words.
etymology: From word + play.

definition: A student's book or booklet containing problems with spaces for solving them.
etymology: From work + book.

definition: A day on which work is done.
example: It will take five workdays to process your application.
etymology: From Middle English werkdai, werkedei, werkedai, from Old English weorcdæġ (“workday”), equivalent to work + day.

definition: A poorhouse where able-bodied poor are compelled to labor.
etymology: From Middle English werkhous, from Old English weorchūs (“workshop, place of manufacture”), from Proto-Germanic *werkahūsą, equivalent to work + house.

definition: A male employee who performs manual or industrial labor.
etymology: From Middle English werkman, from Old English weorcmann (“workman”), from Proto-West Germanic *werkamann, from Proto-Germanic *werkamann- (“workman”), equivalent to work + -man.

definition: A sheet of paper with multiple columns; used by an accountant to assemble figures for financial statements.
etymology: From work + sheet. First use appears c. 1823 in the publications of Isaac D'Israeli.

definition: Space allocated for your work (as in an office).
etymology: From work + space.

definition: Not reassuring; tending to cause anxiety.
etymology: From worry + -some.

definition: Usually used in combination: ‘liverwort’, ‘milkwort’, ‘whorlywort’.
etymology: PIE word *wréh₂ds From Middle English wort, wurt, wyrte (“any herb or plant; herb or plant used as food or medicine; (specifically) cabbage or vegetable of the genus Brassica;

definition: Cause to happen or to occur as a consequence.
example: Wreak havoc.
etymology: From Middle English wreken, from Old English wrecan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“push, shove, drive, track down”).

definition: Small brown bird of California resembling a wren.
Performs some wicked deed.
etymology: From Middle English wrecche, from Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, fugitive, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track, follow”). Doublet of garçon and garson.

definition: Twist and press out of shape.
example: Put the berries into a cheesecloth and wring the juice into a bowl.
etymology: Partly: * from Middle English wring, wringe (“twisting or wringing (of the neck)”), from Middle English wringen, wryngen (verb); and * from the modern English verb. See further at etymology 1.

definition: Get or cause to become in a difficult or laborious manner.
Extract (liquid) by squeezing or pressing.
example: Wring out the washcloth.

definition: Band consisting of a part of a sleeve that covers the wrist.
etymology: From wrist + band.

definition: Moving in a twisting or snake-like or wormlike fashion.
etymology: From Middle English writhyng; equivalent to writhe + -ing.

definition: In an unjust or unfair manner.
example: The employee claimed that she was wrongfully dismissed.
etymology: From Middle English wrongfully, wrongfullich; equivalent to wrongful + -ly.

definition: Humorously sarcastic or mocking.
example: With a wry Scottish wit.

definition: A disdainful grimace.
The 25th letter of the Roman alphabet.
etymology: Attested as wi c. 1200. Of uncertain origin. Perhaps borrowed from Old French ui or gui.

definition: A colorless odorless inert gaseous element occurring in the earth's atmosphere in trace amounts.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange”) + -on, used for all noble gases.

definition: Being one more than eighteen.
Being one more than sixteen.
Being one more than seventeen.
Being one more than twenty.
Being three more than twenty.
Twining plant of Amazon basin having large edible roots.
Talk incessantly and tiresomely.
Distance measured in the aggregate number of yards.
example: What is the yardage of this golf course?
etymology: From yard + -age.

definition: Be wide open.
etymology: Unknown, first attested in the mid-16th century.

definition: Desire strongly or persistently.
example: All I yearn for is a simple life.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English yernen, yern (“to express or feel desire; to desire, long or wish for; to lust after; to ask or demand for”) [and other forms], from Old English ġeornan (“to desire, yearn;

definition: Low-growing annual with yellow flowers dotted red; faintly aromatic of pine resin; Europe, British Isles and North Africa.
Large thorny tree of eastern and central United States having pinnately compound leaves and drooping racemes of white flowers; widely naturalized in many varieties in temperate regions.
The large yellow root of a rutabaga plant used as food.
Yellow-throated American wood warbler.
Of beige tinged with yellow.
A sharp high-pitched cry (especially by a dog).
etymology: Possibly from dialectal yip (“to cheep like a bird”), from Middle English ȝyppe, probably imitative.

definition: Membranous structure that functions as the circulatory system in mammalian embryos until the heart becomes functional.
Distant but within sight (‘yon’ is dialectal).
example: Yonder valley.
etymology: From Middle English yon, from Old English ġeon, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz. Cognate with Dutch geen and German jener.

definition: Distant but within sight (‘yon’ is dialectal).
example: Yonder valley.
etymology: From Middle English yonder, yondre, ȝondre, ȝendre, from Old English ġeonre (“thither; yonder”, adverb), equivalent to yond (from ġeond, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz) + -er, as in hither, thither.

definition: A minority youth culture whose distinctiveness depended largely on the social class and ethnic background of its members; often characterized by its adoption of a particular music genre.
An angular shape characterized by sharp turns in alternating directions.
etymology: Back-formation from zigzag. Compare zig.

definition: The basic unit of money in Zaire.
etymology: Borrowed from French zaïre. Named after the Zaire River, another name for the Congo River.

definition: Strike suddenly and with force.
example: This show zaps the viewers with some shocking scenes.
etymology: 1920s, American English, of imitative origin.

definition: Marked by active interest and enthusiasm.
etymology: From Middle English zelose, from Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus + -ōsus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”). By surface analysis, zeal + -ous.

definition: A slight wind (usually refreshing).
etymology: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).

definition: A wrench for Allen screws.
Having short sharp turns or angles.
etymology: Attested from 1712. Borrowed from French zigzag (attested from 1662), possibly from a Germanic source via Walloon ziczac (although German Zickzack is attested only from 1703).

definition: An ointment containing zinc that is used to treat certain skin diseases.
A mineral ore of zinc.
A yellow to white crystalline fluorescent compound that occurs naturally as sphalerite or wurtzite and is used as a luminous pigment.
A colorless water-soluble powder; used as a mordant or to preserve wood or for the electrodeposition of zinc.
A brief high-pitched buzzing or humming sound.
example: The zing of the passing bullet.
etymology: Of onomatopoeic origin.

definition: Marrow squash plant whose fruit are eaten when small.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino, diminutive of zucca (“squash”). Ultimately related to courgette through the original Latin cucurbita. Compare Sicilian cucuzza.
